Acting Consul-General Green to the Ear! of Malmeshury.—(Received July 11.) 
(Telegraphic. ) 


HER Majesty’s ship “ Cyclops” 
3nd instant, On the evening of the 
Jeddah rose and massacred the 


Alexandria, July 6, 1858, 


arrived at Snez from Jeddah on the 
15th June, the Mahometan inhabitants of 
: Christians. Among the vietims were Mr. Page, 
the English Vice-Consul, M. Eveillard, the French Consul, his wife, and about 
twenty others. The English and French Consulates were plundered. The 
* Cyclops” was anchored about two miles from the town, and during the night 
some Greeks swam off to the vessel. The next morning, two boats sent to the 
town were attacked, and obliged to fire on those who endeavoured to intercept 
their retreat. On the 19th, the ( rovernor-General of t 
Mecea, arrived with 800 men. The | Cyclops” left Jeddah on the 24th, and 
brings up the Christians who escaped, including the daughter of the French 
Sone and the French Interpreter, both badly wounded, and twenty-four 
others, 


he Hedjahs, who was at

The Earl of Malmeshury to Sir UH. Bulwer. 


Forengn Office, July U1, 1858, 
WE have received, this day, news of the massacre by the Mahometans, on 
the Lith June, of the Christians at Jeddah, including the English and French 
Consuls. Tutorm the Porte that the English, and doubtless the French Govern- 
ment also, will require from it the most aiuple reparation for this horrid Olitrage ; 
ind that, in the meantime, Her Majesty's frigute in the Red Sea has been 


ordered to Jeddah to obtain, and if necessary enforce, summary punishment on 
the murderers of the English and French Consuls, 


No. 3. 


The Karl of Malmesbury to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, 


My Lorils, Foreign Office, July 1), 1858, 

L HAVE the honour to inelose to voll Lordships a copy of a telezram, 
received-at 1°80 acs. to-day, from Her Majesty's Acting Agent and Consul- 
Geneval in Egypt,* by which you will perceive that the Mahometan inhabitants 
of Jeddah rose on the (th of June, and massacred the Christians, including 
umong their vietims the English Vice-Consul and the French Consul, This 
intelligence was brought to Suez by Her Majesty's steam-frigate “ Cyclops,” 


' hho, Ls 
(84) 


a 


/ 
P 
‘ 
1 


2 


and assuming that that vessel is still in the Red Sea, and that her force is 
sufficient for the required service, | have to state to your Lordships that it 
appears desirable that she should be ordered forthwith to repair to Jeddah and: 
obtain summary punishment on the murderers of the English and French 
Consuls; and that it should be left to the discretion and judgment of the 
captain of the vousel to use force, if necessary, to secure & compliance with his 
demand, 

And in order that no delay may ensue, I have to suggest to your Lordships: 
that the Admiral at Malta may be instructed by telegraph, which will overtake 
at Malta the Indian mail of the 9th instant, to send on instructions to the above 
effect to the captain of the “Cyclops,’’ and to acquaint Her Majesty's Agent 
and Consul-General in Egypt with the nature of those instructions. Her 
Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople will be imatructed to demand from the 
Porte reparation for the outrage on the British and French authorities, and on 
the Christians at Jeddah in general, and he will be authorized to apprize the 
Turkish Government of the ‘nstructions which are seut to the commander of 
Her Majesty's frigate in the Red Sea; and Lord Cowley will be desired to 
inform the French Government of the despatch of the frigate to Jeddah, and 
that her orders are Lo act in behalf of French as well as of English interests at 
that place.

Inclosure 2 in No: 11. 


Precis of Captain Pullen's Letter to the Secretary to the Admiralty, dated Jeddah, 
June 25, 1858. 


ON the evening of the 15th of June the rising of the Mahometans took 


place. It originated among the Hudramouts, or mercantile community of 


Jeddah. 

The attacks on the English and French Consulates, and the Christian 
inhabitants, were simultaneous. The Christians were principally Greeks. 
Mr, Page, after being cut to pieces, was thrown out of a window, M. Eveillard, 
the French Consul, was shot, and his wife cut down with a yataghan. ‘The 
number massacred amounts to twenty-one, and perhaps more. 

Heard of the rising at 30 par, when two naked Greeks came on board 
ina small canoe. Later at night two more came off, 

The officers of the vessel had been in the bazars up to 6-p.,, without 
observing anything unusual. Thought the Government would be able to afford 
sutlicient, protection, 

Next morning, not sceing the flag-staffs of the Consulates, went with two 
armed boats towards shore. Attacked by the natives, who fired tnto us, and 
tried to intercept our retreat through the reefs, Were obliged to tire; killed 
one, and wounded three. 

Wrote to the Kaimakam, asking after the English and French Consuls, 

Heard from the harbour-master of the fate of these two functionaries. 
Miss Eveillard, the French Consul’s daughter, wounded, but in the Kaimakam’s 


harem, with her maid. M. Emerat, French dragoman, also alive, but badly 


wounded, 

As soon as the rising took place (8,000 people), the Kaimakam went with 
some soldiers to the French Consulate, and sent au officer and men to the 
English Consulate. The English Vice-Consul was killed before their arrival, 
and the Freneh Consul and wilé were murdered in the presence of the Baimukam, 
without being able to assist them. 

The object of the rising said to be the extermination of Christians in thie 
Holy Land. Learnt that some Christians were hid in the town. 

Awaited the arrival of the Governor-General from Mecea, expected on 
the 1th. 

Learnt, on the 20th, that he had arrived. 

Demanded, in the name of the Christian world, that justice should be 
done. 

On the 22nd the Pasha called on me, and requested that. the ship 
“Eyanee” should be delivered up to him, and at his urgent written solicitation 
fave her up. 

Held him responsible for the ship till the decision of Her Majesty's 
Government. 

Have given a pnssage to Suez to a Turkish courier with despatches for 
Constantinople, 

‘The papers of the ship “Rranee,” and the documents connected with her 
seizure, were destroyed at the English Consulate on the 14th. The Pasha states 
that the seizure of the “ Eranee” was the cause of the massacre, The papers 
of twenty other British ships were also destroyed at the Consulate, Both the 
owners of the * Eranee” are British subjects. 

The Pasha states that Saleli Ben Johur, one of the owners of the “ Erance,” 
is an Ottoman subject, although his vessel sailed under British colours. Up to 
the 15th he was considered British. The Pusha wrongly states that the 
“ Branee " only reassumed ‘Turkish colours. By lier register it appears she was 
built at Portsmouth, New Hampshire (America), and seems to have been since 
owned by persons entitled by law to be owners af British ships. 

The proceedings on the “ Evance,” by the Kaimakam’s Commercial Court, 
were protested against by Purud) Yusu (acting for Mr. Page during his: short 
absence), on the plea of its incompetency to judge between two British subjects 
Saleli Ben Johur said he would become an Ottoman subject, and the Karmahkan 
allowed him to hoist the ‘Turkish flag, but, on Furud) Yusu's renewed protest, 
ordercd him to haul it down, He again, however, ufter twelve duvs, hoisted 

Cc 


—— ’ — = = as - = = =

the Turkish flag, and Mr. Page, being then returned, the matter was inquired 
into by him. . 
The Pasha first offered to me to send the parties concerned in these ea 
to Constantinople, but immediately afterwards retracted his offer on the grounc 
of the SEG witness, Furud) Yusu, being his banker. : ct 
The Pasha tries to make it appear that the serzure ol the “ Eranee "wis 
the cause of the massacre. Not so. The English Consul would, in that case, 
have only been murdered. . 
The most probable causes assigned are, that the Mahometans have viewed 
with bitterness Cliristians in their Holy Land, and this rising has for long been 
anticipated. Ans, : A | 
A report is current that a Holy Sheikh trom Delhi had arrived at Mecca 
with sixty followers, ‘This is doubtful. ‘9 
It is said that Saleli Said Ben Johur, Sheikh Abdalgafar, anal 
Moustessib (head of police), Sayd Cagalif, and Sheikh Ah Basabrahim Cadri 
Mollah (priest), incited the people to commit these outrages. a 
The Vakeel of the Grand Scerilf also urged the massacre of all who woul 
not embrace Islamism. ; : 
Twenty-two English ships are now at Jeddah, and thirty more in the 
Red Sea. bound to Suez. . tie ak eo 
On_ account of the weakness of the Turkish authorities in the Red Sea, 
Clivistians are subjected to every kind of exaction and persecution, | } 
‘The whole of the remaining Christians, twenty-six In number, are now on 
hoard.

My Lord, Alecandria, July 7, 1858. 

YESTERDAY evening I received a letter (of which I inclose a copy) from 
Mr. Viee-Consul West, dated Suez, the 5th instant, drawing my attention to 
the uaprotected state of the Christian inhabitants of Suez, and the necessity ol 
precautionary measures, owing to the considerable number of boatmen from 
Jeddah and the coast of Arabia, who frequent the port ot Suez. 

At the same time as I received Mr. West's letter, Captain Johnson and 
Messrs. Barker and Co., communicated to me letters they had received from 
Suez, describing a very bad fecling against the Christians to exist in the bazaar 
of that town. Ver Reet | 

Although I had not much hope of finding the Viceroy in the evening, and 
his movements being so uncertain, | immediately started for Mex (four miles 
from this Consulate), where it was understood he had been spending the day. 
On my arrival there, | learnt that he had left for his residence at Gabarri, to 
which place L followed him, and at last met him in that vicinity driving in his 
carriage, "Taking the liberty of stopping his THighness, | communicated to him 
the information that had reached me, and pointed out the necessity of immediate 
measures being taken, ‘The Viceroy invited me into his carriage, which he 
ordered to drive to the Klectric Telegraph Office ut the railway station. On our 
arrival there, a message from Captain Pullen, of the “ Cyelops,” which Bhd just 
reached, was delivered ta me, and I transhited its contents to the Viceroy, 
I transmit a copy of it, by which your Lordship will observe that, one day later 
than Mr. West's letter, the uneasiness respecting the excitement against all 
Christians had evidently inerensed ; that Captain Pullen had called” on the 
Governor with the English and French Vice-Consuls, and that the Governor 
had stated that he had applied to the Government for on additional force. The 
Viecroy immediately telegraphed to Cairo and Suez fer information, and as he 
assured me thatevery possible precaution should be taken, and that no one heed 
be under any alarm, | took leave of his Highness, thanking him for the prompti- 
tude with which he bad acted, as : 

Captain Pullen having mentioned that he bad visited: the Governor’ in 
company with the French Vice-Consul, | enlled on M. Sabatier, and cormiun- 


7 


‘ated to him the telegraphic message I had received, and also the steps 1 had 
taken in the matter. 

On my return home I found a despatch from Mr. Consul Walne, of which 
I inclose a copy, dated Cairo the Sth instant, by which it would seem that he is 
under considerable alarm as to the safety of the Christians generally at Cairo, 
As this is a subject whicl: concerns us all alike, [ shall consult my principal 
foreign colleagues as to the steps it is desirable to take; for it would no doubt be 
mischievous in the extreme to raise a panic by any hasty or injudicious proceed- 
ings. 

The case at Suez is quite different, and required immediate measures to he 
taken, especially as, from information which hns reached me, the events at Jeddah 
may, I think, be attributed to the jealousy with which the seafaring population, 
and particularly the owners of the country vessels, who derive a large revenue 
from the conveyance of Hadjis between Suez and Jeddah, view the establish- 
ment of the steamers of the Medjidic Company, one of which has alrendy reached 
Sued, 

The number of Jeddah boatmen at Suez, Lam assured may be about S00, 
Our establishments there consist of the agencies and stores of the Peninsular 
and Oriental Company, and the Australian Company, the British Military 
Hospital, the ast Indin Company's agency and Post Office, the hotel, besides 
a considerable number of Englishmen employed in the Transit and Telegraph 
Administrations,

Vices Consul West to adeting Consul-General Green. 
Sir, Suer, July o, PROS. 
| HAVE the honour to submit to your consideration, that the present 
unprotected state of the Christian inhabitants of Suez (the Governor being 
totally unprovided with a sufficient stat! of military or police to maintain order 
in the event of the slightest open shaw of disaffection in the bazar), and our 
continual communications with Jeddah, from whenee a considerable number of 
hoatment and others are daily arriving, would render it desirable that some pre- 
cautionary measures were taken by the local authorities to insure te maintenance 
of order; the more especially that the reports lately brought trom Jeddah by Her 
Majesty's ship “Cyelops, have not, it would appear, filed to cause a rather 
undesirable show of satisfiction among that portion of the population most to be 
dreaded in the event of any disturbanee. [allude principally to the boatmen 
fram Jeddah and the coust of Arabia, and others wha are in daily and direct 
communication with the Hadrmooths of Jeddah. 

Having on a former oceasion experienced some slight disturbance here, 
when native Christians, and even Europeans, were openly insulted by a number 
of natives apparently assembled for the purpose, 1 consider it my duty, in 
cansequence of the late disturbrnees at Jeddah, to submit, for your consideration, 
that some little show of the more immediate power of the Egyptian Government 
to protect the lives and property of those conliding in the widisturbed state of 
the country, might, at this isolated place, prove a most desirable measure for the 
Government of his Highness to adopt. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) GEO, WEST,

Inclosure 3 in No, 12. 


Consul Walne to Acting Consul-General Green. 


Sir, Cairo, July 5, 1808. 


THE intelligence received {rom Jeddah, two days since, of the feurtul 
massacre which took place in that town on the Lath ultimo, has not failed to 
produce a most painful impression on the luropean and, in general, the Christian 
population of Cairo; and those who are best acquainted with Baypt are not 
without some alarm as to the influence which the news may have on the 
Mussulman fanaticism of this city, which is well known not to be extinct, 
though, under the stern rule of Mehemet Aliand the strong Governments of his 
sucecssors, Ibrahim and Abbas, it has been checked and held under control. 

There can be little doubt that, from the breaking out of the revolt in India, 
‘1 which Moslems have taken such a prominent part, there has been here a 
certain sympathy of Mussuliman feeling with that movement; and there is 
reason to suppose than Indian und Persian partisans have done their best to 
‘crease, it not to excite, that sympathy. 

A question very naturally arises + Is the Local Government, which is exclu. 
sively Moslem, in a position at the present time to afford to the Christian 
population that amount of protection which if has enjoyed for the last forty 
years? ‘The only answer that could be given by nine persons out of ten 1s, not 
only that the authorities here cannot he relied on for such protection ; hut that, 
in fact, there exists in Cairo [ttle more than the name or semblance of 
FOVErMIMCHt. 

In the personnel of the Cairo Administrations, as they formerly existed, 
in the material foree at their disposal, the Christian communities had some 
cuarantee that at least active and prompt measures would be taken to suppress 
ineendiariam, pillage, and attempts at massacre, but | must freely confess that, 
in the present state of things, | see neither in the personnel of the autho- 
rities, nor in the few miserable policemen anil soldiers within their call, any 
sufficient security against one or all of these calamities. 

Formerly the Christians were assembled in particular quarters, with a 
certain amount of organization for detence ; they are now, to a considerable 
extent, scattered; and the protection which they have sa long enjoyed has led to 
the abandonment of all organization, and to the neglect of all appliances of 
defence, even in the quarters which are still exclusively Christian. 

Taking into consideration the great ‘nterests which the British and lonian 
residents have at stake, and the danger to whieh those interests may be exposed, 
I feel that I should not do my duty if T did’ not eall your early attention to a 
subject which is now uppermost in the mind of every foreign resident ; and I do 
so with a hope that, by your ‘ntervention in the proper quarters, suitable 
measures inay he taken to ward off evils which are too much within the compass 
of possibility not to merit the most serious attention. 

Lhave, &e. 
(Signed) ALFRED 8. WALNE.

LTTAD, list night, a long conversation with the Grand Vizier with reference 

to the massacre at Jeddah, and his Highness, whose horror is unfeigned, will do 
all in his power to mect the wishes of Her Majesty's Government: and the 
Sultan’s Seeretary has alsocalled upon me this morning, on the part of [is 
Majesty, to say that His Majesty was still suffering from the shock which the 
news had given him, ant to mssure me that there was nothing which he would 
not do to testify his own fecling, and satisfy the British Government. 
__ Lurged on both oceasions the necessity of sendine off Ismail Pasha with 
full powers, without delay, and with a reinforcement of troops. “The Sultan's 
Secreliiry, as well as the Grand Vizier, assured me that Ismail Pasha would 
start immediately, with the powers required, and that troops should be also 
sent, unless the Porte was fully convinced that they were not necessary. 

1 have promised that Her Majesty's Consul-General in Eeypt will aid the 
Pasha by every means at his disposal, in arriving as soon as poss 
nation. ; 

The murderers will be tried by military law, and their fate decided without 
reference to Constantinople. : 

The Grand Vizier thinks, moreover, that Namick Pasha, under such 
extraordinary circumstances, was wrong in not taking upon himself the 
responsibility of summarily punishing the offenders, who, le says, were mere 
rabble ; all the respectable inhabitants depreeating in the strongest manver the

Sir H. Bulwer to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received July 14, 1010 A.M.) 


(Telegraphic. Therapia, July 18, 1858, 4 P.M. 
 -M. THOUVENEL and myself’ are of opinion that, besides the punishment 
of the offenders, an investigation into the conduct of the local eee 
Jeddah should take place, an indemnity be accorded to the ae 0 . : 
sufferers, and a contribution levied apon the inhabitants of the place, # ee 
would make them interested in its future tranquillity. The Turkish flag shoul 
at once be withdrawn from the “Eranee,” and the: fate of that vessel remain 
suspended until the question concerning her. is decided, 


15 


to crush any attempt at disorder in five minutes, Tle, however, added that he 
had warned the authorities to be vigilant, and that he was about to strengthen 
the garrison. His Highness also said that he had sent a company of Regulors to 
Suez, 

Mr. Walne writes to me on the 8th instant:—" The police here appear a 
little more on the alert than usual."’ I hope the natural excitement on the 
receipt of the intelligence from Jeddah will gradually subside. 

Captain Pullen, whe arrived here yesterday from Suez, informs me that he 
met the troops on their way there, and that the number of English steamers and 
sailing-vessels in that port are sufficient to remove any uneasiness as to the 
safety of the Europeans. 

At Captain Pullen's request 1 have addressed a letter to him, stating that | 
think it is desirable that the “Cyclops” should not leave Suca until Her 
Majesty’s Government has had an opportunity of communicating with him, atter 
the receipt of his despatches reporting the events at Jeddah. 

The impression conveyed by the conversations | have held with Captain 
Pullen ts, that the Turkish authorities might, by a display of the slightest 
energy, had they been so disposed, have prevented the massacre of the Christians, 
and that, having cannon at their disposal, a shot or two would have dispersed 
the rioters ina moment. ‘That the rising was talked of long before, was antici- 
pated by the late Mr. Page, and that the proceedings of the Naval Court on 
the ship “Eranee,” which took place on the Lith, and to which the Governor- 
General attributes the massacre, could therefore have had little or nothing to do 
with it, That both the owners of the “ Erance"’ were registered as such at 
Calcutta, and that the attack on the boats of the “ Cyclops,” on the morning of 
the 16th, was a most open and daring outrage by a numerous body of the 
natives; nothing but the courage and coolness of those in the boats enabling 
them to escape. 

L also am happy to learn from Captain Pullen that the “ Lady Canning” is 
armed with four guns, and that no apprehension need be felt respecting her. 

Captain Pullen further informs me that should it be considered necessary 
to have recourse to any measures at Jeddah, of un offensive character, the 
“Cyclops” is well adapted, and perfectly competent to perform, any such 
service that might be required of bees that by lightening his vessel he ein get 
her very close to the shore; that she is very heavily armed, and has alsa 
24-pounder howitzers for the boats, 

The Hadjees will commence arriving here, on their return, in about six 
weeks. I am assured that they are more numerous this year than has ever 
been previously known. 

I have, &e,

Inclosure in No. No 41. 
Memorial, 


To the Right Honourable James orl of Malmesbury, Her Majesty's Secretar y 
of State for Forcign Affairs, 


The humble Memorial of Mary Me Lean, of Liverpool, in the county 
of Lancaster, widow, 
Sheweth, 


THAT Stephen Page, late Her Majesty's Acting Vice-Consul at Jeddah, in 
Arabia, was the last surviving son of your memorialist, by her first husband 
Jeremiah Page, deceased. 

That, about the 15th day of June last, the said Stephen Page was, ns your 
memorialist is informed and believes, assassinated at the Viec-Consulate, or official 
residence, at Jeddah aforesaid, by a fanatical mob of Muhometans, who entered 
the said Consulate or residence for that purpose, and who after murdering the 
said Consul, and throwing his body out of the window, plundered or destroyed his 
property and eclfeets, } 

‘That the authorities of Jeddah aforesaid were cither unable to prevent the 
snid assassination, or were indifferent to its perpetration. 

That the said Stephen Page was for nearly twenty years a merchant in 
Grand Cairo, where he had established a lucrative business. 

That, in the month of March, in the year 1855, the said Stephen Page wos 

ti 


—_ aa Se aes SS 


fal ga 


22 


sprain Her Majesty's Acting Vice-Consul at Jeddah aforesaid, to which 
place he removed and continued to reside up to the time of his assassimition. 
That the said Stephen Page had much extended his business at Jeddah 
aforesaid, and at the time of his death was, as your memorialist believes, if 
receipt of an income of about 2,000/. a year, exclusive of any benefit arising 
from his official appomtment. 

That the suid Stephen Page was a widower, without children, was 41 years 
of age, and of frugal and steady habits, and possessed, as your memorinlist 
belicves, of property in Jeddah aforesaid and in this country, all trace of which 
is lost by the destruction of hts books and papers by his assassins. 

That your memorialist’s said son lost his life not only in the service of Ins 
country, but chiefly because he was her Representative. 

That the said assassination was intended not only as an attack upon the 
Christian religion, but as an insult to the British flag. 

That your memorialist has been twice married, is now and has been for 
twenty-two years a widow, with only two daughters, both of whom are 
married, 

That your menorialist is 67 years of age, and has for the last five years 
been an invalid, . 

That your memorialist has for upward of twenty years been dependent 
upon her son, the said Stephen Page, who was always most liberal and kind: to 
your memorialist. 

Your memorilist, therefore, humbly prays that, after having caused the 
circumstances connected with the said assassination and other atrocities to be 
investigated, ancl justice done to the perpetrators, your Lordship will be pleased 
to remember that the said Stephen Bee had a mother whom he supported, as 
well as a country whieh he served. 

And your memorialist will ever pray, &e. 


(Signed) MARY Me LEAN.

Harl Cowley to the Earl of Malmesbury —(Received July 25.) 
(No. 927.) 
My Lord, Paris, July 24, 1858, 

COUNT WALEWSKI concurs in the suggestions made by Sir Henry 
Bulwer and M. de Thouvenel, as to the exact reparation to be demanded of the 
Porte for the ontrages committed at Jeddah, to which your Lordship's despatch 
No. G76 of the 19th instant relates, and | have informed Sir Henry Bulwer, as 
instructed by your Lordship. 

Count Walewski, when I spoke to him on this matter, read me a telegram 
which he had just received from M.de Thouvenel, mentioning the sum advanced 
by the Sultan for the relief of the sufferers, irrespective of what might be here- 
alter claimed as a just indemnity. 

His Excellency observed that he supposed there could be no objection 
to receiving these sums, [said that it seemed to me that they might he taken, 
and the Governments might decide hereafter whether they should be taken into 
account when the amount of pecuniary indemnity came to he fixed.

Sir H. Bulwer to the Earl of Malmeshury.—(Reeeived July 26, 7°20 a.a.) 


(Telegraphic,) Therapia, July 24, 1858, 10 ve, 

THE Turkish flag is to be at.onee taken down from the vessel seed by 
Namick Pasha, and its ultimate fute decided by an inquiry. : 

On the other points the French Ambassador and myself have both required 
what your Lordship says the British Government demanded. 

The Sultan gives out of his own purse a present to the sufferers, and 
pensions to the families of the Consuls ; but this is not to interfere with the 
imposition of a contribution on the inhabitants of Jeddah, 

The messenger just arrived, In regard to Jeddah, let me clearly explain : 
there is no hesitation here about executing the murderers inany number; but 
the law forbids a Pasha to inflict death without the Sultan's order, ‘This order 
is dispatehed, and will get to Jeddah as soon as possible, What the Grand 
Vizier asks is, to allow of its arrival before requiring the punishment in question : 
because, if it is inflicted by the authority of the Sultan, the Muhometans: will 
probably submit; whereas, if inflicted by the Christian Powers alone, a general 
rising amongst the Mahometans in that part of the world and elsewhere may 
follow: and for the sake of India it seems to myself very important we should 
beable to show clearly that the Sultan, as the head of the faith, is on our side. 
Just think of this, and do not doubt of the intentions of people here. They 


will do anything, but T will continue to hurry them, and keep up. their 
alarm.

Sir -H. Bulwer to the Earl of Malmesbury. {Received July 27, 24.91.) 
(Telegraphic.) Therapia, July 26, 1808, 7 P.M. 

THE troops to be sent to Jeddah are gone; would it not, therefore, he better. 
as the Porte is acting willingly in this affair, to combine operations with her, 
and have whatever force we employ arrive at the same time, or within a few 
days after the force she sends, so that what is done should be done in the Sultan's 
name. The best chance for putting down Muahometan fanaticism throughout 
the Bast, is perhaps in having it punished in an exemplaryspanner by the highest 
Mahometan authority.

Aeting Consul-General Green to the Earl of Malmesbury. — (Received 
July 28, 1015 A.M.) 


(Telegraphic. ) Alexandria, July 24, 1858. 

THERE is perfect tranquillity in Egypt, but considerable excitement among 
the natives on account of the affair at Jeddah, The Viceroy has acted with 
energy at Suez, Cairo, and Alexandria. General Ismail Pasha arrived from 
Constantinople yesterday on his way to Jeddah, ‘Troops are expected to follow 
him in a few days, and the Viceroy has also been applied to by the Porte to 
send troops to Jeddah. 


Vice-Consul Cole to Mr. Hammond.—( Received July 24.) 


Sir, 45, Bloomsbury Place, Brighton, July 25, 1858. 

WITH reference to the late Mr. Page, I beg to inform you that L have in 
my possession a letter to the effect that he had made his will, bequeathing all 
his property to his daughter, and that he had appointed me guardian and executor. 
On this letter 1 am informed that [ shall be able to act, on proof of all docu- 
ments in the Jeddah Consulate being destroyed; I have, therefore, the honour 
to request that you will be good enough to let me know if any official informa- 
tion has been received to that cffcet. 

[am compelled to address you on this subject without further delay, in 
consequence of the very active proceedings already taken by the mother of the 
deceased, with whom, however, he had no communication beyond making her a 
small allowance for her maintenance, and which is to be continued during her 
lifetime. 

Should any information be required with respect to the late Mr. Page, I 
beg that I may be referred to, as being the only person with whom he kept up 
any intimate correspondence. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) C.J. D. COLE.

The Bart of Malmesbury to Earl Cowley. 
(No. 725;) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, July 31, L858, 

I HAVE ta state to your Excellency, in reply to your despatch No. 967 
of the 29th instant, that Captain Pullen, of Her Majesty's ship‘ Cyclops,” will 
act as English Commissioner in matters connected with the outrage on the 
Christians at Jeddah 

Her Majesty’s Government are of opinion that the sum of 3,000,000 of 
frances, which the Government of the Emperor proposes should be levied as a 
contribution on the town of Jeddah, would be too large; and they consider that, 
as the conduct of the Porte, in regard to this affair, las hitherto been satis- 
factory, it is desirable that the Porte should be allowed to enforce its own 
jurisdiction, if possible, by its own means. 

Such is the view taken of the matter in Sir Henry Bulwer's despatch of 
which Linclose a copy," and vour Excellency will inform Count Walewski that 
Her Majesty's Government agree in that view. 

Your Excellency will also inform Count Walewski that Her Majesty's 
Government have had much pleasure in directing the Commander of the 
“Cyclops” to show hospitality, in case of need, to the French Commissioner. 

Iam, &c. 
(Signed) MALMESBURY. 


P.S.—1 add a copy of a letter which I have caused to be addressed to the 
Board of Admiralty on this matter.t

The Queen's Advocate to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received July 31.) 


My Lord. Dacters' Commons, July 31, 1858. 

1 AM honoured with your Lordship's commands, signified in Mr, Ham~ 
mond’s letter of the 2Ist of July instant, stating that he was directed to 
transmit to me a letter from Messrs, G. D. Neroutsos and Co. of Liverpool, 
respecting claims which they conceive they shall have, on account of losses 
which they are likely to suffer in the shape of outstanding accounts al Jeddah, 
in consequence of the disturbances at that place; and to request that I would 
take the inclosed letter into consideration, and report to your Lordship: my 
opinion as to the answer which should be returned to it, 

In obedience to your Lordship’s commands, | have taken the above letter 
into cousideration, and have the honour to report,— 


* No, 62, + No. 68. 


oo 


That I cannot undertake to say what answer can properly be given to the 
letter of Messra. Netoutsos, It does not wppear to me to deserve any answer. 
No legal question is involved therein. 

Messrs. Neroutsos do not state— 

1, Whether they are themselves British subjects by Tnrth, dlesecnt, oF 
naturalization, or whether they are aliens. They are equally silent us to the 
nationality of their agent at Jeddah, 

2. ‘They do not state that they have, in fact, lost any amount or descrip 
tion of property whatsoever at Jeddah or elsewhere, 

8. They do not state that they ever have lind any goods, or any eatablish- 
ment, or agent, or correspondent, resident at Jeddah. 

4. They do not state at what date, or from what place, they last heard 
from their agent. 

4. They speak of losses which they are likely to suffer “in the shape ot 
outstanding accounts,” into which accounts it is ebvious that Her Majesty 
Government cannot enter. 

6. Tam not aware that Her Majesty’s Government has, as yet, determined 
to exact from the Government of Turkey indemnity for losses sustained) iat 
Jeddah by merehants, whether British or foreign ; and Timi not aware whether 
any such losses have been, in fact, sustamed, or under what circumstances (it in 
fact) sustained. 

+ ‘This communication appears to be designedly as vague os possible, 
Neroutsus and Co, evidently do not know whether they have, or have not, lost 
anything whatever at Jeddah, from which they have no reeent intelligence; and 
their letter is probably intended to elicit from Her Majesty's Governiient some 
favourable declaration or guarantee in favour of any vague claim which they may 
suppose themsclves entitled to make hereatter upon whatsoever routs, 

& Under these circumstances I can only suggest that the receipt of their 
letter should be acknowledged, and they should be desired to satisly your 

Lordship: Ist. That they are British subjects; 2Zodly. As to the nationality ot 
their avent at Jeddah, and the nature, amount, and vatuat ion of their property 
there, und how it was destroyed; Srdly. That they have suffered aetual losses, 
and of what nature, or to what definite amount socver, by the disturbances at 
Jeddah. ‘They should likewise be informed that if they are aliens they must 
apply to their own Government, and that your Lordship cannot undertake, ever 
in the event of their being British subjects, to procure them indemmity.

Ne | ON my return from Caifo carly yesterday morning, the Viceroy sent me a 


tnessage that he was anxious to see me at Mex. I immediately proceeded 
there. 

The Viceroy said he wished to consult me confidentially. That General 
Ismail Pasha had arrived from Constantinople, on his way to Jeddah, and tliat 
he had brought him a communication from the Porte, directing him to send 
Egyptian toops there. His Highness said he wished to baye my candid opinion 
as to how | theught Her Majesty's Government would view Eeyptin troops 
being sent to Jeddah, Isaid 1 felt quite sure Her Majesty's Government could 
have no other object in view than that order and security should be re-cestab- 
lished and maintained at Jeddah, and that, consequently, | was contident that 
the presence there of Egyptian troops would be a source of satisfaction to Ther 
Majesty's Government, 

The Viceroy spoke a good deal of the state of affairs in several parts of the 
Ottoman dominions, from religious or fanatical causes, and 1 took the 
opportunity of asking him how the population here ts likely to-act in the event 
of news reaching this that the “Cyclops " has proceeded to extreme measures 
at Jeddah. The population will do nothing wt all,” was the reply, “ Whit 
can itdo? But it won't, be pleased.” 

My own opinion is that it entirely depends upon the military whether any 
disorders are attempted or not, 

The Viceroy subsequently introduced me to General Ismail Pasha, who 
delivered two open letters to me from Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constant 
nople. One of these letters informed me that troops will proceed to Jeddah 
from Egypt, and | translated it to his Highness.

Mr. De Mattos to the Earl of Malmeshury.— (Received August 2) 


My Lord, Jeffrey's Square, London, July 31, 1858, 

IN July 1856, I contracted with the Peninsular and Oriental Steam 
Navigation Company for the delivery of a cargo of 1,000 tons of coals, 
per Blanch,” at Suez, for the total sum of 38,7371, 10s. 

This vessel met with damage on the voyage, and was compelled to put into 
the port of Jeddah, where she was finally condemned and sold by Her Britannic 
Majesty's Vice-Consul, Mr. stephen Page, on the rd October, 1857, the cargo 
having been linded and taken charge of by Mi. Page, for account of whom it 
mught concern. . 

In due course, 67:4) tons were sent on to Suez, and received ly the 
Peninsular and Oriental Company; the remainder, say 932 tons, remaining 
in charge of the late Mr. Stephen Page on my behalf, at the time of his 
lamented death, in the general massacre of the Christians by the inhabitants of 
Jeddah, are tow entirely lost to me. and the value thereof amounts to 3,483/. 7s. 

As all control of my property has thus been lost by the act of a foreign 
Government, or their subjects, | have now to request. that your Lordship may 
he pleased to at once put forward a claim on my behalf to the Ottoman Porte, 
for the said sum of 4483/, 7s., and insist upon an carly settlement, 

Any documents which may be required to substantiate the foregoing facts, | 
shall be prepared to produce when called upon, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WM, NICH. DE MATTOS,

My Lord, Liverpool, August V2, 1858, 

WE are duly in receipt of your Lordship's letter of the Srd instant, in reply 
to our application of the 19th ultimo, and bee herewith to answer the (questions 
contained therein, 

Ist. Our prior, Mr, G. 1D, Neroutsos, is a naturalized British subject, 
settled here since 1844, and married to an English lady, 

anily, Ouragent at Jeddah was originally a Turkish subject from oumelin, 
Aristide Democides, who went out from England, with our merchundize, to try 
to establish 4 regular trade between us and our friends at Cairo, in Keypt, and 
the amount of our finds in his hands was about |400/, the proceeds af our 
manufuctured Manchester goods, which le had sold throuch the house of Suva, 
in Jeddah (the members of whose lirm were all murdered lately), and he had to 
retain the money in his possession, in consequence of the absence of banking 
fucilitivs, and we ean procure duplicate bills of lading, and invoices of the goods 
shipped, which went overland, vil Aden, 

drdly. We have, therefore, suffered to the extent of 14001, as we feel 
certain cur agent is lost, not having received any account from him; and had 


ae 


he eseaped he would have written to us, or he would have been amongst the 
other fugitives on board the English vessel. 

The latter part of your Lordship's letter fills us with anxiety and alarm, 
viz, Where you state that even if we are British subjects your Lordship cannot 
undertake to procure us indemnity. We trust we do not undorstund this 
sentence correctly, for it appears to us incredible that, after carrying on a yery 
extensive business in this country for many years, und paying wcome-tax on our 
profits, that your Lordship will not protect us when we endeavour to extend 
British influence and trade in wew quarters; whilst the French and Austrians 
have had it officially announeed to them, that all claims they may legally put 
forward will be enforeed, 

We apologise sincerely to your Lordship for the trouble we cause you, but 
it is unaverdable; and now, after putting your Lordship in possession of all the 
facts of the case, we trust your Lordship will kindly put forward our claim, or, 
if not yet formal, to point out its irregularities as carly as convenient. 

Apologising again, we remain, anticipating your Lordship’s reply, yours, &e.

Inclosure 2 in No. 87. 


Information odititined ba) Caplain Curling from a Pilot who came off, and boarded 
fl Meat. 


Peninsular avd Oriental Steam-ship “ Bentinck,” off Jeddah, 
July 22, L858, 

THE covering questions and remarks being premised, informant stated the 
Pasha had again left tor Meeea, after spending a few days in Jeddah, taking a 
part of the garrison and the Cadi with him. | 

Before leaving he had caused o great number of persons to be seized, and 


53 


put into prison, and two at least are reported to have been put to death, on 
aceount of the disturbance of the 15th of June. Informant, however, states. in 
his opinion, and as the general opinion of the people of Jeddah, that the imdivi- 
duals seized are in many cases perfectly innocent, whilst others are only guilty 
in wu secondary degree, 

The principals, or instigators of the massacre, he believes to lave been the 
Hadhrami merchants, but these he says the Pasha is atraid to molest, 

Further, he says, the town is governed by the Kaimakam, or Deputy 
Pasha, and all is said to be quiet within and without the walls. 

Informant reports that a French steamer from Magsowah touched at Jeddah 
about a week age, and remained there some tive days. ‘The Captain and officers 
landed, and had an interview with the Kaimakam, but of the result of this inter- 
view informant knew nothing, beyond that the French had heen informed of the 
measures which had been taken to punish the offenders, The French steamer 
leit about five days ago for Sucz. 

There are about thirty merchant ships in the roadstend, chiefly Arab vessels 
under English colours, There is also one small English steamer in port, said 
to have arrived about fifteen days ago from Suez, with some Moslems of 
consequence. 

Informant knew nothing of Her Majesty's ship “Cyclops,” beyond that 
she had taken a number of refugees from Jeddah to Suez. 

His impression seemed to be that the measures which had already been 
token by the Pasha would end the affair of the late massacre. Hut he bitterly 
regretted, however, that the poor and comparatively guiltless should be made to 
suffer for the principal instigators of the recent outrage, which he designated as 
the ** work of the devil.” 

Informant states no more than that the usual number of boats had lett 
Jeddah for Suez within the last month. But the people, however, generally 
scemed to expect reinforcements would speedily arrive for the Turkish garrison 
at Jeddah. 

(Signed) WILLIAM CURLING,

“ Alice,’ hound to Bombay.

Frushard will, no doubt, hear of the massacre, and will proceed immediately to 
Jeddah. The schooner * Mahi” is:at-anchor in Aden harbour, unable to move, 
in consequence of the want of a bowsprit, and | am informe by her Commiuier 
that she is otherwise unseaworthy,

5. I have not had time to sift and compare the various accounts which 
have reached me of this affair, but my impression is, that it was an unpremedi- 
tated, popular ¢meute, which arose from an insult, offered first by a Turk to the 
British flag on board a ship, and which was indiscreetly retaliated by the British 
Acting Vice-Consul at the Consulate on shore: the unfortunate gentleman lost 
his life; his body was severed limb from limb, and east out from the upper 
windows of his house; the mnfuriate populace then proceeded to destroy Christians 
of every sect and nation. It appears that twenty-two were slain, and some 
wounded, : 

6. 1 solicit the indulgence of Government for this hurried and imperfect 
report; but 1 am unwilling to detain the “Alice” a moment longer than is 
absolutely necessary. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) W. M. COGHLAN.

Captain Pullen to the Political Agent at Aden. 
Sir,  Cylops,” Jeddah, June 23, 1858. 


1 BEG to inform you that on the evening of the 15th instant, a rising of 
the Hadramouts and other Arabs took place in the town of Jeddah. 

The following are the particulars of this massacre, as far as T can learn 
them :— 

Simultaneously they altacked the English and French Consulates, and all 
the Christian population residing here, composed, principally, ot Greeks ; they 
murdered the English Viec-Consul, Mr, Page, and threw him trom his window ; 
they shot the Freneli Consul, M. Eveillard, dead, and butchered his wile with 
n yataghan ; Copts and Greeks were alike mercilessly murdered, to the number, 
as | at present learn, of twenty-two. 

Such as have escaped are now on board here, amongst them M. [Emerat, 
the interpreter, and Mademoiselle Eveillard, the daughter af the French Consul, 
both wounded, the latter in trying to defend her father from assassination, 

I send you a list of the murdered, and shall send down to you such of the 
refugees as wish to go to Aden, by the British ship “ Coquet Dale,” the master 
af which will also convey this to you. 

The Governor-General has arrived from Mecca, and order being somewhat 
restored, I have demanded that justice be executed upon all concerned in this 
diabolical massacre, I send you a copy of my letter to him, which will explain 
how matters at present stand. 

The causes of this horrible insurrection are, T think, many. 

|. There appears to have been, fora long time, an evident intention on the 
part of the Hadramouts to expel all Christians from the Mahometan Holy Land. 

© It has been stated that a Sheik, a personage of reputed great holiness, 
had arrived at Mecca from Delhi, with a train of sixty followers. If this meant 
nothing, why should it be whispered about } 

> Tt has been stated that the chief of the bazars had incited the people to 
expel the Christians, as well as the mollah of the town. 

4. It has been attributed to my having seized a British merchant-ship, 
illegally flying Turkish colours; the Consul’s jurisdiction over her being fully 
established, after a Jong inquiry into the circumstances of the case at the 
Consulate, I send you a copy of my report to the Government on the subject. 
The Pasha now states that one of the owners named was an Ottoman subject ; 
that a Court had been held on the matter previously, and that the local autho- 
rities had ordered her to hoist the Turkish colours. 

It is stated by the authorities that the people had no intention to kill any 
one, but that, on going to the Consulate, the English Consul taunted and defied 
them, which infuriated them in such a manner that they rushed into the house 
and murdered him. 

Al these circumstances, however, can never justily the acta committed.

The papers of all the ships (there are twenty-two here at present) are 
destroyed. have given the masters certificales to that effect, for such as have 
applied for them. , | 

There are upwards of 500 tons of coals on shore, belonging partly to the 
under-writers of the wrecked British ship “ Blanche,” and 224 tons to this ship. 

As it becomes necessary for me to proceed to Suez, to report these matters 
to the Government, I trust that you wil see the necessity of sending a vessel 
of the Indian Navy here, as eafly as possible. Claims of all descriptions, on the 
Turkish Government, are now coming in for loss of property, and the Governor- 
eneral assures me that it shall be attended to as soon as possible. 

The various ships and persons here, under British rule, require protection 
also. 

Hadji Furadj Yuser, the principal merchant here, under British protection, 
will give every information to the officer commanding the an which will, | 
hope, arrive here. 1 have given him a sealed letter to establish his identity. 

Be good enough to address the answer to this communication lo Suez at 
your carliest convenience.

Inclosure 4 in No. 88. 
Captain Pullen to Namick Pasha. 


M. Je Gouverneur-Genéral, “ Cyclops,” Jeddah, June 21, 1858. 


ON your announcing to me your arrival at this place yeseney morning, 
you requested, previous to delivering to me the Christians who had escaped the 
hloody massacre of the 15th instant, an interview. 


Your Excellency is aware how readily | went on shore, the first object of 


my solicitude being the safety of all who sought protection of the British flag. 

At my demand, it was arranged with your Excellency that the French and 
English colours should be hoisted the following morning at the main of this 
ship, side by side; that the boats being fully manned and armed, should proceed 
to the landing-place; that the English and French colours, being then advanced 
to the front, should reecive a salute of twenty-one guns from the fort; that an 
armed procession should then form, and, with colours flying, proceed through 
the town, passing the residencies of the English and French Consuls, and, 
finally, thence a funeral party would proceed to the burial-ground, where the 
murdered Consuls lic, the service for the dead read by the Chaplain of this ship, 
and military honours paid to the remains. 

Your Excellency was good enough ta accompany the procession as far as 
the French Consulate, 

[ have now another duty to discharge, and what I then verbally demanded, 
1 now require at your hands. 

Excellency, the blood of the murdered calls for retribution, for a justice so 
stern, so terrible in its example, that throughout the land men will hear of the 
mnassacre which took place, and, at the same time, of the punishment which 
followed, 

Excelleney, ask for this justice, not in the name of England or France 
alone, but in the name of the whole Christian world. Protestants, Catholics, 
Grecks, and Copts, have alike been barbarously murdered, and for all 1 demand 
justice. . 

His Majesty the Sultan, in his proclamation dated Constantinople, Rebiul- 
evvel 4, 1262, commands that, if any conspire against the life or property of 
any, he shall be immediately punished ; but when England and France are both 
insulted by the murder of their Consuls, your Excellency will feel the greater 
necessity for exceuting justice, 

When these terrible events are made known in England and France, it will 
be asked: Is it for these people we have fought and bled at Inkerman, Alma, 
and Sebastopol ? 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WM. I. 8 PULLEN.

Consul Brant to the Earl of Malmeshury.—( Received Auguat 19.) 


(No. 8.) 
My Lard, Bludaw of Damascus, August 2, 1898. 

L THINK it right to inform your Lordship of the effect produced on the 
population of Damascus by the murder of the Consular officers of Great Britain 
and France at Jeddah, 

Correspondents of Damascencs in Arabia have related in terms more or less 
vague or exaggerated the catastrophe and its cause, but these reports can be of 
no interest, since your Lordship will have learned the facts from: authentic 
reports, 

The prevailing fecling in Damaseus among the respectable class of the inha- 
bitants, seems to be rather of indifference in respect to the French, but of regret 
as to the English, The low and unretlecting mob display a certain degree of 
satisfaction that the infidels had been so treated for polluting, by their presence, 
so holy @ city ; but the expression of their feeling is rather subdued and confined 
to private communications or to conversations held by small groups of persons 
in coffee-houses, Some, indeed, did speak of expelling European Consuls and 
Christians from Damascus; and it was remarked that a Consul had been 
murdered at Marash for which no punishment was inflicted: ignorance con- 
founded an agent of the Land Transport Corps with a Consul, and the result of 
the scizure of the guilty parties had never reached Damascus. | remember, 
when reporting from Erzeroom the murder at Marash, that 1 pointed out the 
necessity of a speedy and severe example on the very spot, as the only security 
against the repetition of a similar catastrophe. The punishment of parties 
euilty of such a crime, inflicted at a distant period and locality, is hardly known 
ut the pince itself, and certainly not far beyond it, and thus the effect of the 
example is lost. ‘The safety of Europeans and native Christians depends more 
on the impression that an attack on them will bring down certain and severe 
punishment, thin on the protection of local authorities, wlio have often ne 
power to arrest an outbreak of a fanatical Mussulman population ; if, therefore, 
the punishment be hardly known, this salatary impression is weakened, and with 
it the best safeguard which Europeans possess. 

[ thought it prudent to inform the Pasha, through my dragoman, of what 
was passing among the lower clisses, and to suggest that it would be well to 
take measures to watch them, in order to prevent any outbreak of fanaticism 
against the Christians during the Bairam,. His Excelleney thanked me for the 
information, and adopted the necessary precautions by strengthening the police 
and watching some ill-disposed persons who were pointed out; and Tam happy 
to say that all passed off quietly, , : 

[regret to be obliged to report that all the authorities, without the slightest 
attempt at concealment, receive bribes, and that no post is given away, but for 
4 sum of motiey proportionate to the profit it ts likely to yield by oppressing 
the poor peasants, 


: 59 


A. person who was sent to maintain order in the Haurin, with a large body 
of cavalry, was, alter a short interval, recalled, when. he refused to obey, 
declaring publicly that he had paid a heavy bribe for his post, and would not 
resign it. This is only one among many incidents of the same nature, and 
it may be easily imagined that the Government is neither respected nor feared, 
and that the country is almost in a state of anarchy. 

; I have &e. | 
(Signed) JAS BRANT.

1 WAS afraid if the execution of the criminals were demanded before the 
order af the Sultan could arrive, it would, as contrary to law, be refused by 
Namick Pasha, and |, therefore, ventured to urge that nothing should be done 
until Ismail Pasha had arrived, 


* ha, BG. 


bt 


There are 900,000 pilgrims now at Mecea, and when these return home 
the impression they will produce will certainly be gene ally opposed to a good 
ynderstanding between Mussulmans and Christians. 

The immediate result, of what has taken place is, however, uncertain: it 
may be fear or indignation. For some weeks to come, at all events, no ones 
life, in certain parts of this Empire, will be quite sift. I thought it better to 
speak at once to the Grand Vizier and the French Ambassador ; neither of 
them had then received any information therefrom; but whilst Iwas with Aah 
Pasha a despatch from Musurus was brought to him, 

The French Ambassador replied to me at onee, and in the most friendly 
manner, that he thought the two countries should jointly bear the res vonsibility 
of the event that had occurred, however unfortunate, ‘The Grand Winer on 
the other hand, was alarmed and, in some degree, excited, saying that the Porte 
had done everything in her power, and, with the readiness she had shown, might 
have expected ta have been hotter treated. Te fears the first effects of the 
news, and we agreed to keep the matter, if possilile, secret, until the precise 
truth should reach us. 1 pacified him in some degree by the statement | was 
authorized to make; but if it should appear that, im spite of the willingness to 
do us justice which the Ottoman Clovernment exhibited, we premeditatedly took 
the Jaw into our own bands against a local authority, it is possible that the 
Sultan, sooner than loge all credit with his own subjects, may take up the matter 
‘4a most serious manner, and a protest would then be the first step in his 
proceedings, 

Much, of course, will depend on the tone of other Governments, especially 
of the French Government; but I would recommend an carly explaination or 
exouse, if your Lordship should feel disposed to offer such, m order to anticipate 
demands which it may be difficult for us to assent to, and yet which it may be 
difficult to justify our resisting.

(Telegraphic.) Therapia, August 23, 1858, 5 p.at, 
THE head Dragoman saw the Grand Vizier yesterday, subsequent to the 
conversation I narrated; when his Highness said that the affair of Jeddah bad 
been communicated to the Sultans Ministers, and produced a very sad and 
painful impression upon them, and that he intended, as soon as the details 
reached the Parte, to make a formal and solemn protest against an act which he 
considered neither called for nor justifiable; and which was the more important 
since it might be used as a pretext for similar acts by other Powers, who would 

be glad to quote the example. . é 
| Had the Sultan, said the Grand Vizier, been wanting in offering the mast 
ample reparation, the English Government would have been authorized tn 
taking the law into its own hands, and avenging the bloodshed of its Consul ; 
but such not being the case, the Ottoman Government had a right to_com slain,

No. 105, 


Mr. Fitzgerald to the Seeretary to the Admirolty. 


Sir, Foreign Office, August 25, 1858. 

[ HAVE received your letter dated the 24th instant, in which you state 
that you are commanded by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to call 
the attention of the Earl of Malmesbury to the fuet that ships have been ordered 
from India to Aden to wait further instructions; and to state that my Lords 
would be glad to know whether these ships should be detained at Aden, or 
ordered back. to India, or under what instructions they should enter the 
Red Sea. 

You further state that, should the ships in question not. be required in the 
Red Sea, it is desirable they should return to India, where they are much 
required, 

With reference to this latter point, it is impossible for me to offer any 
opinion whether it is more important that the services of these vessels should be 
available in the Indian waters than in the Red Sea; but until Her Majesty's 
Government are satisfied, by authentic information, that complete satisfaction 
has been afforded, and the claims of British subjects to compensation have been 
settled, it is certainly most desirable that Captain Pullen, who has been appointed 
Her Majesty's Commissioner for that purpose, and is about to return to Jeddah in 
that character, should be supported by an adequate, though moderate, force, 
which should be sent to the spot; and it must rest with my Lords Commissioners 
to decide what that force, under the circumstances, should be. 

In his capacity as Her Majesty's Commissioner, and to support him in that 
character, the nayal force on its arrival at Jeddah should be subject to the 
direction of Captain Pullen, who will receive full instructions for his guidance in 
the duty entrusted to him, and who will be informed that he is to authorise the 
return of the ships to India as soon as their presence at Jeddah is no longer 
required. 

lam, &e.

to be given to the ships ordered to Aden from India, to demand reparation for

of the Admiralty to transmit to you herewith a copy of a letter which has this

ordering that officer to place himself under Captain Pullen, who will conduct 
the negotiations under the authority with which he has been vested; but should 
circumstances arise to render it necessary for Her Majesty's forces off Jeddah 
to act hostilely, for the purpose of enforcing any demands upon the authorities 
at that place, in that case the senior officer will take Captain Pullen wnder his 
orders, and himself conduct the neecssary operations, leaving Captain Pullen to 
resume the negotiations afterwards if necessary. 

Lam also to request that, in laying this letter before the Earl of Malmes- 
bury, you will call hits attention to the fact that, in all probability, the officer 
arriving at Aden will be senior to Captain Pullen, im case he should think it 
desirable that the officer highest in rank should be empowered to act as Com- 
missioner. 

My Lords have, as yet, received no information of the instructions given to 
Captain Pullen in that capacity.

Government, thereupon, lost no time in again telegraphing, through Malta, 
to Captain Pullen to remain at Suez until the arrival of Ismail Pasha, but 
that officer had proceeded to execute the instructions which he received by 
the first despatch, and he had unfortunately quitted Suez, with Her Majesty's 
ship “ Cyclops,” before the arrival of the second telegram directing him to wait 
Isinail Pashas arrival. 

On Ismail Pasha’s arrival at Jeddah, Captain Pullen appears to have acted 
in combination with that General, and to have returned to Suez. 

Tam, &Xc. 


(Signed) MALMESBURY.

Sir, “ Cyclops.” at Jeddah, June 25, 1858. 
TT becomes my painful duty to report to you, for the information of the 
Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, one of the most horrible and bloody 
massacres ever perpetrated in any country + the vietims being unarmed, defence- 
less Christians, living at this place; the perpetrators, the Hadramouts, and 
other subjects of Turkey, ; 

9% Our feelings recoil from deeds so revolting; but when difference of 
religion is considered a justification for these atrocities, we turn with sreater 
detestation from the contemplation of them, and naturally ask, 1f its precepts 
‘nenleate such crimes as virtues, whether those principles should be permitted in 
the world. 

8. It was on the evening of the 15th instant that a rising of the Mahometans 
took place, and the following are the particulars as far as T can learn, 

4, Simultaneously they attacked the English and French Consulates and 
all the Christian population residing here, composed principally of Greeks; they 
murdered the English Vice-Consul, and threw him from his window ; they shot 
the Freneh Consul dead, and butchered his wite with a yataghan ; Copts and 
Greeks were alike mercilessly slaughtered to the number of twenty-one, und 
perhaps more. 

5. ‘The first intimation | had of any rising was at $40 pa. of the 1th 
instant, when two Greeks in astute of nudity came on board ina small canoe ; 
they stated that the mob had possession of the town, and were pulling down the 
Hag-statis at the English and French Consulates; and during the night two 
other Greeks eame on board. 

6. Their joint statement was, that they had left the town at about 6 P.m., 
escaping for their lives, the mob declaring they would murder every Christian. 

7. As [ had only left the town at 5°30 p.at., and as several officers belonging 
to the ship had been at the bazars in the most densely populated parts of the 
town until G Pal, without observing anything unusual, I reasonably doubted 
their statement, which, added to the dithculty of imperfect translation, deter- 
mined me to remain quiet, and not endeavour to take the boats through intricate 
reefs, or the men through narrow unknown streets, until 1 had heard some 
information upon which 1 could rely, considering also that the Government 
would afford sufficient protection to those peaceably disposed. 

8, In the morning, pereciving no flagestafls at the English and French 
Consulates, I proceeded with two bouts, armed, to the town, the arms being 
concealed. When nearing the landing-place, we were beckoned to return by 
some one at the port; at the sume time several shots were fired at us by the 
people, who had collected in crowds about the wharves. I determined, therefore, 
to return, espectilly as it seemed to me the people were in rebellion against the 
Government.

fired at us. fa he Pees

24. Having now detailed every circumstance attending these events, I bee 
to refer again to my letter of the 19th instant, describing the seizure of the 
British ship ‘ Eranee,” which his Execllency the Governor. General states was 
the cause of the rebellion, : 

25, The papers of the ship (together with those of twenty others) were 
destroyed at the Consulate on the evening of the 15th, as well as the notes 
made during the inquiry ; it being intended to complete the depositions the next 
day, and read them publicly to the parties concerned. 

26. I must now draw attention to the letter of his Excellency, in which 
he states that the conduct of the British Consul might have been consistent with 
the laws, if it affceted only British subjects; but 1 was, and still am, assured, 
notwithstanding any declarations to the contrary, that, on the 15th of this 
month, both the owners of that ship considered themselves British subjects. 

27. Again, on the 22nd instant, several merchants, under British protection, 
were on board. J asked them the question; the reply of all was, that the ship 
was a British ship, and the owners British subjects, | 

28. His Excelleney states that, although Salili Ben Johur is an Ottoman 
subject, he makes the admission that the ship tratticked under a British flag. 

29. His Excellency is very wrongly informed, when he states that the ship, 
by hoisting Turkish colours, had done nothing more than return back to her 
first origin. By her register, she was built at Portsmouth, New [ampshire 
(America), anil secins to have been sines owned by persons entitled by law to 
be owners of British ships. 

30, I have made inquiries also into that part of the Pasha’s letter in which 
he speaks of a Commercial Court having been held before the Kaimakam, and 
the following ts the statement of Furudj Yusu:—That he objected to the 
Kaimakam adjudicating on two British subjects; the Kaimakam then said that 
Salili Ben Johur would become an Ottoman subject, and that he then told him 
to hoist the Turkish flag; that Salili Ben Johur then went to the ‘ Eranee,” 
hauled down the English and hoisted Turkish colours; that, thereupon, 
Furudj Yusu went to the Kamakam ant protested against this proceeding, upon 
Which the Kaimakam sent for Salili Ben Johur, and told him to take down the 
Turkish flag, and not hoist any other; that nothing further was hoisted until 
ibout twelve days since, when the ship hoisted a Turkish flag; and Her 
Mujesty’s Consul being then present, the matter was inquired into by him. 

31. At the interview with his Excellency on boanl, he suggested that the 
parties should be sent to Constantinople; to this [ very readily assented, my 
object being to obtain justice for all: but his Excellency afterwards raised an 
objection, on the extraordinary ground that one of the principal witnesses 
(Furudj) Yusu) was his banker. 

a2, As it seems very certain that his Excellency will make the seizure of 
the ship a reason for the rebellion, [ have endeavoured to bring clearly before 
you every object bearing on the case. If such was the only reason, they should 
lave confined themselves to the English Consul, and not attacked, undiscrim- 
nately, all classes of Christians. 

34, | must now trouble you with what is currently considered to be the 
causes of the outbreak :— 

IL, It has been for some time a source of great bitterness that any Christians 
should reside in the Mahometan Holy Land, and it was Known that a rising to 
exterminate them would sooner or later take place. 

2. It has been reported that a Sheikh, or important personage of reputed 
great holiness, had arrived at Mecea with sixty followers from Delhi; this has 
heen whispered about in connection with the affiir, but Lean gain no certain 
knowledge on the subject. 

3. It has been stated that Salili Said Ben Johur, Sheikh Abdalgafar, 
Abdallah Moustessib (head of justice), Sayd Cagalif, and Sheikh Ali Basabrahim, 
Cadi Motlah (priest), had incited the people to commit these outrages. 

4, The Representative of the Grand Scheriff residing here, also inspired by 
the greatest fanaticism, urged the people to slaughter all who would not embrace 
Islamism. 

34. T have now only to repeat what | still firmly believe, that the two 
owners of the ship “Eranee” are British subjects, that the Kaimakam impro- 
verly interfered with them, and did great wrong and injustice by ordering the 
British flag to be struck, and the Turkish placed in its stead. 


if 


35. 1 beg now to inclose a copy of a letter I received from the late Consul 
at Jeddah on the subject of the re-establishment of a monopoly in salt. There 
are at present twenty-two British ships at Jeddah; it is said thirty more will 
soon be in the sea, bound to Suez: nearly the whole of these ships endeavour 
to get a cargo of salt at Jeddah; since the re-establishment of the monopoly 
this is impossible, 

37. Bight fugitive slaves have reached the ship, and are therefore: free. 
Many of them swank a distance of two miles: it may be that many others

Namick Pasha to Captain Pullen. 


(Translation from the Turkish.) 
M, le Commandant, (No date; reecived June 22, 1858,) 

BY the report that the British Consul has sent to you as to the eeizing of 
the ship and taking away the Ottoman colours, which the owners had hoisted, 
you, in accordance, sent persons to tuke the ship, and putting down the colours 
she had fiving, hoisted the English. 

The inhabitants of Jeddah seeing all this done to the Ottoman flag and 
ship, of course took to defend the proprictor of the ship and the colours al the 
Government. In one istance the local authorities and the Medjlis: had sent to 
pequest the British Consul to keep from doing so; but he, instead af trying to 
quiet the people of the town, began to insult them with indecent words, which 
provoked still more the inhabitants, the consequences of which were that they 
attacked him. | 

The Consul on seeing this went so far as to express openly to the mol that 
went to attack him, that had they attempted to do 50, that he would either have 
wounded er killed them. ‘The consequences were that the people, not thinking 
this atkair would take so serious an end, audaciously attacked him. You know 
the rest. and the measures the local authorities took to prevent it; not the less 
of the promptitude which 1 have shown by my coming: from Mecca to: this 
town ; my endeavours of finding and making mysell Gimiliar with the causes of 
this affair; lastly, of the pain and sorrow | really felt at such an oecurrence 

The conduct of the British Consul might have been consistent with the 
laws, if this affair affected an English subject, but Salih Johur is an Ottoman 
subject, native of Jeddah, and had the ship which trafficked to Tndia only uider 
the protection of the British flag; in fact, she has done nothing more than 
return back to her first origin by hoisting the Turkish flag. , 

he British Consul, on leaving this town, appointed Mr. Pura Yussor to 
represent him as his Wahie; a Commercial Court then formed, and itt necord: 
ance with the musbata (trial of the case with witnesses on both sides), a verdict 
given in arbifrio inthe presence ol Mr. Fura Yussor (one of the Judges), and satis- 
Factorily submitted to by both parties, mm causa: it was no use, therefore, alter all 
this had taken place, that the Turkish colours should have been uninasted, and 
seizure made of the ship. ' ) 

1 dread the tearful consequences this affair may yet bring to the country; ut 

has already been the cause of what has happened andawill yet happen, Te 

injure the Government more—a thing which Lam almost sure you would not like 
to hear. : 

|, therefore, beg of you to make over the ship to the proprictor, thrawgh the 

Harbour-master, bearer of this my letter, and be pleased to 07 der that your men 


will quit her. | ree

Inclosure 17 in No, 120. 


Namick Pasha to Captain Pullen, 


(Translated from the Turkish.) 


M. le Commandant, (Received June 24.) 


! HAVE received and understand the letter you have sent me, in which 
you state that the vessel which has been seized will be given into the hands of 
anybody whom I may delegate for the purpose; at the same time informing me 
that the vessel, it being British property, should be kept without any colours 
flying until the entire affair is arranged. 

But the owner of the vessel, Salih Djohur, is an Ottoman subject, and 
therefore the vessel cannot be considered British property; also, he has not 
settled his accounts with his partner, Houssein Djohur, 

I say that Houssein Djohur is also an Ottoman subject, who is placed 
under British protection, [tis necessary, therefore, that the acconnts between 
them should be settled, ’ 

beg then, that the vessel, whose seizure has caused a rebellion, may be 
given up to its owner, Salih Djohur, Otteman subject, and that he may be 
authorized to hoist the Ottoman flag, without whieh it will he impossible for me 
to reecive her, 


(Seal of Namick Pashia.) 


Inclosure 1S in No, 120. 


Acting Vice-Consul Page to Captain Pullen, 
sir, Jeddih, April 2, 1858, 
| AVAIL myself of your arrival at this port to lay before you a statement 
of the serious infraction of our Treaty of Commerce, by the re-establishment of 
the salt monopoly, the which affects British and British-Indian commerce 
almost entirely, and to request, if it is in your power to do so, to render me all 
the assistince you can to abolish it. 

In the year 1854, Mr, Vice-Consul Cole brought this monopoly to. the 
notice of Her Majesty's Consul-General at Constantinople, and an order from 
the Grand Vizier was forwarded through Her Majesty's Ambassador, that the 
sane was to be discontinued. ‘The year 1855 the monopoly was not insisted 
upon, but early in the year 1856, Ramil Pasha, the then Governor, intimated 
that he had reecived instructions from Constantinople to re-establish it. ‘This T 
resisted, having received no orders from Her Majesty's Ambassador to that 
elfcct, and moreover pointed out to him that there were two serious errors in 
the communication he had made to me; the first being, that the salt was the 
produce of a mine, but this is not the ease, as it is made by solar evaporation ; 
and the second, that the salt was the produce of the Island of Souakin, whereas, 
instead of heing the produce of that place, it is collected at a considerable 
distance from it, the small boats collecting it as Salaka, and the larger ones at 
Rowney. I suceeeded, therefore, in resisting the re-establishment of the same 
for that year, viz., 1846,—the produce of these two years being deposited in the 
hands of two of the British merchants, 

At the latter end of the vear 1856, a new Governor-General, Mahomed 
Pasha, being appointed, determined on listening to no remonstrances whatever, 
and re-established the monopoly; «a report of the seme was forwarded to 
Constantinople and the Government of Bombay, 1 beg to state that the Indian 
Government fally approved of my proceedings in: resisting the re-establishment 
of the monopoly in the year 1856.

No. 121. 
Earl Cowley to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received August 28.) 


(No, 1,120. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, August 25, 1858. 

DURING a conversation which I had, yesterday, with Count Walewski, 
his Excellency, in alluding to the bombardment of Jeddah by Her Majesty's 
ship “Cyclops,” said that Fuad Pasha liad just been with him, and had shown 
considerable soreness at the Porte's authority having been superseded by 
Captain Pullen, Count Walewski added that, although he did not wish to raise 
the question in any way with Her Majesty's Government, he must express his 
own regret that Captain Pullen had not waited for the arriva’ of the French 
Commissioner, in order to institute a solemn inquiry into the late occurrences at 
Jeddah. It would, in his opinion, have made a more wholesome impression 
had the participators in the late atrocities been condemned and punished in the 
presence of British and French Commissioners, As it was, his Excellency still 
hoped that an inquiry would be held, and that Captain Pullen would receive 
instructions to that effect. it was impossible to ascertain without such inquiry 
whether the individuals who had been executed were those who most deserved 
it, or whether, as is often the case in the East, those who were without protec- 
tion had not been sacrificed to sereen the more favoured culprits. M. I:merat, 
the Chancelicr to the late French Consul, who was accompanying M, Sabatier 
to Jeddah, could give more information on this matter than any one else. 
Moreover, the question of the amount of indemnity to be paid by the town of 
Jeddah was yet unsettled, 

I replied that, as far as T was acquainted with the matter, L did not think 
that it had been the intention of Her Majesty's Government that Captain Pullen 
should act before the arrival of the Commissioner sent by the Porte with full 
powers to punish in the Sultan’s name; or that he should then do more than 
vive the Commissioner all the assistance that should be required of him, Her 
Majesty's Government had felt, as I had already had the Renate to inform: his 
Excellency, that if the Porte was willing to act, it would be proper to let the 
Sultan vindicate his own authority. I could only account, therefore, for Captain 
Pullen’s proceedings, by supposing that he had mistaken the nature of his 
‘astructions. ‘There certainly had been no intention on the part of Her Majesty's 
Government to obtain satisfuction to the exclusion of Ghana co-operation. 

Your Lordship is, probably, aware that the French press has commented 
in no measured terms on Captain Pullen’s conduct, maintaming that that officer 
ought not to have acted until the arrival of a French ship to join him, If the 
French Government entertain such a pretension, they do not put it forward 
openly; for some time must clapse before the steam-frigate, dispatched about ten 
days ago, can reach the roadstead of Jeddah. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.
