No. 133. 


Mr. Fitzgerald to the Secretary to the Admiralty. 


Sir, Foreign Office, September 1, 1898. 
oe I fe directed by the Earl of Malmesbury to acknowledze your letter of 
28th ultimo, received yesterday, in which you state that, with reference to the 
instructions which have been addressed by the Secretary of State for Foreign 
Affairs to Captain Pullen, on his appointment as Commissioner for the settie- 
ment of the demands of Her Majesty’s Government, on account of the recent 
outrages at Jeddah, the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty are in doubt, 
looking to the tenour of my letter of the 25th instant, whether those instructions 
were forwarded by the mail of that date from the Foreign Office. 

On referring to that letter, it appears to Lord Malmesbury that it purported 

to convey to you a copy of the instructions that had been addressed to Captain 
Pullen, and that it was, therefore, sufficiently apparent that it had been sent by 
the mail of that date direet from this Department. 
x¢ You further inform me that you are directed to suggest that, for the future 
instructions to naval officers employed in diplomatic commissions should be sent 
to them by the Board of Admiralty, and not by the Department by which they 
are appointed, and under which, as such Diplomatic Agents, they act; and, ina 
subsequent letter you forwarded to me, as a precedent which, in their Lordships’ 
opinion, should, in future, be followed by this Department, a letter, addressed by 
Lord Clarendon to the Board of Admiralty, in which their Lordships transmitted 
a copy of a despatch which his Lordship proposed, with the concurrence of the 
Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, to address to Captain Prevost, with 
reference to a survey in which he was to be engaged, and as to which Lord 
Clarendon desired to be informed whether my Lords concurred in the proposed 
instruction. 
But it does not appear to Lord Malmesbury that the duties which Captain 
Prevost was to perform, and which were of a professional character, are at all 
analogous to those which un officer entrusted with a diplomatic commission. is 
called upon to fulfil, or that the case referred to can be at all considered a 
precedent as to the course of proceeding which should be adopted in cases 
similar to that under consideration. 

__ Tam directed by Lord Malmesbury to state that it would, in his inion, be 
highly inconvenient that instructions to an officer employed on an important 
diplomatic service, and whieh, in this particular instance, had received the 
epprotelion of the Prime Minister and of the French Government, with whom 
ter Majesty’s Government are now acting, should be forwarded by any but this 
Department, under which he ts called upon to act; and still less that the 
concurrence of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty should be required 
to instructions which are framed upon considerations, and with reference to 
circumstances, of which it is possilile their Lordships may have no cognizance 
and as to which they would, probably, hesitate to express an opinion. a 

Lord Malmesbury believes the only result of the adoption of the course 
suggested by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty would be to exclude 
naval officers from appointment to diplomat ic commissions of a highly honour- 
able and important character, z 

Lord Malmesbury is therefore of opinion that the more convenient course 


is that instructions to naval officers employed on a diplowiatic service, and

which are to guide them in the execution of the duties that service imposes on 


them, should be gent directly from this Department, but should, in oll cases, be

With reference to the possible ‘nconvenience that may eccur from the fact 
of Captain Pullen being a junior officer in command on the station at Jeddah, 
while Lord Malmesbury admits that possible embarrassment may ¢nsue from 
this fact, he must remark thet this arises only from the particular circumatances 
of the case, and that this difficulty might have been more advantageously

Inclosure in No, 137. 


Captain Pullen to the Secretary to the Admiralty. 
Sir, “ Cyclops,” Suez, Auquet 22, 1858, 
MY letter of the 12th instant placed you in possession of my proceedings 
ta that date, and of my intention to complete provisions, &c., from Malta, as 
speedily as possible, to be in readiness for the French Commissioners and 
proceed to Jeddah, 

Experience every day assures me of the fact, that the bombardment of the 
town of Jeddah, and, above all, the destruction of a number of buggalows there, 
has been attended with the desired effect. Pilgrims and others are constant! 
arriving at this place, and whilst they spread exaggerated accounts of the 
bombardment of Jeddah, and of the execution of the murderers, they are not 
forgetful that for their sakes the bombardment was discontinued, they treated 
with every facility, and were allowed to proceed to their homes: thus a spirit of 
submission has gained ground, coupled with a wholesome dread that, as soon as 
any crime is altempted, its punishment, sooner or later, will fall on the guilty, 
the town, and the buggalows, 

The Turkish troops are now concentrated at Jeddah, and I consider this is 
& moment ta mete out justico—a justice aimed not alone at the unfortunate 
ignorant fianaties, but to those who, holding situations of trast, were found 
wanting in their duty at the time of the massacre, 1 believe a delay will be 
attended with bad results ; it will keep alive ill-fecling towards Christians until 
itis disposed of, whilst, on the other hand, the speedy and solemn decrees of 
Justice, unmixed with anything approaching vengeance, will give them a fear and 
respect for our character, our firmness, and our power, and the bombardment 
will teach them also a lesson which will never be forgotten. 

With the Mahometans of this part of the world two things are necessary to 
show authority: first, the bombardment of the town and destruction of their 
vessels ; and secondly, indemnification to the greatest extent, that is, as far as 
the inhabitants can bear it,

1 trust therefore, my Lords coinciding with these opinions, will either direet 
me to proceed forthwith to Jeddah, or that the French Commissioner may be 
sent to Suez as early as possible to accompany me. 

I am very anxious also to proceed to Yembo, and such other ports as may 
be necessary, where the presence of a vessel of war for a few hours may be 
attended with good cflvcts,but my stay here is now dependent on their Lord- 
ships’ orders.

Vice-Consul Calvert to Acting Consul-Goneral Green. 


Sir “Cyclops,” at Sea, off Jeddah, August 8, 1858, 


1 HAVE the honour to inform you, that in obedience to your instructions, 
I left Alexandria on the afternoon of the 16th of July, and arrived at Suez at 
about 6 o'clock pat. on the following day, I immediately made oyer to 
Mr. Vice-Consul West the despatch for the Commodore of Her Majesty's ships 
and vessels in the East Indies, and without loss of time proceeded on board at 
Her Majesty's steam-frigate “ Cyclops,” and delivered the despatch addressed to 
Captain Pullen, ‘That officer having expressed a wish that I should HEME DY 
him to interpret for him, | availed of the permission you cera granted me, 
just before leaving Alexandria, and 1 at once placed myselfat his Li as shes 

Captain Pullen would have left that same evening for Jeddah, to carry 
out his instructions, but your telegram, announcing that further onlers had 
reached you for him, caused him to delay his departure until the following alter-

Jeddah, that a force of thirty-five armed buggalows was about to proceed to

We reached Jeddah early on the morning of the 23rd of July, and there 
found the Honourable East India Companys steamer * Lady Canning” 
(Lieutenant-Commanding Peevor) and also about twenty-five or thirty large 
merehant-vessels, mostly British Indians, At 11730 a.a., Captain Pullen sent 
off. a letter to the Kaimakam of Jeddah, inclosing a despatch for the Governor of 
that place, Mehmet Namick Pasha (then absent at Mecca). The Captain therem 
informed the Pasha, that he had come to demand, on the part of England and 
France, the immediate execution of the murderers of the British and French 
Consuls; and he pointed out a spot in sight of the ship where it was to take place; 
he granted the Pasha thirty-six hours, from the time of landing his despatch, 
for a reply ; and stated, that if his demands were not then complied with, he 
would be compelled to carry out, to their fullest extent, the orders he had 
received ; he furthermore assured the Pasha, that he had not come to make war 
against the Ottoman authorities, but to insist on the punishment of a race of 
cowardly murderers, and that so long as the fortifications did not molest him in 
the execution of his orders, he would respect them, but would immediately open 
fre upon them if'a shot were fired. 

Eantain Pullen stated that the compensation for loss of property to 
British und French subjects was a matter which he did not intend to enter 
upon, as it would, of course, be settled later by the respective Governments 
concerned; and he also informed the Pasha that he would not allow any native 
bont to leave the place, and, if any attempted it, he would sink her: and in 
order to carry out this measure, the “ Cyclops " and “ Lady Canning ” took up 
positions commanding the two channels among the coral reefs. 

‘At 2 o'clock in the afternoon, a Secretary of the Kaimakam’s came on 
board, being the bearer of a letter from the Kaimakam, acknowledging the 
receipt of the Captain’s letters, and stating that, being in Freneh, they were not 
understood. Their contents were, therefore, translated to the Secretary, and the 
Captain granted additional time for the Pasha’s reply, to make up for the delay 
thus occasioned. At the same time he informe the Secretary that, to his 
surprise, he pereeived the ‘Turkish flag flying on board the ‘* Eranee,” notwith- 
standing Captain Pullen's former protest to the Pasha, and proposal that that 
vessel should not show either British or Turkish colours ; and he desired that 
the Turkish flag should be at once hauled down: this was immediately carried 
into effect by the local authorities. From what the Kaimakam told Captain 
Pullen, the Turkish colours had been hoisted on board of the “ Eranee,” 
by order of the Pasha, on ihe very day when the “ Cyclops” left Jeddah for 
Suez, 

The time granted by the Captain having more than elapsed without a reply 
from the Pasha, the “Cyclops” opened fire on the town at half-past 3 o'clock in 
the morning of the 25th of July, by three rounds of shot and shell from two 
68-pounders, and two B4-pounders (hollow shot), At about 5 o'clock a.m. 
four more rounds were fired, the fortress being silent on both these and on all 
subsequent occasions (it 1 doubtful whether the Turkish guns would have had 
sufficient range to reach the ship). At a quarter to 7 o'clock a.m., a Bimbashee 
and the Kamuikamys Secretary came on board, and begged that the bombardment 
should be suspended for at least fourteen hours, on the chance of a ren 
reaching from the Pasha within that time. Captain Pullen did not consider 
himself justified in granting this delay, but allowed sufficient time for the return 
‘of the officials to the shore. At 10 o'clock a.a., the boats of the “ Cyclops ” 
and ‘ Lady Canning" were sent to destroy some bugealows anchored in a bight 
not far from us. ‘This order was soon effectually performed, and, aided by the 

uns of the two steamers, it resulted in the sinking or burning of about filteen 
Ehaealows, some laden with manufactures. nie hae 

Ata quarter past 11 a. a Secretary of the Medjlis of Jeddah came on 
board, and brought a letter from Namick Pasha. acknowledging Captain Pullen's 
letter to him of the 23rd instant, and stating that the property plundered from 
British and other subjects had heen recovered in part; that diligent search was 
being made for the rest; that fourteen persons were now imprisoned at Jeddah 
for having been concerned in the massacre; that he had not the power of lile 
and death, and could not act without reference to Constantinople; that, by 
blockading the port and firing on the town, Captain Pullen would cause the

Arab tribes to rise up in open rebellion against the Sultan, as it would be impos- 
sible to convince them that England and Turkey were not acting in concert 
arainst them; and that our bombardment would ‘destroy British, French, and 
"Tarkish property. He, therefore, begged the Captain to desist, until orders 
came from Constantinople. 

To this letter the Captain replied that his instructions were imperative to 
demand the execution of the murierers ; that those instructions must be obeyed; 
and that a squadron from the East Indies might shortly be expected here to 
support and conclude whatever he might leave untinished. At about half-past 
noon, we made another attack on the town with rockets and great guns; this 
desultory firing at irregular intervals being intended to inspire a wholesome 
dread among the natives, and to prevent them from remaining inthe town, In 
this we perfectly succeeded, for Jeddah was in a few hours quite deserted, and 
the inhabitants were seen flying in all directions to the neighbouring villages. 

On the morning of the 26th of July, the “ Cyclops” again tired fifteen or 
twenty shot and shell into the town, most of whieh appeared to do much 
damage; and we learnt in the afternoon that a moorsom shell had killed a 
family of five persons in one house, including a person called Sheikh Sady, an 
Arab. Another shot had killed two female black slaves. After this bormbard- 
ment, Captain Pullen went on board of the “ Lady Canning,” and sent for the 
masters or mates of the East Indiamen anchored in the rondstead, to inquire of 
them whether they considered they would be sale after our departure. ‘They 
replied they were not sure, now that the town had been bombarded, Captain 
Pullen had, on the day of our arrival at Jeddah, recommended them to put to 
sea, to be out of the way of danger; this, however, they were unable to do, as 
most of the masters und seamen were at Mecca, and the ships were in want of 
water and provisions, and had not even ballast. 

In the afternoon, a Turkish officer came on board, with a letter from 
Namick Pasha, stating that the bearer understood French, and was authorized, 
on his part, to confer with Captain Pullen (the officer had left Mecca before the 
news of the bombardment had reached that place). The object of lis interview 
with the Captain was, to renew the request already given by the Pasha for a 
suspension of hostilities; and the same arguments previously advanced were 
again brought forward, but with no better success, for, shortly after sunset, the 
« Cyclops’ boats, mounting three howitzers and two rocket-tubes, were sent in 
among the coral reefs; and, having got tolerably close to the town, opened fire 
on it with shot, shell, and rockets, 

On the 27th of July, eight buggalows having arrived, bringing from Suez 
about 500 Albanian Bashi-Boxzouks, Captain Pullen impressed both on their 
commanding officers, and on the Kaimakam, the necessity of restraining them 
from plundering or committing any disorder, 

Namick Pasha arrived on the 28th of July from Mecea, and immediately 
sent a message to Captain Pullen, to say that, although ill and futigued, he 
would come on board to see him, whenever it might be convenient. His Excel- 
lency therefore came off on the 29th, and had a long interview with Captain 
Pullen, He dwelt with much earnestness on the extreme difficulty of his 
position; he said that it was impossible for him, without the sanction of the 
Porte, to put any one to death ; such an unauthorized act would be his infallible 
ruin, and might cost him even his life. He said that, after the departure of the 
“Cyclops” for Suez, the Kaimakam had discovered and imprisoned a number 
of persons concerned in the missacre, and had recovered some of the plundered 
property; but that the detailed report of these proceedings had not yet gone 
forward to Constantinople, for want of an opportunity. 

The Pashia said that many pilgrins were now daily arriving at Jeddah from 
Mecca, but that the fear of another bombardment had the effect of preventing 
them ftom laying in a stock of provisions and embarking, and thet the bakers 
had closed their shops, and had tled, causing great distress among the pilgrims. 

Captain Pullen said, in reply, that, taking these circumstances into consi- 
deration, he would allow them till the 8nd of August, at noon, to make their 
preparations, and embark, ‘The interview ended without the Pasha having 
acceded in-any way to Captain Pullen’s demands, with respect to the execution 
of the murderers. 

In the afternoon of the Slst of July, the * Lady Canning "left for Yembo, 
having the Moorish Princes and their suite on board. One of the Princes had

died of apoplexy at Mecca. ‘The Princes were now proceeding on their pilgri-

were to leave Yembo for Suez, in the “Lady Canning.” 

At Captain Pullen's request, Namick Pasha furnished him, on the 31st of 
July, with a copy of the “ mazbuta” which is about to be sent to Constantinople, 
containing the list of persons imprisoned on a charge of having bean implicated 
in the murder of the Consuls and other Christians, and the depositions of the 
witnesses, 


From this document, it would appear that sixteen persons lave been 


arrested on suspicion, one of whom has lately died, and another is dangerously 
ill: ‘The prisoners are mostly tradesmen, with a‘ saraf” (or banker), two harbour 
pilots, and two slaves. Among them are those who are accused of having 
murdered the British Consul, the French Consul and his lady, and Mr. Sava, 
the merchant. The testimony of the witnesses, except that of a slave of Sava's, 
consists chiefly in the prisoners having been heard by them to have declared 
that they had each killed one or more Cliristians or had murdered the Mnglish 
or the French Consul. Indeed, one of the accused confirmed openly to several 
officials the truth of his having killed Sava. 7 believe that, in Mahometan law, 
such a confession is alone sufficient to constitute guilt. 

Captain Pullen having previously obtained from the Kaimakam a nominal 
list of the prisoners, and not perceiving among it the name of several persons 
of rank who were pointed out to the captain as the instigators of the massacre, 
requested the Pasha to make inquiries respecting them, 

The Pasha, in reply, stated that some were not known to him (probably 
because the names had been mis-spelt, and were not identified) ; that others, so 
far from inciting the mob, had afforded shelter to British subjects (not Christians) ; 
and that another was so infirm and old, and his house so far from the seene of 
slaughter, that the suspicion cast on him was quite unmerited, 

On the morning of the 2nd of August, Captain Pullen wrote a letter to 
Namick Pasha, stating that, in consideration of the constant influx of Hadjis 
into Jeddah, he would prolong the suspension of hostilities until the evening of 
the 4th, but that if, by the following morning, no favourable reply were received, 
he would, by more stringent and severe measures, strive to obtain justice, He, 
moreover, threw on the Pasha all the consequences of a refusal. Before a reply 
was received, or the time had clapsed, the Ottoman steamer “ Gabarri ” arrived 
from Suez, having on board 480 Egyptian troops, and Ismail Pasha, an officer 
sent expressly from Constantinople with full powers to act in a manner beat 
calculated to satisfy the just demands of England and France. Ismail Pasha 
forthwith came on board of the * Cyclops.” His Excellency assured the captain 
that, on the present occasion, it was the wish and intention of the Porte to act 
in concert with England and France for the punishment of the guilty. The 
arrival of this officer relieved the authorities of Jeddah from an embarrassing 
position, us they dared not act without orders, Captain Pullen's conduct 
throughout this affair has been must judicious, and he has adhered to.the tenour 
of his instructions as closely os his peculiar position would permit. The arrival 
at Jeddah of thousands of Hadjis, among whom there were many natives of 
British India and Algeria, was the main cause of Captain Pullen being shackled 
in his movements ; and I believe he selected the only course left open to him, 
equally consistent with his orders and with humanity, The bombardinent of 
Jeddah has occurred at a most opportune moment; for no pilgrims were then 
in the place; and they can now tell in every remute corner of the Mahometan 
world how England and France avenge the murder of their Consuls and their 
other subjects. 

On the 3rd of August, Captain Pullen was officially informed by Namick 
Pasha that he had received un Imperial firman, ordering him to satisfy the 
demands of Englind und France by the immediate decapitation of the persons 
convicted of participation in the massacre of the 15th of June last. Namick 
Pasha stated that he was ready to fultil the orders of his Government, as soon 
as Captain Pullen would indicate the spot selected by him for the execution ; 
and he invited him to interrogate the prisoners. The Captain replied that any 
examination by him was unnecessary, as he felt certain the Local Tribunal had 
done all that justice required. 

On the following day, Captain Pullen sent an officer to point out to the 
authorities the place of execution, It was on a dry spit of coral reef, running

out into the inner harbour, and so situated as to be visible both from the town 
and from the merechant-vessels, ‘The next morning (the Sth) the execution took 
place at about sunrise, eleven criminals being belicaded, in the presence of a 
large portion of the ‘‘ Cyelop's” crew, fully armed and drawn up on the beach, 
and in that of the boats of the Anglo-Indinn ships in the port, called together 
by order of Captain Pullen, whose motive in so doing was that this instance of 
retributive justice should be known in Indin. ‘The officers of the Cyclops" 
described the execution as a sickening and appalling scene of butchery. Most 
of the culprits openly acknowledged their guilt before dying, and not a shadow 
of suspicion exists in the minds of any one that innocent blood has been shed. 
The whole affair only occupied ten minutes. The total number of prisoners 
was sixteen, Of these, eleven were executed, ns above stated; one died in 
prison; and the remaining four, not having been convicted of actual murder, 
though accessories, are to be sent to the galleys at Constantinople, 1 inclose a 
list T have drawn up, respecting the prisoners, by which you will perceive that 
the murderers of the Consuls have not escaped their well-merited punishment. 
There are, no doubt, many murderers and instigators still unpunished; but 
Captain Pullen considered that a further effusion of blood would be unnecessary, 
and he, therefore, wrote to Namick Pasha to declare that the deniands of Great 
Britain and France having now been satistied, he left the uuthoritics to deal 
with sany other criminala in the way they judged best. At 8 o'clock, the 
*Cyelops*” saluted the Turkish flag at her fore with twenty-one guns. ‘This 
salute was immediately returned by the fort with an equal number of guns, when 
the British and French colours, flying side by side, were displayed at the 
Cyclops’ main. The same afternoon, Namick Pasha sent his Secretary, 
Nazmy Bey, on board, with two letters for Captain Pullen: the one, explaining 
satisfactorily the reason of the four criminals, already referred to, not having 
been executed ; the other, stating that Ismail Pasha had received orders from 
the Porte to examine into, and settle, the dispute about the “ Eranee,” and 
inviting Captain Pullen to send a person to represent him at a Council about to 
be convened for that purpose, ‘To this the Captain, of course, objected, reply- 
ing that he had no authority to do so, and he did not consider the local autho- 
rities competent to decide a question in which British subjects and a British 
vessel were exclusively concerned. Not to lengthen this report. and to keep 
different subjects separate, I shall, on my arrival at Alexandria, draw up a 
despatch on the subject of the * Eranee.” 

On the 6th August, Captain Pullen, at Namick Pasha’s request, left with 
him o letter addressed to Commodore Watson, of Wer Majesty's ship “ Chesa- 
veake ” (and to be opened by any officer of the Royal or Honourable Company's 

vavy visiting Jeddah), explaining that satisfaction had been fully obtained by 
England and France for the murder of their Consuls. 

At 8 a.m. on the 7th Aucust, we left Jeddah, having on board a ‘Turkish 
officer bearing despatches from the Pasha to his Government. It was fortunate 
there was nothing further to detain Captain Pullen at Jeddah; tor disease, said 
to be cholera, was committing ravages among the pilgrims, and the dead bodies 
were carelessly thrown overboard from the vessels anchored near us, and flouted 
about the ship, thus endangering the health of the crew, whow it was expedient 
to remove at once from this pernicious atmosphere, 

The Kaimakam, on calling to make his farewell visit, told Captain Pullen 
and myself, in confidence, that the authorities had the names of other persons 
implicated in the murder of the Christians; but that these culprits now keeping 
away, the only chance of their being arrested was by seeretly and patiently 
awiiting a proper opportunity, : 

In concluding this despatch, | may, perhaps, be allowed to offer a few 
remarks respecting the massacre of the 14th of June last, Io am told that 
rumours had, for some time previously, been prevalent at Jeddah of an inten- 
tion to exterminate the Christians from the Mahometan Holy Land; the 
existence of several taverns kept by Christians had given great uinbrage to the 
fanatical portion of the population, aad there were other grievances, real or 
imaginary, which kept up a feeling of irritation, when the lowering of the 
Turkish flag on board of the '‘ Eranee” was seized upon as a plausible pretext, 
and the massucre was effected hefore the small garrison (about 100 Artillerymen) 
were in time to gave more than half the Christians, Jt will be no easy matter 
ta discover and convict the chief instigators, if they were persons of nank and

The Hedjaz seems to be but feebly garrisoned, the troops scarcely sufficing 
to defend themselves against the Arabs, much less to afford adequate protection 
ta the pilgrims, who are yearly plundered and murdered by those lawless tribes. 
I believe that the Turkish authorities and troops sincerely rejoice at the execution 
of the murderers having taken place under the guns of the “Cyclops,” as the 
population of Jeddah have now learnt: how completely they ever must be in the 
power of any vessel of war appearing off their port, and how necessary, there- 
fore, it is for them to curb their fanatical passions ; for the town mamnly depending 
on supplies by sea, the blockade by even a single gun-boat would, at any time, 
suffice to greatly distress the population, and reduce tt to obedience.

the promoters of the massacre of the Consuls and resident Christians, have, uy

Inclosure 3 in No. 139. 


Mr. Ayrton to Consul Walne. 


Sir, Cairo, August 17, 1858, 

MESSRS. MIRIALACHI, A. d'Antonio, and Co,, and Messrs, Duca 
Paleologo, Cochilani, and Co.,.on whose behalf I write, having learnt, within 
the last twenty-four hours only, that Captain Pullen, commanding Her 
Majesty's ship “ Cyclops,’ has been appointed Her Majesty's Commissioner for 
obtaining from the town of Jeddah a sum of money to cover the tnderanity due 
to the sufferers by the late outbreak, and the interests of the above-named firms, 
and of the persons dependent on them, being of large extent in connection with 
Jeddah, as more fully explained in the letter addressed by each of the firms to 
you, for transmission to Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople, on the 
l¥th instant; I have the honour, by their special desire, to request that in the 
event of its being contemplated to effect anything like a final settlement of cases 
by the Commission, of which Captain Pullen is to be a member, you will move 
Hier Majesty's Acting Consul-General to bring, if possible by the present mail, 
to the notice of Her Majesty's Government at home, the large interests 
belonging to these firms at stake, and the impossibility of arriving at anything 
like a just estimate of their losses, before they have had time to collect their 
accounts and advices from their correspondents at various ports of the Ked Sea, 
besides Jeddah, and that they hope they may be favoured with such notice of 
the meeting of the assumed Commission as will admit of their making due 
arrangement for being represented before it, 

I am further requested to state, on behalf of the firms mentioned, that they

Captain Pullen to the Secretary to the Admiralty, 


Sir, " Cyclops,” Suez, August 13, 1858. 

I BEG to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of 2nd instant, with its 
various inclosures, for my instruction, to act as British Commissioner, in matters 
connected with the late events at Jeddah. 

As the health of the officers and men of the ship has become extremely 
enervated by the intense heat experienced at Jeddah, I am very desirous of 
giving them, for as long a period as possible, the benefit of this, comparatively 
speaking, cool place. 

I have also demanded provisions from Malta, of which I am greatly in 
want, and part of which it will be necessary for me to receive before leaving 
Duez, 

In the meantime I shall take on board coals, and be prepared to proceed. to 
carry out their Lordships’ orders with as little delay as possible after the arrival 
of the French Commissioner, to whom it is my intention to offer the hospitality 
of this ship, in the name of Her Majesty's Government. : 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) W. LS, PULLEN.

No, 146, 
The Secretary to the Admiralty to Mr, Filzqerald,—{ Received Seplember 4.) 


Sir, Admiralty, September 3, 1855, 

[ HAVE received and laid before my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty 
your letter dated the Ist September, respecting the instructions given to Captain 
Pullen, of Her Majesty’s ship “ Cyclops,” as Commissioner for the settlement 
of the demands of Her Majesty's Government on account of the outrages at 
Jeddah, 

While my Lords regret to be under the necessity of troubling the Earl of 
Malmesbury. with further observations upon this subject, they are constrained to 
remark that the words “will be sent,” used in your letter of the 25th ultimo, 
conveyed to them only the expression of an intention to furnish Captain Pullen 
with dull instructions for his guidance as Her Majesty's Commissioner. On the 
28th ultimo, and after the departure of the mail of the 26th ultimo, my Lords 
received, with your letter of the 26th ultimo, a copy of those instructions, 
which were then stated to have been addressed to Captain Pullen; but their 
Lordships were still in doubt as to the fact of the instructions having been 
actually forwarded on the 25th ultimo, more especially as they considered, and 
are still of opinion, that the practice of forwarding such instructions without the 
concurrence, or, at least, hous the timely knowledge, of their Lordships, to 
naval officers on actual service afloat, is calculated to produce inconvenience to 
the public ¢ervice. 

My Lords are very far from wishing it to be understood that they are to 
be in all cases consulted as to the nature of the instructions to be addressed to ii 
naval officer acting as Her Majesty's Commissioner, under the authority of the 
Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and they fully concur in the reasons stated 
by Lord Malmesbury in objection to such a course; bot when the same. officer 
is also acting in command of a naval force, and is an officer for whose conduct 
my Lords are of necessity responsible, they deem it essential that every care 
should be taken to avoid the inconvenience of his receiving conflicting instruc- 
tions, and that, unless from unavoidable necessity, no instructions should be 
forwarded by the Secretary of State without the knowledge and, to that extent, 
without the concurrence of their Lordships. 

With this understanding, my Lords see no reason to object to the employ- 
ment of Captain Pullen as Her Majesty’s Commissioner ; but they must observe 
that, in the first intimation which they received of his appointment as such by 
the Secretary of State, they were also informed that the arrangement had been 


already announced to Lord Cowley, and to the Government of the Emperor of 
: ! 


the French, 
Lam, &c. 
(Signed) W. G. ROMAINE,

Prompt and decisive measures, under all circumstances here, I considered

15, As the boats were on the point of shoving off, | observed the Turkish 
colours hoisted, and dipped occasionally, at the port. Imagining it might be a 
communication from the Pasha, it was answered; and at 7°45 a Turkish official 
(Colonel) and the Kaimakam’s Secretary came on board, and requested that. the 
bombarding would cease for fourteen hours to wait the Pasha’s reply. This J 
(id not consider myself justified in doing, and refused; allowing them to get on 
shore again, when | sent the bonts away to destroy the buggalows. Two cutters 
from the “Lady Canning” assisted, and with an occasional gun from the two 
ships, Lieutenant Armstrong, to whom I had entrusted this service, carried my 
intentions out successfully, by burning and sinking fourteen or fifteen of these 
craft in the course of a couple of hours, 

LG. Ata quarter past 1] a Secretary of the Town Council came on board, 
and brought a letter from Namick Pasha, acknowledging the receipt of my 
despatch of the 24rd; but not considering it satisfactory or decisive, | could not 
consent to its request, and replied accordingly. This Secretary requested I 
would give a written promise not to fire on any mosques, fortifications, hospitals, 
or public building; I declined, but in arrangement for communication which | 
sent toin to the Kaimakam, promised as far as possible to respect Government 
property and hospitals, where they were to hoist the colours. At 345 r.a., 
this officer having landed, I opened fire on the town again with shot, shell, and 
rockets, ceasing at 4. 

17. At 9 a.m, the next morning, the 26th, [ again opened fire with shot 
and shell, continuing only for ten minutes; and learnt m the afternoon, from a 
Turkish officer who had arrived from Meeca, that we had done much damage in 
the town, and driven all the inhabitants out of it to the surrounding villages. 
This. officer brought a letter from the Kaimakam, stating that the bearer spoke 
French, and was authorised to treat with me on the part of his Excelleney. He 
had left Mecea before the news of bombardment had arrived, but met it on the 
road, and now requested that I would suspend further proceedings. In reply, | 
referred him to my letters to the Pasha, and until those demands were complied 
with I should go on. 

He had no authority to aceede to them; and he stated the Turks, from 
the smallness of their force, could hardly hold the country; that if the 
bombarding continued, the Arabs would rise and murder them all, as they could 
not convince them they were not in league with us: for which reason the 
Kaimakam would not come off, nor hoist any fing on his quarters. Considering 
this might be one cause for their not complying with my demands for the 
execution of the murderers, I addressed a proclamation to the inhabitants of 
Jeddah, with which the officer left the ship; and on arrival on shore, after 
allowing full time to get out of the town again, I sent the boats inside the reefs 
to open fire when within range. Sire 

18. Lieutenant Armstrong, senior of this ship, conducted this duty most 
satisfactorily, leading the boats in amongst the shoals (at the best of times a 
most: difficult business), and taking up a position of from between 1,100 and 
1,200 yards from the fort, and throwing shot, shell, and rockets into the town 
with good effect, returning to the ship about an hour after dark, 

The next morning, the heat being so intense, | determined on mooring the 
ship to the southern part of the harbour, where we might get more the benefit 
of the wind, and lay in deeper water, and to act as cireumstances would direct 
in further bombarding; for the town would still be within range of the guns. 
Accordingly she was moved, and shortly after anchoring ight large buggulows 
came in from Suez with troops. 

20, These troops left Suez a few days before the “ Cyclops,” and had been 
daily expected since our arrival. ‘They were Albanians (Bashi-Dozouks), and, 
not to delay their landing, | signalled to the shore a wish to communicate, and 
stated verbally that 1 would allow thirty-six hours for the purpose. The 
Kaimakam requested, by the officer that came off, that 1 would impress on the 
commanding otlicer of these troops the necessity of keeping them in order, and

The Indian ships also required water, and I directed them also to be

22. On the morning of the 28th the Pasha arrived, announcing it by 
letter, and that he will not fail to come off and confer with me whenever | 
will appoint a time. I did so by return messenger, saving, any day his Excel- 
lency thought proper; but if he could arrange it for to-morrow, about noon, I 
should be happy to see him. 

23, Accordingly, on the 29th, his Excellency Mehemet Namick Pasha eame 
on board, and had along interview with me. He dwelt with much earnestness on 
the difficulty of the position he was in, saying how impossible it was for hin to 
execute those he had in confinement without orders from Constantinople: such 
an act would be bis utter rnin, and might even cost him his life. He stated 
that many pilgrims were daily arriving from Mecca, subjects not only of Turkey, 
but France (Algerines), in fact, people from all parts of the world; and also one 
of the widows of the ex-Sultan Mahomed, on her way from Mecca. None of these 
had been concerned in the events of the 15th of June, but the fears of nnother 
bombardment detained them on their way, causing much suffering and privation ; 
also uncertainty of being able to get the necessary provisious for their voyage at 
Jeddah. He also ndverted to the unworthiness of a British man-of-war firing on 
an unresisting town, and destroying a few harmless bugenlows. ‘To this [replied 
that I had come here in compliance with orders to demand the punishment of 
ofa set of ruthless murderers; failing this, 1 was to bombard, which I hoped 
would not only strike terror into the hearts of the aseassins, but prevent the 
recurrence of such horrible atrocities. And the same with the buggulows: he 
could not know how fully armed they were in every particular; and, as it was 
my intention to take these arms away from them, | would hand them over to 
him, requesting therefore that he would send an officer in the boats on this 
service, ind to reecive them. 

And now, taking all the circumstances of the case into consideration, and 
forthe sake of humanity, 1 told his Exeelleney that I would discontinue any 
further acts of hostility until Monday noon, the 2n:l; and the interview ended 
without his having aceeded to my demands, as far as the murderers were 
concerned; but all clse he was ready to comply with: promised to send coals 
off to the “ Lady Canning; would receive all arms taken out ol the buggalows, 
sending an officer to accompany our boats on the service. The shipping were 
acquainted with thisextension of time, and, through them, the merchants on 
shore under British protection. 

84. On the morning of the 80th the merchant-ships commenced hauling out 
ta the fairway, and, i accordanee with my intention, the pinnice was sent away 
to disarm the buggalows, By the evening, a large collection was arranged on the 
quarter-deck ; iron guns, of various calibre, mnuskets, matchlocks, and sabres of 
all sorts and sizes, and delivered aver to the Captuin of the Port. Large stores 
of powder were started overboard, Some, however, I found out belonged to boats 
of the Persian Gulf, though under Arab colours, bearing a pass from British 
authorities; to these their arms were returned, 

95, The Pasha sent off the coals to the * Lady Canning 7” and Licutenunt

sailed for Yermbo about noon of the Bist. One of the Princes died at Mecea, 
and it was reported that cholera had broken out there amongst the pilgrims, 
but it was subsequently denied, 1 waited on the Princes before they lett.

27. On the morning of the 2nd, the Kaimakam was sent off by the Pasha

29, Directly she had anchored, a boat was sent to board her: soon returnin 
with an order from Viee-Admiral Fanshawe, inclosing the two telegrams Pacaivad 
by him from their Lordships on the same day, the 15th of July, but at different 
hours. 

30. ‘The boarding-officer reported that the steamer was the “ Gabarri ;” had 
on board Ismail Pasha, with 480 troops, and that he would be happy to come on 
board to confer with me, if I wished. In reply, I sent the boat back imme- 
diately, and stated that, if he would do ine the honour, she was at his disposal. 
Accordingly, at 440 p.a,, this officer returned in the pinnace. 

3], lamail Pasha informed me that he had come express from Constantinople, 
with full powers to act in the best manner to satisfy the just demands of Great 
Britain and France, assuring me that it was the wish of the Sultan to act fully 
in concert with the two Powers for the punishment of the guilty, and he hoped 
that all would now be settled satisfictorily. 

49, On Ismail Pasha reaching the shore he was saluted by the fort with 
seventeen guns; and the next morning, the rd, I received a letter from Namick 
Pasha, saying that he was now empowered to act summarily, and satisly my 
demands ; requesting L would point out a spot where the execution should take 
place, and it should be carried out directly he could make the necessary arrange- 
ments. 

33. To this replied by letter; and considering how requisite it was that 
all who were now here, and present when the murders took place, should be 
witnesses to this stern act of justice (the ships, too, all Indian), I pointed out a 
place in the harbour on one of the dry reefs, where it could be-seen by them as 
well as the inhabitants of Jeddah. ‘Therefore, at sunrise on the morning of the 
Sth, the armed boats’ crews of this ship, a boat's crew from each of the 
merchant-ships, besides the guard of Albanians, assembled on the spot, and the 
murderers were executed by beheading, 

84. Lieutenant Armstrong commanded the boats, and on return to the 
ship reported to me that only cleven were executed, making, with the one who 
died in the prison, twelve, out ot the sixteen confined; when [ saluted the 
Turkish flag with twenty-one guns, as an acknowledgment of the justice done 
on the murderers of the Representatives of England and France, which was 
returned with alike number from the fort; the “Cyclops” flying the British 
and French ensigns from the main. Addressing a letter to his Excellency stating 
this, and requesting to know the reason why the four persons were spared, he 
sent me a satisfactory reply, intimating that by the law they were not proved 
cuilty of murder, though having taken part in the rising, but would be sent to 
Constantinople, there to be dealt with; aud the Kaimakam assuring me, on his 
last visit to the ship, that neither the Pasha nor himself would spare their exer-

tions in having others arrested who might be suspected of any participation in 
the afiair, The authorities had the names of many persons who were now

suddenly arrest them on their return to the town, ‘The inclosed list is a return 
of the sixteen criminals, with the particulars concerning them, 

35. This business having now been so far brought to a close, | decided on 
leaving for Suez, more particularly as numbers of pilgrims have left for ths 
port, it would be well fora ship of war to be here as a check on any disturbance 
likely to arise on their arrival, Moreover, our sick list was daily increasing from. 
the éffects of such a climate, which doubtless would be getting worse from the 
decay of many human bodies floating about the harbour who had shed, anid 
been thrown overboard from the pilgrim ships. 

36. Lintimated my intention to the Pasha, stating that 1 would carry any 
despatches for his Government; and left with lim wu Tetter for Commoilore 
Watson, or any naval officer that might arrive at Jeddah, sequainting ther with 
the position of affairs; and steamed out of the port on the morning of the 7th 
of August, 

37, In carrying out this business, my endeavour was to impress on the 
people of Jeddah that 1 had been sent to punish, and thar they could not 
eommit such deeds without paying for them. For T cannot banish the idea that 
they have fancied from their position, and almost considered in the character af 
a holy city, from its nearness to Mecea, that they might do many things with 
impunity. I trust this will be a lesson they will not soon forget ; and although 
it would bea work of time to raze the town, yet they cannot but know how 
areatly they can be distressed by stopping all the supplies from the seaward 
ports on which they are so dependent. Gun-boats will be the best vessels for 
service in this sea; and 1 strongly recommend, for their Lordships’ considera- 
tion, that two, at least, should always be in it. 

38. The bombarding happened at a time when no pilgrims were in the 
town; and they will be able to carry to all parts of the Mahometan world how 
England and France avenge the murder of their subjects and Representatives, 
and also how the hostilities ceased as much for their sakes as for other const- 
derations. And taking into account the state of affairs in Tndia it was one great 
reason why [ insisted on the execution taking place in sight of the ships. 

39, Ismail Pasha’s endeavours to get all satisfactorily arranged appeared to 
be increasing; he wrote to ask whether [ considered the Kaimakam (brahim 
Aga) and other officers had performed their duty. How to hear testimony on 
this subject’ I hardly knew, more than the first-named officer, 1 thought, had 
done all he could to quell the rising; and his endeavour to protect the French 
Consul, the eare he took of his (the Consul’s) daughter, and the surviving 
Christians, until given up to me, were commendable. The troops he had were 
miserably few, not more 100 at the most; and what could they do against 
thousands? Others I know nothing of, except Yusuf Aga, the Captain’ of the 
Port, whose conduct throughout from the first of our visits to Jeddah has been 
everything that could be wished, ready at all times to be of service, and in any 
way required. , 

40, In conclusion, 1 cannot too strongly speak of Mr. Vice-Consul Calvert's 
services, both as an interpreter and adviser; they were invaluable, and 1 could 
not have done without him, for all the correspondence from the authorities was 
in Turkish, and he fully put me in possession of the sense of the letters ; and the 
conduct of my officers and crew throughout has been most priiseworthy, for 
working under a burning sun, with only a knowledge that they were inflicting 
punishment for the cowardly and brutal murder of fellow-Chiristions, some ton 
having been their shipmates, sustained them at such atime, But Lieutenant 
Armstrong, the senior of the ship, [ beg most particularly to recommend. to 


their Lordships’ consideration, not only in this affair, but throughout the time of 


commission. His exertions have been unceasing to get the crew in good 
training, and at this particular time not only had charge of the bouts’ operations, 
but was in the cutter, and accompanied me in my gig on the morning at the 
[6th, when we had to force our way out from the town; and although: se 
attacked, his encouragement of the men and show of forbearance could not fail 
of mecting my warmest commendation. 

41. 1 had prepared a letter for the Commodore to meet him at Aden, to. be 
sent off by the first mail leaving after my arrival; but she passed us in Mi Gulf,

Inclosure 2 in No, 148. 
Acting Consul-General Green to Captain Pullen. 


Sir, Alerandria, July 16, 1858. 


AS it is of the utmost importance that [should be aware of the nature of 
your orders, which could only not have been sent under flying seal to me by 
inadvertence, [ have opened the inclosed despatch addressed to you by Admiral 
Fanshawe, and which has just this moment been handed to me by Captain 
Pechell, of Her Majesty's ship ‘* Wanderer.” 

The important nature of its contents induces me to require of the Egyptian 
Riese Administration the means of forwarding it to you without a moment’s 

elay. 

The most singular intelligence from Suez has reached this, during the last 
twenty-four hours, as to the approach of armed boats, &c., from J eddah, 

Not having heard from you, or Vice-Consul West, on the subject, no doubt 
there is no truth in it; but should any such boats be navigating, with hostile 
purposes, there can be no question as to the way in which they should be 
treated by you: that is to say, as pirates. 

I have kept a copy of your instructions in case of any accident happening 
to the messenger by which I send this. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) J. GREEN, 


P.S.—I have decided on confiding this despatch to the charge of Mr. Vice- 
Consul Calvert, who has also charge of the despatch for the Commodore of Her 
Majesty's ships in the Kast Indies. 

J. G,

Inclosure 3 in No, 148. 


Captain Pullen to the Commanders of the Peninsular and Oriental steamers 
“Candia” and * Suez." 


Sir, * Cyclops,’ Suez, July 17, 1858. 

YOU will, doubtless, have heard intelligence of the late events at Jeddah, 
and of the barbarous murder of the English and French Consuls there. More 
or less there are several reports in circulation affecting the safety of the Chris- 
tian residents in Mahometan towns. 

It is my ay to acquaint you also that a report has eained circulation that 
thirty-five buggalows, armed, and manned with a large number of Arabs, are 
proceeding to Suez with hostile intentions ; and 1 even apprehend they may 
attach any ship at anchor, 

Vor the safety, therefore, of the ship under your command, you will be 
prepared to defend her, or to render assistance to others; and in the event of

your falling in with these vessels, and being assured, by their numbers, of their 
illegal purposes, you will use all aggressive acts against them, destroying both 
men and ships to the best of your ability, and you will report to me, fully, any- 
thing you may do in reference to this direction. ; 
| have, &c.

Inclosure 4 in No. 145. 


The Political Agent at Aden to Captain Pullen. 


Sir, July 5, 1858. 

YOUR letters to my address, dated the 23rd ultimo, with inclosures, 
reached me yesterday by the barque ‘* Coquette Dale.” 

9. It happened that a ship was in our outer harbour on the point of 
departure for Bombay, I instantly sent orders to detain her to convey my 
despatches. She sailed in the evening, carrying your letters, and a request 
from me.to the Government of Bombay that an. efficient war-steamer may he 
sent to Jeddah as soon as possible, 

3. This is all that is in my power, for I have no ship of war available; the 
steamer “ Laily Canning” is not efficient a5 a vessel of war, but she may he 
useful to vou; she ought, as fam informed, to have arrived at Jeddah about 
the 29th ultimo. 

4, The Honourable Company's sloop " Elphinstone ” will probably arrive 
at Massowah about this date. Captain Frushard, hearing the state of affairs 
at Jeddah, will, no doubt, instantly proceed thither, 

5, The Honourable Company's schooner “ Mahi’ 1s here ; I would dispatch 
her to your orders, but she, unfortunately, is unfit for sea. 

6. M. Henri Lambert, the Consular Agent of France at Aden, procecds 
immediately by buggalow to Jeddah; I have requested him to communicate 
with Captain Frashard, if he should be able to do so. 

7. 1 do not perceive that any further meastres can be adopted from this 
quarter, It is clear from the narrative of your proceedings, that British honour 
and jnterests are safe in your hands, and that your judgment will guide you 
rightly in the difficult position in which you are placed by the tragedy of the 
14th ultimo; but, in stating this impression to the Government of Bombay, 1 
have added that you may require support, and, therefore, it is desirable that an 
eficient war-steamer be dispatched immediately. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) W M. COGHLAN.

Inclosure 6 in No, 148, 
Captain Pullen to Namick Pasha. 


ixcellence, “Cyclops,” Rade de Djeddah, le 23 Juillet, 1858. 

EN vous annoncant mon retour dans cette rade, il est de mon devoir de 
vous prévenir que je viens maintenant, non seulement en ma qualité de Capitaine 
Wun bitiment de guerre de Sa Majesté Britannique, mais comme le Représentant 
de Angleterre, muni de pouyoirs d'agir énergiguement, et de demander en son 
nom, et en celui de la France, la punition des Miches et brutaux assassins qui 
massacrerent les Consuls Anglais et Francais et autres personnes dans la nuit du 
15 Juin passé, 

En un mot, je demande qu'une justice ample. et sévére soit exercée, tant 
sur ceux dont les mains ont été actuellement trempées du sang de nos com- 
patriotes, que sur les instigateurs de ces horribles atrocilés, 

2. Je viens done réitérer les demandes di faites aux autorités de Djeddah 
pour la punition des coupables, et afin de m/assurer de leur accomplissement, 
jindiquerai plus tard un endroit see sur un des récifs dans le port, que jinsiste 
devra @tre le lieu du supplice. 

3. Je ne doute pas que votre Excellence connaisse les auteurs et instigateurs 
du massacre ; mais avant de passer la peine de mort sur qui que ce soit, il faut que 
des mesures solent prises pour identifier les individus, afin que les innocents ne 
souffrent pas au lieu des coupables. 

4. Si mes demandes ne sont pas satisfaites, dans un espace de. temps 
raisonnable, espace dont jo me considére seul le juge, et qui ne doit pas dépasser 
trente-six heures A dater du débarquement du cette dépéche, je serait contraint 
davoir recours aux dernidres extrémités, et de mettre en exécution dans toute 
leur étendu Jes ordres de mon Gouvernement ; et comme le bruit a couru que des 
embarcations armées s‘équippent, ou se sont équippées dans ce port pour se 
rendre A Suez ou 4 d’autres endroits of il pourrait y avoir des habitants Chrétiens, 
je ne permettrai le départ d’aucune embarcation jusqu’ ce que ma demande ait 
été satisiite, 

5. Votre Excellence est done price den prévenir immeédiatement tous ceux 
que cela pourra intéresser, et si un bitiment ou bitcan quelconque tentera de 
désobéir cet ordre, i dater d'une heure aprés le débarquement de cette lettre, je le 
forcerai de se retirer ou je le coulerai. De méme, si des batiments ou des 
embarcations en certains nombres oseront s'approcher des hatiments de guerre 
Britannique, je les envisagerai comme une force hostile, et je les traiteral comme 
telle, Je dois, cependant, observer que cette mesure ne s'appliquera pas & une 
communication entre la ville et les bitiments de guerre par des embarcations 
isolées, et afin qu'il n'y ait pas de méprise, je vous prierais d'arborer de jour 
le pavillon de guerre Ture sur la chaloupe qui pourrait me porter des communi- 
cations de votre part, et de montrer, de nuit, une lumiere. 

G. Je prie votre Excellence de croire que je ne suis pas venu ici avec des 
intentions hostiles envers le Gouvernement de la Sublime Porte, mais pour 
demander la justice de vous; et tant que ies fortifications ne me molesteront pas 
dang l’exécution de mes ordres, je les respecterai, mais 4 la premiére hostilite de 
leur part, je dirigerai mes canons contre elles, 

7, La compensation des pertes oceasionnées aux sujets Anglais et Francais, 
est une question qu'il ne m'appartient pas d'entamer; c'est un sujet qui sera 
décidé plus tard par les Gouvernements dela Grande Bretagne et de la France ; 
mais j'insiste, tres formellement, sur l'exécution dé ma présente demande, 

8. Je prie votre Excellence de vouloir bien me répondre en Francais ou en 
Italien, et d'une manitre décisive, 

Agréez, &e,

Inclosure 7 in No. 148. 
Captain Pullen to the Commander of the “ Lady Canning.” 


Sir, “Cyclops,” Jeddah, July 23, 1858. 

IN pursuance of instructions from the Honourable Company’s Political 
Agent at Aden, you are herelfy requested and directed to place yourself and the 
ship under your command, under my orders, to assist me in my determination to 
carry out the orders of Her Majesty’s Government in obtaining ample justice 
from the murderers of the English and French Consuls, and other Christians at 
this place on the night of the 15th ultimo. 

I have related to you the whole of the circumstances, and also read to you 
the instructions under which I am-acting. 

It is stated that thirty-five armed buggalows are fitting, or have fitted out 
at this port, intending to attack Sucz. a 

There is also a report that an attack on the “Cyclops” 1s, or was, I 
contemplation ; you will therefore fire into, and sink, any boats approaching you. 

You will proceed to the Northern Canal, and prevent any boats leaving the 
port, firing into and sinking any who attempt it. 

Should my demands not be complied with, [ shall hort the signal of 
Marryatt’s code 207, upon which you will endeavour to burn, sink, or destroy, 
every buggalow in this harbour; the boats of Uns ship will be sent with guns 
and rockets to assist in this operation, br, 

Having accomplished this serviee, the destruction of the town will be the 
next object ; in this, however, I must depend upon my own guns, those in the 
“ Lady Canning” not being of sufficient size to reach the place. :. 

It may be possible that the ships here muy open fire upon the “ Cyclops 
or the “ Lady Canning?’ in such case it will be your duty to destroy them, 
Any signal made to the “ Lady Canning” will have over it the Union Jack, and 
Marryatt’s code will be invariably used. A prompt attention to signals is 
desirable. 

Lam, &c. —s 
(Signed) W, I. 5. PULLEN,

| The origin of this massacre appears to be the seizure of a ship, and 
imprisoning the owner of her. About five hours after these events took place, 
outbreak occurred. Amongst the persons you have mentioned, Said Cagalit 
and Sheikh Ali are not known; as for the others, they ure amongst the well-

known and respectable persons of the country, and are members of the Council, 
atid when the people rose to commit these deeds, Abdallah Massif was in his 
house, and the others were with the Kaimakam, Sheikh Abdalgafar with Said 
Abdallah Baharoum were sent down to the wharf, te prevent the people going 
to the ship, Abdallah Moutessib was sent by the Kaimakam to Mr. Vice- 
Consul Page's, to prevent the crowd from hauling down the British flag: before 
he could reach the Consulate the crowd fell upon him, and commenced beating 
him; he was taken home in a dangerous state, and remained so for some days. 

The Cudri Mollah is the Chief Magistrate here, and did not leave his house 
during the disturbances. Abdallah Massif is a very old man, and quite incapable 
of meddling in such affairs; he is a very charitable, hospitable man; he is one 
of the members of the Council, and his infirmities often prevent him from 
attending to his duties, On the mght of the massacre he saw the erowd 
pouring into Hadji Furudj Yusu’s house, which is opposite his own ; he imme- 
diately collected his family and friends, and told the crowd that Hadji Furudj 
Yusu was his friend, and he would protect him. 

No one knew anything of the affair, and no one. anticipated such a 
proceeding; and the Government knew nothing of it: if they had, they would 
have given notice cf it. 

Had I had any suspicion that the persons you mentioned were implicated, 
I would have immediately imprisoned them, without taking into consideration 
their rank, 

The daughter of the French Consul said, that since Abdallah Massif had 
the power to rescue Hadji Furudj Yusu, he might also have been able to rescue 
her family; and M. Emerat told me that some of the persons above men- 
tioned had the Christians. Had Abdallah Massif not wished to reseue the 
Christians, why did he rescue Forudj Yusu? The faet is, Abdallah Massif's 
house was so far from the seenes, that he could not do anything, the rising 
being so sudden. M. Emerat’s remark was only the result of the feeling for 
the moment, made under an excited state. 

T have made inquiries, both privately and openly, und feel satisfied that 
these persons are not implicated in the murders. If you do not believe my 
assertions, it is easy for o Commissioner to be sent from Constantinople to make 
inquiries. 

According to your request I send you a list of persons who are imprisoned, 
with their professions. Having been absent when the disturbance took place, 
the Kaimakam can better give you any details you may require. 

(Seal of Namick Pasha.)

Inclosure 19 in No. 148, 
Namick Pasha to Captain Pullen. 


(Free translation from the Turkish.) 


IN reply to your letter of the Sth instant, 1 beg to forward the reasons 
why four of the prisoners charged with the murder of Haevaja Sava’ have not 
been executed. 

Salim Bunaja’s slave, Bilal, and Mehmet Noovar, were not the actual 
murderers of Sava, they having only used sticks, or bludgeons. 

Abdullah bin Ali Afesh, and Mustafa bin Dervish Kharad, had no proof 
of their having been the murderers of a Christian, as they made use of clubs ; 
the murder was committed by a Bedouin with a pistol, and he escaped. 

According to Mahometan law the above four prisoners are criminals of the 
second degree of guilt, which is not punishable by death. They are to be sent 
to the galleys at Constantinople. | 

(Seal of Namick Pasha.)

No, 155, 
The Queen's Advocate ta the Earl of Malmeshury.—(Received September 11.) 


My Lord, Doctors’ Commons, September 8, 1858. 

T AM honoured with your Lordship’s commands, signified in Mr, Fitz- 
gerald’s letter of the 21st August ultimo, stating that he was directed to transmit 
to me a letter from Messrs. Neroutsos and Co., containing replies to the several 
questions in my report of the 31st of July, respecting their claim to compensa- 
tion on account of the late outrages at Jeddah; and to request that | would 
take this letter, together with the former papers, into consideration, and report 
to your Lordship my opinion thereupon. 

In obedience to your Lordships commands, I have taken these papers into 
consideration, and have the honour to report— 

That Mr, Neroutsos, the principal in this firm, should be requested to 
forward a copy of his certificate of naturalization, and a correct description of 
the names and nationalities of his partners. 

It is by no means certain, although very probable, that Messrs. Neroutsos 
have lost the 1,500L, the proceeds of goods sold at Jeddah, which they state 
was in the hands of their agent (Aristide Democides) supposed to have been 
murdered at Jeddah, They should, at all events, satisfy your Lordship, by 
reasonable proof, and not by mere conjectural assertions, that this is the fact, 
and should show that their agent had this money in his possession at the time 
of the massacre. 

Upon their doing this, by stating all particulars, and furnishing copies of 
the communications from Jeddah, upon which they rely for information as to 
the facts which they state (viz., the sale of their goods and the receipt by their 
agent of the money in question), their claim may be considered in common with 
that of others. 

The invoices and bills of lading of the goods which they offer are of no use ; 
these goods had been converted into cash, and it is this cash which they claim. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) J. D. HARDING.

My Lord, Bludew of Damascus, Auqust 21, 1858. 
I HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that the public mind has

this affair was, that the woman’s husband was murdered, some months ago, in a 
mysterious manner; his body was found, early one morning, in a sechided lane 
among the gardens, with the head cut off and carried away; but neither arms, 
clothes, nor purse were taken, and his horse was grazing near the spot. 

All inquiry as to the author of the murder was fruitless; but, after the 
dragoman was discovered in the house of the woman, the Koords declared that 
they could prove that he was the instigator of the crime. The dragoman was 
arrested about midnight, and imprisoned in the Serai, and next morning the 
Pasha gave notice to the Prussian Consul of the fact, and offered to send him to 
the Consulate, but the Consul said that he might remain in prison, ‘Twelve 
hours after the Consul claimed the dragoman, but was informed by the Pasha 
that it was no longer possible to send him to the Consulate; for his Excellency 
feared that he would either be murdered by the infuriated populace on the road, 
or, if he got there safe, the Consulate might be attacked. 

The whole Koordish population, armed, bad surrounded the Sera, and 
clamoured violentiy to have the man given up to them. 

The authorities were perplexed what course to pursue; and the European 
Consuls were invited to meet them and the Conneil to consider the matter, No 
Consul attended on the invitation. ‘The French sent word that he had no right 
to sit in judgment ona colleague, but that, if his opinion were desired in a 
private unofficial manner, he would wait on the Pasha, whieh offer was accepted. 

The Pasha admitted the Consul’s right to have the dragoman delivered up, 
but he feared the result, After several messages between the authoritivs and the 
Consul, it was arranged that the dragoman should, in the night, he conveyed, 
under an escort, from the Pasha, accompanied by a cavass of the Prussian 
Consul, to Beyrout. 

When the Koords next morning discovered that the dragoman had been sent 
away, they dispatched cighty horsemen in pursuit, to murder him on the way; 
fortunately he was taken by the road to Sidon, while: his pursuers followed the 
direct road, and thus he escaped, The Vali spread a report that he had sent 
the man into exile, which appeased the natives, and the Koords, finding that 
they were satistied, gradually calmed down, 

It was the assassination laid to the drmgoman’s charge which caused the 
violence of the excitement: although he is a notorious debauchee, he is not 
believed to have heen accessory to the murder, und ifthe Koords had possessed 
any clear evidence, it would have been brought forward at the time; but it was 
easy to suborn false witnesses to swear to the guilt of the dragoman. Ile is a 
Jew, and was, a few years since, a domestic servant: he is now reputed rich, 
notwithstanding he has squandered much money in his lieentious indulgences ; 
he was not a person to have been placed ina post of trast, such as dragoman to 
a Murepean Consul, which he has grossly abused, 

Had either the Vali or the Military Pasha possessed energy, they could 
have easily arrested the excitement at its commencement; but they cannot, in 
this instanee, be reproached with more than weakness. “Uhis quality, however, 
affects their power of governing well, such a population as that of Syria; and 
when to this is added in ordinate and undisguised venality, they are regarded with 
contempt and dislike, so that even a trifling cause of discontent might be followed 
by serious results. 

Some of the fanatics tried to get up a memorial of their grievances agninst 
the Christians; but the principal Beys, Aghas, and religious Sheiks, whom they 
consulted, seriously advised them ta remain quict, as, if anything happened to 
the European Consuls, or their subjects, their Governments would not hold the 
Sultan responsible, as his weakness was so well known; but the punishment 
would be inflicted on themselves; this prudent discouragement caused the 
memorial to be suppressed, For some days the Christians were much alirmed, 
an did not venture out of their houses,

No. 158. 
Consul Brant to the Earl of Malmesbury.—- (Received September 15.) 


(No, 12.) 
My Lord, Bludau of Damascus, August 28, 1858. 

1 HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that the news of the 
bombardment of Jeddah produced a feeling of depression, rather than of excite- 
ment, ameng the Mussulmans. The authorities, however, seem to have thought 
it prudent to disclaim their belief in it, as they pretended not to have received 
the news; but the intelligence spread immediately throughout the city: and it 
is probable that not a person was ignorant of the event an hour after the post 
arrived, 

I think that the public tranquillity will not be disturbed, unless, indeed, 
some new and strong motive should oceasion it, in which case, the authorities 
could hardly be relied on for its suppression; the Vali being wanting in 
decision, and the Mushir apparently not trusting his troops, in the event of their 
being called upon to act against the Mussulman population. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) JAS, BRANT,

The Secretary to the Admiralty to Mr. Filzgerald.—( Received September 25.) 


Sir, “ait Admtralty, September 18, 1858. 
wo H reference to your letter of the 17th instant, stating, by desire of the 
Earl of Malmesbury, that Her Majesty's Government consider that Captain 
Pullen, and the senior naval officer in command of Her Majesty's ships off 

Jeddah, should be instructed not to have recourse to anv act of hostility, exeept 
in self-defence, without first referring to Her Majesty's Government for instruc- 
tions, and that you had conveyed such opinion to Captain Pullen by the mail of 
the 17th instant ; and further requesting that my Lords Commissioners of the 
Admiralty would address a similar instruction’ to the senior oflicer; [am 
commanded by their Lordships to acquaint you that, in compliance with the 
request of Lord Malmesbury, orders have been sent to the senior officer at 
Jeddah, not to engage in any act of hostility, except in self-defence, without first 
referring to Her Majesty’s Government for instructions. My Lords have alsa 
sent @ copy of these orders to the senior officer at Aden, in case the vessels 
ordered to Aden and Jeddah should not have lett the former place, 

My Lords are reluctantly compelled to again draw Lord Malmesbury’s 
attention to the novel and inconvenient practice of forwarding orders, direct 
from the office of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to a naval officer in 
active command of one of Her Majesty's ships of war under the orders of the 
Board of Admiralty. 

_, The order “not to engage in any act of hostility, except in self-defence, 
without first referring to Her Majesty's Government,” was one which, in their 
Lordships opinion, should only have been sent to Cuptain Pullen, by their 
Lordships, after timely information had been given to them of the wishes of the 
Secretary of State for Foreien Affairs, 

_ Captain Pullen, though acting as Diplomatic Commissioner under the diree- 
tion of the Seeretary of State for Foreign Affairs, is an officer for whose conduct 
my Lords are justly lield responsible ; and they consider that publie inconve- 
mence would be oceasioned, and the direet and immediate responsibility of naval 
officers to them would be weakened, by their receiving orders from other 
Departments of the Government, without such orders being transmitted through 
the Board of Admiralty. ; 

_. My Lords would further remark that, in consequence of the late hour last 
night, at which the letter conveying the request of Lord Malmesbury arrived at 
this office, the orders of Captain Pullen might very probably have reached him 
through the Foreign Office, by the mail leaving last night, whilst either no 
Instructions or contradictory ones might have been sent by their Lordships. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) W, G. ROMAINE.

THE first part of this despatch relates to the movements and embarkation 
of the troops. ] 

[ beg to report, for your information, that I found Jeddah quict. His 
Excellency Ismail Pasha had left, a tew hours before my arrival, in one of the 
Medjulie steamers, for Yembo, taking with him thirty-six prisoners, of low rank, 
charged with having been implicated in the late massacre at Jeddah, He may 
be expeeted at Suez in the course of two or three days. = 

At Hodeida, where the “ Feraze" and“ Zenobia” touched on their way up 
to Jeddah, it was publicly stated that the man chiefly implicated—in fict, the 
instigator of the late outrages —was perfectly well known, but that, having wealth 
at his disposal, he had been able to obtain the protection of the Turkish autho- 
nities. 

The Greek merchant Theotini, of the Jeddah-house of Sava, told me this, 
assuring me that the pilerims that were daily arriving from the North spoke of 
as an undoubted fact, and even named the sum for which he purchased his 
immunity, This man is Abdullah Furrau, who commenced life, as his name 
implies, as a baker,has risen to be the Mohtessib of Jeddah, and, I firmly believe, 
took advantage of the excitement occasioned by the hauling down the Turkish

colours on bourd the “ Eranece” to gratify the bitter enmity he had towards the

the Consuls! and, though probubly not present in person at the massnere, it 
would appear that a comsiderable portion of the wealth in Thoma’s shop found 
its way to the Mohitessib’s toflers. 

[was glad to find, on my arrival at Jeddah, that this individual had been

ae Therapia, September 20, 1858. 
| HAD the honour of receiving your telegram of the 13th instant, and the 

immediate veply which 1 gave thereto was probably sutticient to explain the 
nature of the mistake which appears in some wily or other: to have occured 
and, at all events, I think it better to take this opportunity of preentid . pon 
Lordship with more ample ia a to the subject to which your Jordsnip s 
Jecraphic communication reterred, eee 
pec ete ufter the news of the massacre at Jeddith reached Constantinople, 
MI. Thouvenel spoke to me os to the widvisability ol addressing to the orte, Ni 
addition to the communications of a general nature which we had een \ me ts 
a geries of specitic demands, and he communicated to me a paper he had drawn 
up in the shape of Articles, for this purpose, 


I] 


Had the news of the events which had taken place at Jeddah reached the 
respective Embassies at Constantinople betore it had reached London and Paris, 
I inight have thought that [and M. de Thouvenel could, upon our own respon- 
sibility, have, without inconvenience, made such demands as he sugested, and 
even have adopted the form for doing so, which he had chosen; always leaving 
the sum to be claimed, in ‘the way of indemnity, undetermined, wntil the lnases 
which had taken place had been ascertained. But, as it so happened that it was 
through our respective Governments that we were ourselves informed of what 
had taken place at Jeddah, it appeared to meé that we could not advisedly enter 
into the detailed treatment of a question with which our Governinents might, at 
that very moment, be oceupied ; and on which it was possible that, with respect 
to details, they might adopt diflerent views from those which we individually 
entertained. 

M. de Thouvenel agreed, upon consideration, as to the soundness of this 
opinion, and the paper he had drawn up was laid on one side. But inmediately 
alter this decision had been taken by us, a note from the Porte, offering the 
Governments of France and England full and ample repanition, wits presented 
to the two Embassies. This note created a new state of things, and offered a 
motive for M. de Thouvenel and myself to point out, though in a general 
manner, the particular interpretation which we were disposed to give to il, since 
we telit thus beable to inform our respective Governments whether the Porte 
assented or objected to that interpretation. 
| Hence the document inclosed in iy So. £8. "That document speaks for 
itself: nor could any mistake concerning it have arisen, hail not M. Thouvenel 
in his communications with his own Government, sent home, not only a copy 
of the piper that hid been written and delivercd to the Porte, but also a copy 
al the paper which he bad drawn up, but whieh tad never been made use df, 
fi, is: true that in forwarding this latter, M. Thouvenel observed that it had not 
been adopted, But I conelude that this observation escaped Count Walewski’s 
notice ; and! that misunderstanding the real character of the inelosure trans 
mitted to him, he was Jed to believe that to be «valid and official document 
Which was in reality a plece af waste paper, 

I go into all these particulars, in order that vour Lordship should see 
clearly what appears to me the origin of the misconception on the part of the 
French Govertiment, to which your communication of the both allies; but, at 
the same time, Linay state that the note which wis subsequently written by 
M. de Thouvenel and myself contains all the principles, although it omits the 
details, which M. Thouvenel’s first note set forth; and DP think your Lordship 
will agree with me that, with respect to those details, we could not properly 
énter inte them, when the course whieh [er Majesty's Government imght take 
in regard to them was not known to us, and when even the precise nature ot 
the occurrences at Jeddah was not fully Known to Her Majesty's Government. 

Alter recent occurrences, it appears to me, | countess, that we should be 
dealing horshly with the Ottoman Government, and with the town of Jeddah 
itselt, were we to exact any indemnity in the way of punishments but it is 
still undoubtedly justifinble for Her Majesty’s Governinent t6 insist upon an 
indemnity in the way of compensation for loss sustiined, and, if the twa 
Governments adopt this course, | think your Lordship will deem, as | do, that 
the amount of compensation to be required can only be justly determined by 
the Commissioners who have been sent to Jeddah, and who will hive tir better 
opportunities than any persons not on the spot can have, for establishing whiat 
that amount should be,
