No. 200. 


The Kurloaf Malmesbury to Karl Cowley. 
(No, 929.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, October 14, 1858, 

YOUN Excellency will have observed, in Sir Henry Bulwer’s despatch 
No. 208 of the 20th of September, which passed through your hands a few days 
ago, that he was of opinion that we should be dealing harshly with the Ottoman 
Government, and with the town of Jeddah itself, if we were to exact any 
indemnity in the way of punishment. But the recent advices from Captain 
Pullen, and the despatch from Commander Cruttenden to Mr, Consul-General 
Green, which were transmitted to you in my despatch No, 902 of the Sth instant, 
elearly show that the Arab merchants were the instigators of the massacre, even 
though they might not have actually committed murder; and it is manifest that, 
unless a fine be levied on the town, the richest culprits will escape with 
comparative impunity, 

Her Majesty’s Government are, therefore, of opinion, anid your Excellency 
will state this opinion, and the grounds of tt, to the French Government, that a 
fine ought to be levied on the town, although the amount of it should be 
modified according to the sun) to be paid as indemnity for the destruction of 
property. 

I have stated this opinion to Sir Henry Bulwer; and I have also desired 
him to insist on the conduct of Abdullah Furrah being investigated, as you will 
lave seen by Commander Cruttenden’s despatch above alluded to, that he is 
accused of having taken a very active part in the outrage, and of having obtained 
a large share of the plunder, although, by means of lis great wealth, he had 
succeeded in sereening himself from apprehension and adequate punishment. 

lam, Xe, 
(Signed) MALMESBURY,

No, 201. 


The Eorl of Malmesbury to Sir H. Bulwer, 
(No. 259.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, October 14, 1858. 

YOU will have seen, by my telegram of yesterday, of which I inclose a 
copy, that Her Majesty's Government do not agree in the opinion expressed in 
your despatch No. 208 of the 20th of September, that an indemnity should not 
he exacted from the town of Jeddah, by way of punishment. 

Her Majesty's Government consider that the exaction of such indemnity 
affords the only means of punishing the richest of the culprits, such, for instance, 
as Abdullah Furrah; and Her Majesty’s Government entertain no doubt that 
the Arab merchants were the instigators of the massacre, although they may not 
have actually committed murder. 

Her Majesty’s Government think, therefore, that a fine ought to be levied 
on the town, although the amount of it should be modified according to the sum 
to be paid as indemnity for the loss of property. 

1am, &e. 


(Signed) MALMESBURY.

capacity as guardian to the daughter of the late Mr, Page, his Excellency 
informed me that he had applied to your Lordship as to who was the. roper

No, 210. 
The Law Officers of the Crown to the Earl of Malmeshury.—(Received October 21.) 


My Lord, Doctors’ Commons, October 19, 1853, 

WE are honoured with your Lordship's commands, signified: in Mr. Ham- 
mond’s letter of the 12th October instant, stating that he was directed to 
transmit to us the accompanying papers explanatory of the case of the 
* Pranee,” asserted to be a British vessel, and guilty of illegally hoisting Turkish 
colours at Jeddah ; and to request that we would take these papers into consi- 
deration, and report to your Lordship our opinion whether, under the cireum- 
stances of the case, Her Majesty’s Government would be justified in instructing 
Captain Pullen to take posssession of this vessel, without the consent of 
the Turkish uuthorities, and to remove her from Turkish jurisdiction to the 
jurisdiction of a British Viee-Admiralty Court for trial, 

In obedience to your Lordship’s commands, we have taken these papers 
into consideration, and have the honour to report— 

That we are of opinion that Her Majesty’s Government would not be 
justified in instructing Captain Pullen to take possession of the vessel in 
question without the consent of the Turkish authorities, or to remove her 
without such consent from Turkish jurisdiction to the jurisdiction of a British 
Viee-Admiralty Court for trial. 

We have no doubt, upon the statement before us, that this vessel is a 
British vessel; and she appears to have become forfeited to Her Majesty, who 
may properly claim her at the hands of the Turkish Government, but may not 
take forcible possession of her whilst within the territory and jurisdiction of 
Turkey; more especially after the formal delivery up of the vessel by Captain 
Pullen to the Turkish authoritics in his letter No. 14 of the 23rd June, 1858. 

We have, &e. 
(Signed) J. D, HARDING. 
FITAKOY KELLY, 
H. M. CAIRNS.

No. 215, 
The Karl of Malmesbury to M. Musurus. 


M. Ambassadeur, Foreign Office, October 21, 1858, 


HER Majesty’s Government have had under their consideration the 
despatch addressed to your Excellency, om the 22nd of September, by the 
Turkish Minister for Foreign Affairs, explaining the feelings of the Sublime 
Porte on the subject of the bombardment of Jeddah by Her Majesty's steamer 
“ Cyelops,” and stating the considerations which alone have induced the Porte to 
refrain from formally protesting against that proceeding. 

I have to assure your Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government have 
observed with the highest satisfaction the friendly and conciliatory tone of 
Mahmoud Pasha’s despatch, and have learnt with sincere pleasure the decision 
at which the Porte has arrived. 

When the news of the outbreak of Jeddah, and the lamentable cireum- 
stances attending it, reached Englaud, Her Majesty's Government had no 
alternative as to. the course they should pursue. me 

The murder of the English and, French Consuls, and of other Christian 
subjects; aud the pillage of their houses, by a lawless and fanatic mob, ealled for 
prompt and signal punishment, and Her Majesty's Government were obliged to 
instruet Captain Pullen to proceed to Jeddah, in Her Majesty's steam-vessel 
Cyclops,” and require the immediate punishment of the murderers at the 
place ating their atrocious crimes were committed, 
It was the more indispensable for Her Majesty’s Government to take this 
course without delay, inasmuch as they had reason to apprehend, and the 
result proved that their apprehension was not without foundation, that the 
excitement oceasioned among the Mussulman population on the Red Sea by the 
intelligence of what had happened at Jeddah, might lead to similar calamities 
in other quurters, which could only be averted by proving that severe and 
immediate punishment would overtuke the authors of such crimes, 

But when it was known that the events which had taken place at Jeddah 
were viewed at Constantinople with as great horror as they were here, and that 
the Sublime Porte was about to take immediate measures to punish the guilty, 
and to grant compensation, as far as possible, for the loss of life and property, 
fresh orders were sent without loss of time to Captain Pullen. to: await the 
arrival of the Turkish forces which were‘on the point of being despatched: to 
Jeddah, 

Unfortunately, however, that officer had left! Suez: betore those counters 
orders reached him, and on his demands for satisfaction not being complied: with 
hy the local authorities, he proceeded to enforce them by firing on the town,

Inclosure | in No, 216. 
Str H. Bulwer to Mr, Pisani. 


Therapia, October 10, 1858. 


WHAT L wished to understand was, how Ismail Pasha came to state that 
he had no authority to act as Commissioner when the Porte said ‘that he had 
authority. It would consequently be desirable to ascertain when the Porte’s 
wuthority was given to, him. 

Much as 1 desire at all times to smooth away difficulties, and prevent 
complications, Lam sorry to say that I cannot promise anything to his Highness 
the Grand Vizier with respect to delaying Captain Pullen's action, simply on the 
plea that the Porte is waiting for Ismail Pasha to get'out of quarantine. It is 
not simply the case of a man disobeying his orders, but of a promise given to 
Great Britain, the performance of which promise has already been unwarrantably 
postponed. It ought, therefore, to be now, with excuses for and explanation of 
that delay, to. be fulfilled forthwith, If I were to propose to delay its fulfil- 
ment further, on the plea that the Porte wished, before fulfilling it, to talk to 
Ismail Pasha, Her Majesty’s Government would most probably consider itself 
insulted, and could not, at all events, attend to such a nest. 

The sending back of the prisoners must be immediate. Any explanation 
as to the conduct of Ismail Pasha might then be delayed until that officer was 


here, and able to state his own case. | 
(Signed) HENRY L. BULWER.

No. 238, 
Lord A, Loftus to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received November — .) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, November 10, 1858. 

COUNT BUOL has just stated that he must refer to correspondence before 
replying to the question concerning Austrian claims at Jeddah. 

His Excellency appeared ignorant on the matter, observing that, probably, 
their Chargé d’Affaires had been instructed, if others claimed and received 
indemnity, to reclaim the same for Austrian subjects. He denies existence of

My Lord, Doctors’ Commons, November 13, 1858. 

1 AM honoured with your Lordship’s commands signified in Mr, Hammonds 
letter of the 1st of November instant, stating that he was directed to transmit 
to me the accompanying papers relative to the conflicting claims of the repre- 
sentatives of Mr. Page, late Her Majesty’s Consul at Jeddah, to his property, 
and to a pension granted by the Porte to his heirs, on account of Mr. Page's 
murder in the month of June last; and to request that I would take these 
papers into consideration, and report to your Lordship my opinion as to the 
course which Her Majesty’s Government should follow im this case. 

In obedience to your Lordship’s commands I have taken these papers into 
consideration, and have the honour tu report— | . 

That 1 do not clearly understand whether the Turkish Government desires 
to leave to Her Majesty's Government the selection of the persons who are entitled 
to receive the pension or indemnity which the Sultan 15° disposed to grant, m 
whatsoever precise form or words, to “ the heirs” of the late British Consul at 
Jeddah ; or whether the Turkish Government is disposed to determine this 
question, and to select these persons for itself. Dit oe 7 cop 

At present, it does not appear to me that Her Majesty's Government 15_in 
a position to determine the question for itself, or that it has any voice im the 
matter, Ido not observe amongst the papers any application from the ‘Turkish 
Government or Legation to Her Majesty's Government, asking even for infor= 
mation or advice as to the persons entitled, whether legally or morally, to receive 
the indemnity in question. ‘The precise nature of the indemnity 18 not settled ; 
no indenynity, fund, or pension is as yet disposable by Her Majesty's Government, 
or is even in existence, ! 

Under these circumstances, it may be the most proper, or indeed the only 
course open to Her Majesty's Government, simply to reler all the applicants to 
the Turkish Government, which may distribute its bounty at its own discretion ; 
and this is the course which I should, at the present moment, recommend Her 
Majesty’s Government to adopt. ; 
mae however, Her Majesty's Government is to be considered as entitled or 
called upon to decide upon the disposal of this indemnity as between the appli-

No. 249, 


Captiin Pullen tothe Earl of Malmesbury —(Recewed November 19.) 


(No. 6.) 
My Lord, * Cyclons,” Jeddah, November 3, 1858. 

[ HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that I left Suez on the 
7th ultimo, accompanied by M. Sabatier, the French Commissioner and suite, 
and arrived here on the 12th, 

My despatch No. 3 of the 28rd of September last, informed your Lordship 
of the return of Ismail Pasha from this place, with thirty-six prisoners, said to 
have been concerned in the massacres, and of the intention of M. Sabatier and 
myself urging upon him the expediency of his being present here with us: he, 
however, refused ; his reasons being that he was merely the bearer of an order 
for the execution of the murderers, and that he was subject to the authority of 
Namick Pasha, 

M. Sabatier has, since bis arrival here, received a letter from lis Govern- 
ment, expressing their surprise at Ismail Pasha leaving this place. 

On arriving here | addressed a letter to Namick Pasha, who was at Mecea, 
a copy of which is inclosed marked No. 1, to which I received an answer in 
Turkish, to the effect that he had no knowledge of the appointment of a Turkish 
Commissioner, but that as soon as he arrived he would come to Jeddah, and in 
the meantime he had taken steps to prevent the escape of the persons therein 
named, 

M. Sabatier also addressed a letter to his Excellency in similar terms. 

He, however, arrived here on the 17th ultimo, and at an interview he agam 
stated he had no knowledge of the appointment of a Commissioner, and that he 
had no authority to act in the matter. 

As the Medjidie Company's steam-vessel “ Gabarri’’ was expected with 
the Grand Scheriff of Mecca, it was considered probable that the Turkish 
Commissioner might be on board her; but she arrived on the @&th ultimo, with 
only the former functionary and his suite. 

~ But, my Lord, it is manifest that the protestations of the Turkish officials 
are not in accordance with their acts. As tar back as July last, the Minister for 
Foreign Affairs of the Sublime Porte thus writes to Her Majesty’s Ambassador 
there :— Sans perdre de temps sempresse d’employer les mesures fortes pour 
chatier les coupables, tous ceux qui scraient connus comme ayant pris part a 
cet outrage, ou y étant compromis, ou bien qui sont dans de grands soupcons.” 

How, my Lord, has this been carried out? The execution of eleven, and 
sending to Constantinople of thirty-five persons of the poorest class and the 


- lowest station, and I believe that amongst those sent away are some who would 


give evidence against influential people. 2 

1 may mention a few cases with regard to persons who are officially or 
otherwise of great power here. 

The tardy manner in which Namick Pasha came to Jeddah after the 
massacre, and his withrawal of a greater part of the force available for the 
security of that place, are alike inexcusable. AT 

The next case is that of the Kaimakam (Ibrahim Agha}. It is said he was 
formerly a kaiquejy ” (boatman) of Constantinople. I have before me sworn 
evidence that, in May last, during the feast of Bairam, when Mahometans are 
more than usually fanatical, he threatened a Turkish soldier with punishment for 
being seen in the shop of a Christian ; thus showing openly the hatred in which 
he held them. Again, on the l5th of June last, he held a conference with 
merchants whom he knew were most inimical to Christians; and whilst he 
knew that crowds were collecting outside the building in which they were, 
uttering cries against the Kafirs. Does he seck toullay these turbulent elements ? 
No; he orders his own followers to load ther fire-wrins : he stands outside the 
house, and with gestures points to the Consulate. With this approval of their 
conduct the crowd rush forward, aud the result we too sadly know. 

‘J must, however, state that, after the rising, 1 believe the conduct of the 
Kaimakam was consistent with his duty, as far as the means at his disposal 
allowed, and that by his means the lives of Mademoiselle Eveillard and 
M. Emerat were saved. 


V1 


The nextis that of Abdallah Mohteasib, a man possessing extreme influence 
over the masses. Although a letter, purporting to be an order from the Gand 
Vizier to suspend him and bring him to trial, has beeu received, he is still at 
lurge in the town, His conduct on the 15th of Juné was marked with the 
greatest fanaticism: he harangued the crowds; he led them to the British 
Consulate, where, from his position, he knew of there being large sums af 
money deposited, i 

_ ‘Fhe next is the Sheik Anti Ba Haron, Sheikh al Laoda, a Hadramont. 
It ts sworn that he led the crowds to the house of Sava and Co., exclaiming, “ On 
them, the Kafirs !” 

Then, again, there is the Sheikh Abdal Gaffhr Ba Gaffar, a Hadramout, 
Chief of the Tribunal of Commerce and Shehbendee of the Merchants. It is 
sworn he led the crowds to the French Consulate, the people yelling, “ Down 
with the flag; destroy them!” 

And, lastly, we find that the Cadi not only did nothing to prevent the 
massacres, but, on a Christian having promised to embrace Islamism on 
condition of his life being spared, being brought before him, he suid, “ Why have 
you brought him tome? "Take him away: after having commenced to kill them, 
kill this one also.” 

Thus, my Lord, it would appear that the conference amongst the Sliciklis 
was not of the manner in which the rising was to be prevented or put down, but 
to concert measures for carrying their diabolical intentions more fully into 
effect. 

_ such, my Lord, is the substance of information gleaned in the endeavours 
of M. Sabatier and myself in tracing home the guilt to the really guilty» and, on 
occasionally comparing the intelligence we gain, we find there is little difference, 
thus showing the accuracy of it, 

TI shall, without doubt, receive much more information; and should the 
Turkish Commissioner not be able to bring home the guilt to the really guilty, 
M. Sabatier and myself will then bring forward our evidence. J 

| have now to take the attention of your Lordship back to the events 
detailed in my letter to the Seerctary of the Adimiralty dated the 2th of fast 
June, reporting the massacres of this place, and the causes which, it is said, led 
to it, 

One of the causes was stated to be, that “a Sheikh, or important personage 
of reputed great holiness, had arrived at Mecea with sixty followers from Delhi,” 
Although this was whispered about at the time, no information could be 
obtained to throw further light upon it, or to account for the foundation of the 
report. 

However, on the 31st ultimo, I received letters from Brigadier Coghlan, 
the Political Resident at Aden, copies of which are inclosed, marked respectively 
Nos. 2 and 3, which leaves little doubt but that the person named in his letters 
is the same said to have been concerned in the massacres, 

1 hesitated not, therefore, to place myself in communication with the 
Governor-General, Tleaftected, at first, to be ignorant of the existence of such 
a person, but afterwards admitted that a man, answering the description [ had 
given of him, was, at present, living between ‘Tai and Mecea, und that about 
two years sinee he hud gone to Suez, thence hy sea to Aden, with the intention 
of going to Ladin; being frustrated in his desizns, however, by the authorities at 
Aden, he left for Yemen, and shortly afterwards arrived at his present pluce af 
abode. 

I requested the Pasha to deliver this person to me; he sat, in reply, that 
the pubhe seizure of Syud Fug) would cause the inhabitants of Mecca and 
the Arabs to rise against the Government, thus acknowledging the influence 
possessed by the tungul, 

Although the right to demand that person is undoubted, vet T am-anxious 
that the authorities here should not be embarrassed, and the assurances given 
to me by his Excellency, that he will deliver him quietly to me, if possible, or 
put it stop to his propagating his pernicions doctrines, will meet, for the present, 
the object in view, | 

1 have written to the Brigadier, stating this, and also of my intention to 
bring the matter before Ller Majesty's Government; and L have pow to request 
the instructions of your Lordship, whether [shall insist upon the tungul beter 
given up, or proof of his removal to a distant part of the Turkish dominions, 


= 


172 


This is undoubtedly the worst place in the world where any of the people 
should reside, 

The next subject 1 have to lay before your Lordship, is the question of 
indemnity for losses sustained, An abstract has been drawn up of the claims 
presented to me; they are all very volumnious, and many most complicated, 
that of Sava and Co, being particularly so. Their principal transactions were of 
a commission character: thus their losses have taken with them, those of 
numbers of other persons: it involves heavy questions, with regard to money, 
jewels, pearls, diamonds, securities, &c.; everything being either destroyed or 
rendered useless. 

M., Sabatier has, himself, many claims on this house, for losses sustained by 
French subjects ; and he agrees with me in the necessity, that as soon as affairs 
are settled here, and every information obtained, that Mr. Whillier, the Secretary 
to the British Commissioner, should proceed to England, to lay the various 
accounts before your Lordship, and the explanations thereto, and be at hand to 
meet the extraordinary demands which, from what is now seen, will be doubtless 
brought forward. 

1 agree with M. Sabatier that the final decision shall, in each case, be 
made by our Governments; but he observes, that his accounts are exceedingly 
simple, and of small amcunt, whereas he is also aware that those of Savas are 
of the most complicated nature. 

Mr. Whillier, by proceeding to England, will be able to bring with him the 
amounts which the coals of Mr. Mattos, of London, will realize, and settle his 
claims, as well as other money belonging to the late Viee-Consul, which has 
been received: as also his will, which I consider too valuable to be intrusted to 
the post, 

With reference to the claim of Mr. Page, it will be seen, that 10,0001. is the 
sum fixed; and | have reason to believe, that this sum is rather under, than 
over, the amount he was possessed of at the time of his death; it is my intention 
to claim, in addition thereto, a certain sum for the loss of his life. 

Ofall these measures, I request the approval of your OED 

I would also sugeest to your Lordship that the indemnity, when obtained, 
which will he conveyed to Suez in this ship, should be also sent in charge of the 
Secretary to England; but on this matter I beg the decision of your Lordship. 
My reason for suggesting it is, that after affairs are settled here, it would be 
unwise to keep up the recollection of events, which undoubtedly are best 
forgotten, and that, therefore, the final payment should be made through Her 
Majesty's Government in England. 

The ‘ Chesapeake,” ' Pelorus ” and “ Roebuck,” are here, and M,. Sabatier 
and myself have agreed, that in order to afford the Turkish Government every 
facility, a ship of war should be despatched to Suez. I have, therefore, requested 
the senior officer to despatch the “ Roebuck” to that place on the 4th instant, 
where she will await the arrival of the mail-steamer due from Constantinople at 
Alexandria on the 16th of the month, should the Turkish Commissioner not 
have arrived before, 

On learning, by telegraph (which will be conveyed to the Commander of 
the “ Roebuck” by Her Majesty’s Consul-General at Alexandria, to whom I 
have written on the subject), that the Turkish Commissioner had not then 
arrived, the “Roebuek ” will return to this place, and my French colleague and 
mysell have determined to act forthwith to carry out the views of our respective 
Jovernments; but we both foresee great difficulties in the task before us, and 
as we tread onward, step by step, we shall find greater difficulties placed 
purposely in our way by those whose interest it is to keep every event as 
concealed as possible. ee 

The appointment of Namick Pasha will not lessen such ditheulty, for he 
declares, in the event of being appointed as Commissioner, he will decline acting 
ais one. 

Thus | have endeavoured to convey to your Lordship the feeling entertained 
by the ‘Turkish officials, and as, by your instructions, | am not to proceed to acts 
af hostility, yet l venture to suggest to your Lordship whether it will not be 
necessary to inquire whether similar instructions liave been issued to M. Sabatier 
by the French Government, as it would place each of us in an unenviable 
position were he to order the guns of the *Duchnyla” to be opened on the 
town when she arrives here, and the English squadron to be lookers-on, 


7s 


Lastly, L can assure your Lordship, what, T have no doubt, you will have 
learnt by the perusal of the foregoing, that the niost perfect cordiality and unity 


of ideas exist between M, Sabatier and myself.

I beg respectfully to submit to your Lordship that this is the first intima-

officially notified in July lagt that I was the representative of Mr. Page as executor

that I might be referred to. 

It could not be supposed that there were no claims on his account; and 
under the circumstances I humbly conceive that I had reason to expect that 
when any arrangement was determined on, for the settlement of these claims, | 
should receive some notice of the same. I therefore trust your Lordship will 
exonerate me from any negligence in the matter; for, being entirely without 
information, I had no idea there was any time fixed for sending in claims; and 
likewise that your Lordship will take into consideration the peculiar difficulties 
of the case, for lam still unable legally to appoint an agent, in consequence of 
not having yet received Mr. Page's will in the original,

No. 258. 
Earl Cowley to the Earl of Mabneshury.—( Received November 22.) 


(No, 1,482.) 


My Loril, Paris, November 21, 1858, 

COUNT WALEWSKI informed me yesterday that he had received 
intelligence from M. Sabatier, which showed that the real promoters of the 
massacre at Jeildah had, as yet, escaped punishment, and M. Sabatier enter- 
tained but little hope of justice being done, unless the decision of the dilferent 
cases was to depend on the Commission appointed to inquire into the whole matter. 
If the cases are to go before the tribunals the greatest criminals will escape, 
Count Walewski is anxious, under these circumstances, that greater latitude ol 
action should be allowed the British and French Commissioners; in fact, that 
ulterior proceedings should be left very much in their hands. THe requested me 
to bring this opinion to your Lordship'’s knowledge. 

1 had the honour to receive this morning your Lordship’s despatch No, 1,095 
of the 20th instant, in which you desire me to ascertain whether instructions 
have been addressed to M. Sabatier desiring him not to have recourse to hostile 
measures without previous reference home. 

Count Walewski will not be in town again before Wednesday next, but | 
shall then put the question to his Excellency, 

[ have, &e, 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 259. 


The Earl of Malmesbury to Earl Cowley. 
(No. 1,109.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 23, 1858. 

HER Majesty’s Government. agree with Count Walewski that if the trial 
of the parties who are now accused of being the active instigators of the massacre 
ai Jeddah is left to the Turkish authorities alone, as was the case in regard to 
the parties already executed, there is too much reason to apprehend, considering 
the influential position of the parties now implicated, that their acquittal will 
take place. At the same time, however, it would not be possible for the two 
Governments to insist that the parties should be tried by their Commissioners 
alone; and it therefore would seem that the only course open for us to pursue 
is to require that, under the peculiar circumstances of the ease, the English and 
French Cowmissioners should be associated with the Turkish authorities, in the 
game manner as under the Capitulations, when 4 British subject is tried in 
Turkey on a charge of murder, the British Consul, and I believe, in a corre: 
sponding case, the French Consul would hear and decide, together with the 
Turkish Judge, as to the guilt or innocence of the accused party. ; 

‘At all events it is clear that the English and French Commissioners must be 
present at the trial of the accused, and must have the right to produce the 
evidence by which they consider the charge 1s substantiated ; and that a verdict 
of acquittal, if given contrary to the opinion of the two Commissioners, must be 
revisable by the Porte, so us to secure, in case of need, a final heaving by a Court 
uninfluenced by local prejudices. 

Her Majesty’s Government, in the event of this course meeting the views 
of the Imperial Government, will instruct Her Majesty's Commissioner— 

lat. ‘To require to be admitted to take part in the trial of the accused on 
the same footing as the Turkish authorities ; : 

Badly, If that is refused, to insist upon being present at the trial, and upon 
being allowed to produce such evidence as he may deem proper ; and 

Srdly. ‘To insist, in case of acquittal contrary, in his opinion, to the evidence, 
that the whole of the proceedings shall be referred to onstantinople, for the 
final judgment of the Porte; the accused being retained in custody until the 
result of the reference to Constantinople is known. | re 

And Her Majesty's Government will make known by telegraph to Sir 
Henry Bulwer the nature of the instructions given to Her Majesty's Commis- 
sioner, and will direct him to communicate the substance of them to the Porte, 
and press upon the ‘Turkish Government the determination of that, of Her 
Majesty to have the principal criminals openly and fairly tried, and, if found 
guilty, punished according to law; and to state to the Porte that Her Majesty's 
Government are much dissatisfied with the remissness which has been shown by 
the Turkish Government in this matter, and trust that they shall have no longer 
occasion to complain of the dilatory and evasive proceedings of the Turkish 
authorities. , Sh ae 

But your Excellency will state to Count Walewski that Her Majesty's 
Government are desirous of tryin oe means to induce the Porte itself to do 
justice to their legitimate demands betore they give any such latitude. to the 
British Commissioner as would authorize him to have recourse to forcible 
measures, 

In the first instance it was important at once to convince the Mussulman 
mind that the Christian Powers would brook no delay in obtaining, at all events, 
a partial reparation for the horrible outrage committed upon the Christians at 
Jeddah; and the accounts which have reached Her Majesty's Government from 
different quarters show that the promptinude with which measures were taken 
against the offending city produced «a most salutary effect, more especially under 
the circumstances of the time, when numerous pilgrims were returming to their 
homes from the holy cities, But there is no-longer any occisin® for such speedy 
action, and Her Majesty's Government preter to hold under their own control 
the issue of the orders, if unfortunately they should. be called for, to resort again 
to active operations against Jeddah, ni a) 

The mail for the Red Sea will be made up in London on Thursday the 25th 
instant, and I should therefore wish to know by telegraph the general result ol

your communications with the French Government in this matter, even though 
time should not admit of your forwarding to me a detailed report; so that | may 
be enabled to send instructions to Her Majesty’s Commissioner without further 
delay.

YOUR proposed instructions for Jeddah (see your No. 1,109) are entirely 
concurred in. In using the word ‘* Commission,” I had intended to include the 
Turkish Commissioner, as well as the British and French, The latitude which 
it was proposed to give to the two latter had reference simply to proceedings 


with their Turkish colleague, and was never meant to extend to resumption of 
hostile measures.

_ HER Majesty's Government have been in communication with that of the

implicated in the late massacre at Jeddah; and among whom, Captain Pullen, in 


his despatch No. 6 of the 8rd of November, describes the following as most 
prominent, viz. :— 


. The Kaimakan, Ibrahim Aga. 

- Abdallah Mohtesstb. 

. Sheikh Aali Ba Haron, Sheik al Laoda, 
. Sheikh Abdal Gatfar Ba Gaffar, 

» The Cadi. 


_ These seem to be the chief participators, though, it may be, in different 
degrees, in the murders ; and, besides these, Namieck Pasha’s conduct must be 
inquired into, as having, by alleged culpable negligence, omitted to take early 
precautions to suppress the disturbance. 

But Her Majesty’s Government, and that of the Emperor of the French, 
apprehend that, if the trial of these partics, or of any others against whom 
eviilence can be obtained, is left to the Turkish authorities alone, as was the case 
in regard to the parties already executed, their acquittal is likely to be secured 
beforehand, in consequence of the influential position which they occupy; and, 
therefore, in conformity with the understanding which has been come to with 
the French Government, I have to instruct you to require;

manslaughter, that vou shull hear and decide in common with the Turkish 
authorities the cases of the several parties brought before you.

No. 279. 
Ear! Cowley to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received November 27.) 


(No. 1,509.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 25, 1858. 

COUNT WALEWSKI having been in Paris yesterday for a few hours, [ 
was enabled to communicate to his Excellency, without delay, the substance of 
your Lordship’s despatch No. 1,109 of the 23rd instant, relative to the course 
to be pursued by the British and French Commissioners sent to investigate the 
circumstances connected with the massacre of Jeddah. : 

I have to express my regret that my despatch No. 1,482 of the 21st instant, 
to which your Lordship’s despatch is an answer, should have led you into error 
as to. the objects of the Imperial Government. There is no desire on Count 
Walewski’s part to deprive the Ottoman authorities of their proper jurisdiction 
in this matter, but he wishes that the investigation which is yet to take place at 
Jeddah should be conducted before the Commission appointed for the purpose 
(including of course the Turkish Commissioner), inasmuch as he is convinced 
that justice will not be obtained before the ordinary tribunais. And in recom- 
mending that greater latitude of action should be allowed to the British and 
French Commissioners, it was with reference to their dealings with their ‘Turkish 
collearue that Count Walewski spoke, and not with w view of placing in their 
hands the power of having recourse to force. nie 

Under these circumstances, his Excellency has no difficulty in agreeing to 
the instructions which your Lordship proposes to address to Mr. Walne, as I had 
the honour to inform you by my telegram of yesterday's date, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

WITH reference to your letter of the 2let ultimo, inclosing a copy of a

Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to transmit to you herewith, for the 
information of the Earl of Malmesbury, copy of a letter dated the 2nd instant, 
which my Lords have this day received from Captain Pullen, reporting that he

Captain Pullen to the Secretary to the Admiralty. 


Sir, “ Cyclops,” Jeddah, November 2, 1858. 

I HAVE the honour to acquaint you, for their Lordships’ information, that 
in consequence of having sent. the British ship “ Eranee” off to the first Viee- 
Admiralty Court, at Bombay, T have to request that her register, sent home last 
August. may be returned, in the event of its being pees the copy only 
accompanying her, with other pe relating to her illegal proceedings; and of 
this intention I acquainted his Excellency Namick Pasha, on arrival here on the 
12th instant. | 

Furthermore, for their Lordships’ information, 1 beg to lay before them my 
reasons for so acting; in fact, I intimated in my despatch of the 12th of August 
last, that could J have ballasted her after the bombardment, I should have sent 
her off then. cK 

1. When I returned to Jeddah, in July last, she was again wearing 
Turkish colours, and they were only hauled down by the authorities at my 
demand, acquainting me at the same time that it was by the Pasha’s orders 
she had them fying. This was contrary to my protest to his Excellency. in 
June last, 

2, On entering the port on the 12th of October, Commander Adams, of 
the Honourable Company’s ship “ Assaye,” informed me that the * Eranee” had 
been loading salt; but in consequence of a letter from me from Suez, addressed 
to the senior naval officer present, saying that she was not to leave the enenoree 
he had stepped her proceeding after getting about 200 tons on board. This 
led me to infer that it was the owner’s intention to put to sea directly he had 
sufficient ballast on board, in which conjecture 1 feel more assured, as Namick 
Pasha informs me himself, that after the “Cyclops” last left this port he had 
given the ship up entirely to the owner. 

I, therefore, in order no longer to prolong a discussion that can only be 
settled in n Vice-Admiralty Court, decided at once on taking this final step, and 
that she should leave as soon as she could be got ready, when Lieutenant 
Wilkinson, an Assistant-Surgeon, and Second Master, with twenty men from 
this ship, were placed in charge to navigate her to Bombay, and she left this 
morning, towed by the “ Assaye,” : Zee 

Trusting that my proceedings may meet their Lordships’ approval, | 


have, &c. (Signed) W. 1. 8. PULLEN.

Inclosure 1 in No, 285. 

Sir H, Bulwer to Mr. Pisani, 
Sir, Pera, November 18, 1858. 
YOU will read the substance of the inclosed despatch to Fuad Pasha. 
You will remind him of the frequent and repeated remonstrances | made, 
in the most formal manner, against the delay that took place in naming a 
Commissioner to Jeddah, and against the delay which subsequently occurred in 
sending one off. You will remind him also of the various promises I, from time 
to time, received on the subject; promises of which I did not full to: inform 
Her Majesty’s Government, and of which I saw the execution constantly deferred 
with the deepest regret. 

I am not prepared to say that there was any want of good farth on the part 
of the Ottoman Government. On the contrary, the character of the individuals 
who compose that Government convince me that this is altogether impossible ; 
neither am I prepared to estimate the various difficulties in detail which have 
caused that procrastination in arranging so important a matter, of which I had 
so often reason to complain. But still 1 must affirm that days and days, and 
weeks and weeks, have been allowed to pass by without doing that which, under 
the pressing nature of the circumstances, should have been done at once; and 
although I entertain a hope that the fact of the departure of Seid Pasha may 
prevent any of those steps being taken which the Earl of Malmesbury threatens 
to adopt, I must, nevertheless, add that Her Majesty's Government will be fully 
and entirely warranted in pursuing the course which the inclosed telegram 
points out, and that the responsibility of any varied accident that may arise 
therefrom will rest with the Porte—a fact of which | have long since, as you are 
well able to state and to prove, frankly normed the Gand Vizier. 

am, &c. 
(Signed) HENRY L. BULWER.

Inclosure 2 in No, 285. 
Mr. Pisani to Sir H. Bulwer. 


Sir, Pera, November 18, 1858. 

IN obedience to your Excellency’s instruction of this day's date, I commu- 
nicated to Fuad Pasha the substance of the Earl of Malmesbury’s telegram of 
November 15th, instructing your Excellency to state to the Porte that the 
Commissioner had not reached Alexandria on the 4th instant, and asking an 
immediate explanation. I also communicated m exfenso your Excellency’s 
instruction to me, 

Fuad Pasha expressed much regret at the delay which had occurred in the 
departure of the Commissioner, and stated that this delay was owing in great 
part to the recent changes which had taken place in his Exeellency’s depart- 
ment; and, secondly, because the Porte was anxious that the Commissioner 
should start simultaneously with the new Governor ; but circumstances, which 
could not be controlled, prevented the Governor from conforming to the Porte’s 
desire. 

However, the Commissioner, as your Excellency is aware, left for Alex- 
andria on Saturday, the 14th instant, nob being able to start on Wednesday, as 
intended, on account of the state of the weather. Fuad Pasha ventures to 
hope that Her Majesty’s Government will be satisfied with the explanation, and 
will make some allowance for the causes which delayed the departure of the 
Commissioner, in indulgently refraining from pursuing the course pointed out m 
the above-mentioned telegram. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) ET. PISANI.

My Lord, Foreign Office, November 30, 1858. 

THE instructions to Her Majesty’s Commissioner at Jeddah, authorizing 
him to investigate the claims of Austrian subjects, will have led him to ever 
that, in conformity with what your Lordship stated in your telegram of the 
LGth instant, and in your despatch No, 316 of the same day, those claims would 
be officially laid before him by the Austrian Consul-General in Egypt, as a 
euarantee that the parties were, bond fide, Austrian subjects. fs 

Count Apponyi has since observed to me, with reference to a similar state- 
ment which { made to him in my letter of the 23rd instant, that the Austrian 
Consul-General could know nothing about these claims, and that it was desirable 
that Mr, Walne should not be restricted to inquire into those only which might 
reach him through the Consul-General. 

Your Lordship will ascertain from Count Buol what it is that the Austrian 
Government really wishes in this respect; pointing out to his Excellency, if 
necessary, that Mr. Walne can scarcely investigate claims without receiving 
some official assurance that the parties who seek his aid are really entitled to do 
so under the consent given by Her Majesty’s Government to the wishes 
expressed by Count Buol.

No. 295. 
The Queen’s Advocate to the Earl of Matmesbury.—(Received December 6.) 


My Lord, Doctors’ Commons, December 4, 1858. 

1 AM honoured with your Lordship's commands signified in Mr. Hammond's 
letter of the 27th November ultimo, stating that he was directed to transmit to 
me a letter and its inclosures from Messrs. Neroutsos and Co., in answer to one 
which was addressed to that firm in consequence of my report of the 8th of 
September, upon their claim for losses at Jeddah, together with the former 
papers relating to this case; and to request that I would report to your Lordship 
any observations which I may have to make on Mr. Neroutsos’ communication 
of the 25th November ultimo, — 

In obedience to your Lordship’s commands, I have taken these papers into 
consideration, and have the honour to report— tae 

That I have to observe that, it appears from this letter and its inclosures 
from Mr. Neroutsos, that this claim is not at present in such a shape as that 
Her Majesty's Government would be justified in supporting It, 


21 


The claim, if for anything definite, appears to be for 1,500L, proceeds of 
goods sold, and alleged to have been in the hands of an agent named Democides, 
who was murdered at Jeddah. 

There is no proof whatever beyond the assertions of the claimant— 

1. That Demoeides was his agent at, Jeddah; or was murdered at Jeddah ; 
or that he is not now alive, and in possession of the money ; 

2. That Democides had in his custody at his death, in cash, this 1,500/., or 
any other sum in cash, the property of Mr. Neroutsos. There is not a letter, 
account, or particle of writing produced from Democites. Democides is missing, 
and may have been murdered at Jeddah, and probably was indebted to the 
claimant, and he may have had some money of the claimants in his possession ; 
but this is all that appears, and it is obviously insufficient. 

The certificate of naturalization contains an express exemption of any rights 
and capacities of a ‘ natural-born subject out of and beyond the dominions of 
the Bintish Crown.) our Lordship might not be inclined, however, 1m this 
case, to insist strictly upon this exception, if the material facts were satisfactorily 
established ; but at present this is obviously by no means the case, especially 
when the suggestion of ‘serious losses in the shape of outstanding accounts,” 
made in Mr. Neroutsos’ letter of July 19,1858, is borne in mind; and, upon 
the whole, I cannot advise your Lordship to support this claim against the 
Turkish Government, 

I have, &e. 
yoigned) J. D. HARDING.

IN pursuance of an Act passed in the session of Parliament holden in the 
seventh and eighth years of the reign of Her Majesty Queen Victoria, intituled 
“An Act to amend the Laws relating to Aliens :” 

I hereby certify that Paleologo Doucas, calling himself Doucas Paleclogo, an 
alien, now residing at Manchester, in the county of Lancaster, in that part of 
Great Britain called England, with intent to settle therein, has presented to 
me, George Grey, Bart., one of Her Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State, a 
memorial, stating: that he isa native of the Island of Lemnos, in the Greek 
Archipelago; that he came to this country the 13th May, 1846; that he has 
been for the last three years a partner in the firm of Athanasio Paleologo and 
Co., merchants in Manchester ; that he is married and has four children; that 
he intends to continue to reside in this kingdom; and praying me, as such 
Secretary of State, to grant to him the certificate therein mentioned. 

And whereas I have inquired into the circumstances of the case, and 
have received such evidence as I have deemed necessary for proving the truth 
of the allegations contained in such memorial : 

Now, in pursuance of the power and authority given to me, as Secretary of 
State, by the said Act, I hereby grant to ‘the aforesaid Doucas Paleologo, 
merchant (upon his taking the oath prescribed by the said Act), all the rights

Mr. Fenwick to Mr. Hammond.—(Received December 14.) 


Sir, 17, Exchange Alley, North, Liverpool, December 13, 1858. 


I AM obliged by the receipt of your letter of the 11th instant, and with 
reference thereto beg leave respectfully to observe that, as nothing in writing 
has passed between the Turkish Government and Her Majesty’s Ministers, it 1s 
important to know what arrangements have been made by the Porte for the 
regular payment and remittance of the annuity to Mr, Pages heirs, the amount 
of which annuity, as 1 understood from Mr. Ewart, was fixed at 4801, to 
commence from the date of the massacre. Six months have almost clapsed 
since that event, and 1 submit it is time the matter should be settled. 1 shall, 
therefore, feel obliged by your affording full information, and stating when 
particulars of claim are to be sent in, as much time will necessarily be lost in 
obtaining the proofs.

Ineclosure 1 in No. 316, 


Instructions given to Seid Bey. 
(Translation.) 


TIE Governments of France and England having requested n completion 
of the inquiry into the well-known conspiracy against the Consuls of England 
and France at Jeddah, as well as a complete execution of the measures called 
for, they have respectively deputed a Commissioner to go there. 

It is indispensable, and it has been stipulated, that a Commissioner of the 
Sultan’s Government should be present, in order to complete the requisite 
investigation, and to put into execution the sentences which may be awarded, 
The Licutenant-General Ismail Pasha having recently returned to Constanti- 
nople, the General of Brigade Seid Pasha has heen chosen and appointed ta 
conduct the necessary investigation, jointly with the other Commissioners, and 
to perform the acts required.

; Inclosure 2 in No. 416, 


Fistrial Instructions to Seid Pasha. 
(Translation.) 


AS you are well aware, it was laid down in the first clause of the instruc- 
tion relative to your mission, on your departure from here, that the inquiries and 
cross-examinations to be held on the deplorable event, were to be conducted 
conjointly with the Commissioners appointed by England and France. | 

As the crimes which have been committed have been so committed on 
the subjects and functionaries of the other purty, it is in accordance with practice 
and Treaties that in sucli trials the magistrates of the plaintifls’ side should be 
present, 

It is, therefore, requisite that they should be invited to the Court of 
Judgment and Inquiry, and that the examinations should be conducted whilst 
they are present. 

Such persons as shall be produced by the plaintiffs’ side, to give evidence 
in substantiation of their plaint, shall be accepted. , 

As it 18 laid down in the second clause of the instructions, such persons as 
shall be put on their trial before the Court, and shall be shown to be offenders of 
the first class, that is, as shall be proved to-have actually committed murder, 
shall be put to death, according to the Imperial firman previously issued on this 
subject, and their sentences shall be executed on the spot. 

puch suspected persons as shall not belong to the first class, that is, as ‘shall 
not be deserving of death, but shall belong to the second class, must be sent 
here to receive their punishment, They shall, therefore, be sent here, along 
with the file of their cases, when their crime has been proved. ? 

Such persons as shall be asserted, on the one side, to be guilty, and on the 
other, to be innocent and undeserving of condemnation, shall be considered as 
“disputed; allthe particulars and documents showing both sides of the case 
shall be inserted and inclosed it ‘‘mazbatas;’ their persons will be kept under 
the surveillance of the poliec, in such manner that they shall not be able to 
escape, and the subject-matter will be reported here for the issuing of a detinitive 
sentence, : 

Above all, it is essential in this matter to give proofs of the justice and 
impartiality of His Majesty's Government. 

The way to realize this desideratam is to conduct the cross-examinations 
ancl Inquiries in such o perfectly fair way a5 to leave no room for remark on 
either side. 

In accordance with your discretion and intelligence, you will bestow your 
exclusive attention on these points of detail, and perform the duties of your 
mission by applying yourself ta the proper execution of the things required hy 
the clauses above cnumerated,

(Signed ) MEHMED EMEIN AALI.

No. 317. 
Sir H. Bulwer to the Earl of Malmestury.—(Heceived December 18.) 


(No. 417.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 7, 1858. 


YOUR Lordship will observe that by the later instruction, translation of 
which is inclosed in my No. 415 of yesterday's date, the Turkish Commissioner 
at Jeddah is distinctly instructed to attend to the following points :— 

1, That all inquiries and cross-examinations to be held at Jeddah, shall be 
conducted conjointly with the Commissioners of England and France. 

2. That the British and French Commissioners shall be present at. the 
trials. 

3. That if these Commissioners are dissatisfied with the sentence, the 
matter shall be referred to the Porte, | 

These provisions, I think, meet the instructions of Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment on the subject, but will not, 1 apprehend, satisfy those of the French 
Commissioner, who is, I believe, for making the three Commissioners, in form 
and fact, the persons who are to institute the inquiries, bring up the witnesses, 
and judge the case, 

Such e course of proceedings would hardly be: justified by usage or Treaty, 
and though this Government will consent to give whatever the English and 
French Governments demand in an indirect shape, I doubt whether it would 
consent to surrender the whole functions of Government at Jeddah directly and 
clearly into the hands of the Commission. 

At the same time there is, undoubtedly, one difficulty under which 
M. Sabatier and Mr, Walne will labour, even after the instructions which the 
Porte has given, 

The Tribunal will probably be composed of leading persons of the place, 
subject to local influence, and possibly the present Governor, whose conduct 1s 
not very clear, and who will not then be replaced, will exercise some influence 
over it, But as the Tribunal and Governor will always be under the restraint 
which a knowledge that their sentence may be reconsidered will inspire, and the 
Commission will have the power of rejecting from the Judges any suspected 
individuals, I trust that the result will be satisfactory, 

I have, however, brought the tase I have suggested under the consideration 
of the Porte, and urged in the strongest terms the prompt departure of a new 
Governor, respecting which a certain difficulty exists, since [ learn that the one 
first named has declined the post, and others to whom it has been offered have 
followed this example.

(Signed) HENRY L. BULWER,

Captain Pullen to the Earl of Malmesbury.—( Received January 15, 1859.) 
(No. 10.) 
My Lord, * Cyclops,” Jeddah, December 12, 1858. 

IT HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Lordship’s letter 
No, 6 of the 8th ultimo, directing me to make over to Mr. Walne, Her 
Majesty’s Consul at Cairo, the instructions with which I have been furnished, 
as well as all papers connected with the Commission entrusted to tne, 

This [ accordingly have done, and have given Mr, Walne every information 
in my power, both verbally and in writing. 

I have also handed to Mr, Walne full statements of the claims for indem- 
nity, as far as they had been received, with my opinion of the amount they 
claim. 

I further offered to Mr. Walne the services of Mr. Whillier, the Secretary 
to the Commission, who, I felt assured, would be found most useful in assisting 
Mr. Walne by his knowledge of every event that has taken place. 

He informed me, in reply thereto, he had provided himself with an Inter- 
preter and Secretary. 

I cannot close this despatch, however, without recording the sense I enter- 
tain of Mr. Whillier’s services during the protracted time which has. clapsed 
since the commencement of this sad business. His efforts to gain every infor- 
mation tending to throw light on every occurrence, and unremitting attention 
throughout, calls for my highest praise, and particularly when the intense heat 
of such a climate is so much against exertion, 

I trust Tam not asking too much in requesting your Lordship to bring this 
officer’s services under the notice of the Admiralty, 

I have, &c.

I HAVE the honour to report my arrival here on the 28th ultimo, im 
company with Seid Hamdi Pasha, the Turkish Commissioner, who, with his 
Staff, embarked at Suez on the 24th, 2 tf 

I immediately put myself in communication with my French colleague, 
M. Sabatier; and the result of two or three conversations that I have had with 
him is, that our joint representations have induced the Turkish Commissioner 80 
far to meet our wishes as to consent to a parliamentary meeting of the Commus- 
sion, which is to be held on the 4th instant, On that oceasion 1 hope that we 
may clearly ascertain the powers of Seid Hamdi Pasha, and that we may be able 
to remove the objections which he entertains to entering on inquiry and negotia- 
tion previous to the arrival of the newly-appointed Governor-General of the 
Hedjaz, who, it is represented, mity be shortly Ste 

Namick Pasha, the present Governor-General, received me the day after my 
arrival at Jeddah, and immediately afterwards withdrew to Mecca, 

Captain Pullen, whom your Lordship has directed me to replace as Her 
Majesty’s Commissioner, has handed to me your Lordship’s instructions and 
other papers, which may be considered as forming the archives of the Commission, 
together with copies of such despatches from the Admiralty a3 have reference 
to it.

No. 3a0. 


Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Reeeived January 15, 1859.) 
(No. 4.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, December 22, 1858. 


ON the 2nd instant I had the honour of reporting my arrival at this place, 
with the ‘Turkish Commissioner, Seid Hamdi Pasha. bel 

The first meeting of the Commission was held on the 4th to settle prelimi- 
naries ; and M. Sabatier and myself then learnt, with more regret than surprise, 
that the Turkish Commissioner, though professing to have extended powers as to 
criminal questions, had received from the Porte no authority whatever to exact 
an indemnity from the town of Jeddah; his instructions being limited to confer- 
ring with the Governor-General of the Hedjaz, and reporting to the Porte on the 
claims advanced. ‘. 

Since then the sittings of the Commission have been held daily, with the 
exception of Fridays and Sundays. We have examined separately all the local 
authorities, except Namick Pasha, and subjected to a severe interrogatory all the 
persons who ure under suspicion of being instigators or active agents in exciting 
the mob of Jeddah to the deplorable massacre of which this town was in June 
last the melancholy scene. . 

Of the mass of evidence that has been brought before the Commission, there 
ia little that would interest your Lordship were it possible for me to forward a copy 
of the proceedings; and I limit myself, therefore, to reporting that, although our 
labours are not yet completed, we have succeeded in establishing, by the state- 
ment of Sheikh Abdallah Baharoun, and the subsequent admission of Abdallah 
el Mohtessib, the important fact that the latter caused to be summoned to the 
Custom-house at sunset on the 15th of June, an armed mob of Hadarum ; and 
that the order was given by him, in the name of Ibrahim Aga Kaimakam, the 
Lieutenant-Governor of Jeddah. How far the Kaimakam may have been the 
dupe of Abdallah el Mohtessib, obviously the prime mover 1n this frightful drama, 
admits of doubt; but the conduct af that officer has, 1m any case, been so 
highly reprehensible that the Commission has not hesitated to order his suspen 
sion anid arrest. | 

| hope that in a few days the Commission will be at liberty to enter on the 
examination of claims for losses sustained by British and French subjects and 


29) 


protégés; but as to the mode of proceeding in this inquiry, the preliminaries 
have yet to be settled. 

M. Sabatier and myself have, however, considered it indispensable to adopt 
two measures of some importance to the parties interested, namely, first: to 
intimate the abandonment, for account of the Sublime Porte, of all the merchan- 
dize und effects of which the local authorities had taken possession since the 
events of June; secondly, to. present an official demand for such an instalment 
of the indemnity to be raised the town of Jeddah, as should not exceed 
the amounts of British and French claims which must, in any case, be 
admitted. 

Linclose, for your Lordship's information, copies of the notes upon these 
subjects which, with translations, have been presented by myself to the Turkish 
Commissioner, as well as copies of the notes sent by M. Sabatier. A translation 
of Seid Pasha’s answer to the last note is also inclosed. 

With regard to the merchandize and effects, | may observe that I have 
myself acted on the requisition of the principal parties interested. Many of the 
goods are, doubtless, more or less damaged, and most of the chattels are reduced 
to a.worthless condition. It has even come to our knowledge that the local 
authorities, some weeks since, took upon themselves to sell some of the goods 
to traders, who exported them. 

On the subject of the instalment of indemnity to be levied on the town of 
Jeddah, M. Sabatier and myself have found a ifference im our instructions 
which has not.been without embarrassment, placed as we are ab a distance from 
our respective Governments, and deprived of regular postal communications, 
M. Sabatier’s orders were explicit and positive, to make a demand of 3,000,000 
of francs, and to insist on payment within fifteen days; with the power of 


resorting, without further reference, to coercive measures. My instructions were, 


in effect, to demand only such a sum as should indemmify the ascertained losses 
and injuries of British subjects. 

Finding, on consultation with my. colleague, that the British and French 
losses united, must necessarily exceed 3,000,000 af francs, | have agreed with 
M. Sabatier to claim the sum originally fixed, and he on his part has vonsented 
to waive the question of payment within fifteen days. Looking to the insuffi- 
cient powers of the ‘Turkish Commissioner, and to the means of coercion at the 
disposal of M. Sabatier, I have thought it best to prevent any unnecessdly 
collision between the French and ‘Turkish authorities, whilst preserving the 
appearance of perfect agreement between my colleague and myself, I trust that 
the course pursued, in circumstances af some delicacy, will have your Lordsbip’s 
approval. 

I fear that the abstract of claims, forming on inclosure in Captain Pullen's 
Report of the 3rd November, may have somewhat misled your Lordship as to 
the amount of losses really sustained by British subjects, for, on examination of 
the papers, I ain at a loss to understand upon what data some of his conclusions 
have been arrived at, In the first place, the necessity of abandoning, for 
account of the Sublime Porte, all goods in the hands of the authontics, appears 
not to have occurred to Captain Pullen, and he has not sufficiently calculated on 
their deterioration. In the next place he has looked to immediate losses, 
without sufficiently calculating the damages that must arise from the suspension, 
‘f not breaking up, of commercial establishments, of which some of the members 
have been murdered, or of which the agents and employés have been driven 
away, under circumstances that render their return highly improbable, Though 
freely admitting that some of the eluims are greatly exaggerated, 1 cannot adopt 
Captain Pullen’s estimate, or hope to make reductions to the extent which he 
has indicated : but my best attention shall be directed to etfect such an equit- 
able adjustment of all demands, that, without pressing hardly on the Porte, the 
sufferers may receive a just indemnity for their injuries and losses. 

Among the claims of which a list has been forwarded to your Lordship, is 
one by Farag Yusur, a British subject, for the lors of two bughilehs (large boats), 
valued at 4,000 dollars, which were amongst the vessels destroyed by the boats 
of the “Cyclops” during the bombardment of Jeddah. Similar claims, both 
French and British, will doubtless be brought forward: and 1 regret that, upon 
this subject, | have not received your Lordship's instructions; and am scarcely 
likely to receive them belore the labours of the Commission terminute. 

It appears to me very questionable whether the Porte will ever saat the

fall amount of indemnity from the town of Jeddah, There are many indica 
tions of weakness on its part with regard to the port of Mecca, and I conceive 
it possible that the Ottoman Government may find it more convenient to make 
panes in some other place. Such indulgence would probably be dangerous 
hath to the authority of the Porte in this province, and to the lives and pro- 
perty of Enropeans who may settle here. Jeddah has not yet paid the penalty 
of its crimes, and the least punishment that can be inflicted on the wealthy 
instigators and abettors of massacre and pillage is, that they should be) muleted 
in their purses, since the law, as adininistered, is inadequate to touch their 
persons. 

It is much to be regretted that the Porte has exhibited so much dilatoriness 
in sending out the new Governor-General of the Hedjaz, ap ointed to replace 
Namick Pasha, The latter has withdrawn to Mecca, and, though invited by 
the Turkish Commissioner to return, obstinately remains there, on the plea of 
indisposition, ‘The instructions of Seid Hamdi Pasha impose on him the 
necessity of consulting with the Governor-General, a8 well as of referring to 
Constantinople; and months may thus be wasted when, with proper arrmange- 
ments, a few weeks would have sufficed to indemnify the injured, punish the 
guilty, and re-establish such order and authority as should enable the important 
trade of the Red Sea to return to its ordinary cHannale 

1 understand from M. Sabatier that as soon as the claims for’ indemnity 
have been considered by the Commission, and reported on, it is his intention 
to proceed to Suez in the ‘Duchayla.” My own movements will, of course, 
be regulated by the instructions that may reach me in the interval; but, in the 
absence of instructions, it is probable that I may find it convenient to adopt a 
similar course, in order to have the advantage of direct communication with 
the Foreign Department, of which, under existing circumstances, T am wholly 
deprived, IT have, &c.

Inclosure 1 in No. 380. 
Consul Walne to Seid Pasha. 


Jeddah, December 13, 1858. 

THE Undersigned, Her Britannic Majesty’s Commissioner, has the honour 
to inform his Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, Commissioner for the Sublime 
Porte, that, looking to the responsibility of the Sublime Porte to indemnify all 
British subjects and protégés who, directly or indirectly, have been injured.in 
their person or property by the massacre and pillage which took place in Jeddah 
on the 15th of June last, and for which that town must, by the Porte, be beld 
civilly responsible, he abandons, on behalf of the parties interested, as well as 
in virtue of the mission confided to him by Her Majesty's Government,. all 
merchandize, chattels, or property of whatsoever description, of which the local 
authorities may have taken possession during or subsequent to these events ; 
leaving such property to be disposed of by the said authorities, as to them shall 
seem best, for account of the Sublime Porte. 

Conformably, however, with a suggestion of the British claimants, the 
Undersigned has to submit to the consideration of his Excellency Seid Hamdi 
Pasha whether, at sale of the merchandize and chattels by public auction, an 
original holder, if purchaser of merchandize or chattels formerly his property, 
might not, for the mutual convenience of the Sublime Porte and the parties 
interested, be entitled at once to reecive such merchandize or chattels against a 
written acknowledgment by him for the purchase money, the amount of which 
should be subsequently deducted from the indemnity finally assigned to him. 

The Undersigned reserves to himself the right to select and withdraw from 
the articles collected by the authorities, such objects belonging to the late 
Acting Vice-Consul, or other victims of the massacre, as may, in his opinion, 
have a personal interest as souvenirs of the deceased, and which it may be 
considered proper to forward to their relatives. 


The Undersigned, &e, 
(Signed) ALFRED 8. WALNE.

Inclosure 2 in No. 330. 


Consul Walne to Seid Pasha. 


Jeddah, December 20, 1858, 
THE Undersigned, Her Britannic Majesty's Commissioner, has the honour 
to inform his Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, Commissioner of the Sublime 
Porte, that he has received instructions from Her Majesty's Government to 
obtain complete satisfaction for the injury and losses sustained by British 
subjects and protézés from the massacre and pillage which occurred at 
Jeddah in June last, for which that town must by the Porte be held civilly 
responsible ; and that, though the damages cannot be exactly estimated, till the 
claims have been subjected to an inquiry, which will be entered on in a few days, 
it is already ascertained that the British and French losses considerably exceed 
the sum of 3,000,000 francs. The Undersigned has, therefore, to invite lis 
Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha to take such measures as may be thought 
necessary to make an early provision for satisfying these claims, by demanding 
of the town the amount above mentioned, as an instalment of the indemnity due ; 
reserving to himself to call, at a future time, for such further sums as may be 
necessary to complete the indemnity, whenever the claims have been finally 
adjudicated. 
The Undersigned, &c. (Signed) ALFRED 8S. WALNE.

Inclosure 5 in No. 330. 
Seid Pasha to Consul Walne. 


(Translation.) 16 Gamad-Avvel, 1275. (December 22, 1858.) 
(After the usual compliments.) 

1 HAVE had the honour of receiving your note dated the 20th December, 
requesting me to recover immediately from the inhabitants of Jeddah the sum of 
4,000,000 francs, on account of damages sustained from the outbreak which 
oecurred: and this previous to decision on the amount by our respective 
Governments. 

In answer, I beg to state that according to the instructions which I have 
received from the Ottoman Government respecting the losses sustained from the 
outbreak, it is the business of the Commissioners to estimate and fix the amount 
of damages; but the recovery, acceptance, imereasé or decrease, ure matters to 
be decided on by the Sublime Porte. . 

The Commissioners, in conjunction with the Governor-General, are to 
ascertain the exact damages, and discover those who have caused them. 

1am distinctly instructed to submit to the Sublime Porte the “mazbata " 
or statement of the damages as estimated and established. As to their recovery 
from the inhabitants, there is nothing in my instructions. To put in execution 
what is not found in the said instructions, 1 must apply for authority from the 


Sublime Porte. : 

I beg vou to aceept my excuse, and the assurance of my esteem. 

(Signed) SELD HAMDI PASHA, 
Turkish Commissioner for the affairs of Jeddak.

Consul Walne to the Earl of Malinesbury.—(Reeeived January 15, 1859.) 


(No. 7.) 
My Lon, : Jeddak, December 24, 1858. 

SINCE my arrival here I fiave had several applications from lonians and 
other persons under British protection, who have returned to this port with a 
view of carrying on trade, and who have experienced, on the part of the local 
authorities, dificulties not warranted by the ‘Treaties existing between Great 
Britain and the Ottoman Empire, and which assuredly would not be met with in 
any province of Turkey, near the centre of Government, 

In a few instances I have ventured s0 far to interfere, by verbal eommuni- 
cations with the Lieutenant-Governor, as partially to remove those difficulties ; 
but looking to the possibility of our trade with Jeddah being gradually resumed, 
and to the necessity of our traders having the full rotection to which they are 
entitled, I have respectfully to submit to your Lordship whether it would not be 
desirable that a Consular officer should, as early as possihle, be sent out, and 
Consular authority re-established, 

It may be worthy of the consideration of your Lordship, whether in future 
the Consular officer in Jeddah should not be prohibited from trading; whether 
he should not have that jurisdiction in criminal cases which can be exercised 
legally only in virtue of a commission ; and whether it might not be advisable to 
obtain for him the exequatur of the Sultan, and put him in every respect in & 
position equal to that of his French colleague. 

For a long time to come British authorities in the Red Sea will require the 
support of an armed force, and | consider it my duty to suggest to Her Majesty's 
Government the advisableness of maintaining there such a squadron as will 
enable the officer in command to keep, at least, one vessel-of-war stationed at 
Jeddah, as well as cruizers looking in from time to time at the other ports of 
trading importance, . | 

There is every reason to believe that, immediately after the events of June, 
the conspirators of Jeddah intended to effect a massacre of all the Christians at 
Massowah, and actually sent arms there for that purpose. The arrival of a 
bugleh in ballast excited the suspicion of the French agent, and this nefarious 
scheme was providentially frustrated. 

Thave, &c. 
(Signed) ALFRED 8. WALNE.

Mr. Hammond to Mr. de Mattos. 


Sir, Foreign Office, January 17, 1859. 

LAM directed by the Earl of Malmesbury to acquaint you that Captain 
Pullen has reported that the coals belonging to you at Jeddah have been sold 
under his authority, and have realized the net sum of 2,035/, 13s, 2d., from 
which is to be deducted a sum of 8/. for the expenses of taking charge of the 
coals for six months, and the hire of a person to weigh them, leaving a balance

No. 350. 
Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received January 21.) 


(No. 10.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, January 2, 1859. 


HAVING pushed, as far as appeared advisable to my French colleague and 
myself, the inquiry as to who were the instigators and accomplices in exciting 
the population of Jeddah to massacre the Christians, and pillage their establish- 
ments, on the 15th of June, as well as to the conduct of the local authorities on 
that occasion, the Commission closed the procés-verbaue of its interrogatories on 
the 28th of December. . 

But although several meetings of the Commissioners were subsequentl 
held, it was only yesterday that a decision was adopted as to the terms in whic 
the Commission should put on record the results of its inquiry. 

Considerable diserepaney between the instructions sent to the French and 
British Commissioners by their respective Governments ; the want of an exact 
knowledge of the powers given to the ‘Turkish Commissioner by the Porte; 
sone little diflerence of ideas as to procedure, when examined from a French, 
Turkish, or English point of view; the absence of a Governor-General ina 
position to offer efficient and willing concurrence: such ure the cireumstances 
which have embarrassed the Commissioners during the last week, and led to 
repeated discussions on questions that, under a well-regulated Government, 
might have been safely confided to the decision of the constituted tribunals. 

I considered it my duty to repudiate the idea of the British and French 
Commissioners exercising judicial functions as to the cases brought before the 
Commission. It appeared to me that it was perfectly within our attributes to 
he members of a Board of Inquiry, and, ina barbarous country like this, to go 
to extreme limits in expressing our opinion, not only as to the result of that 
inquiry, but as to the course which ought to be pursued in punishing the guilty. 
But at the conclusion of our inquiry, I have been careful in leaving to the 
Turkish Commissioner the responsibility of giving to further proceedings such 
lecal forms as may, in his opinion, satisfy the ends of justice, without over- 
stepping the powers delegated to him by the Sublime Porte. My French 
colleague has, in general, on reflection, agreed with my views, 

| have now the honour of inclosing, for your apt information, 
translation of the report of the Commission sitting as a Court of Inquiry. It is 
the draft framed by M. Sabatier and myself, and finally accepted by seid Hamad 
Pasha, After the signature of that report, the functions o the Commissioners 
in regard to the criminals must necessarily differ. It will be the duty of 
M. Sabatier and myself to call for the punishment of those whom we conscien- 
tiously believe to be guilty; it will be the duty of Seid Hamdi Pasha to satisly 
the ends of justice, so far as he can do, by the Bay delegated to him, and 
with whatever executive means may be, reluctantly, placed at his disposal by 
Namick Pasha, whom the Porte has already judged fit to remove from the 
Government of the Hedjaz, 

That Namick Pasha has been culpably negligent, if not somethmg worse, is 
sufficiently clear from the now. established tact, that the so-ealled tribunal 
constituted to try the poor wretches exeeuted by Ismail Pasha at the time of the 
bombardment included in its members the very individuals that’ our recent 
inquiry has proved to have been most criminal, whether a8 instigators or abettors 
of the massacre, 

Whilst consenting to allow of Ibrahim Aga, Kaimakam, being sent to 
Constantinople, where probably his punishment tay be commuted to imprison 
ment, it is the clearly expressed intention of M, Sabatier and myself that 
Abdallah el Mohtessib and Sheikh Amoodee shoald be immediately executed here 
as an example calculated to produce a salutary effect upon the town of Jeddah, 
where suel an example appears to be much required. 

Verbal communications, which my colleague and myself have just received 
from the ‘Turkish Commissioner, lead us to expect that the fatter will receive 
from Namick Pasha the least possible aid, if, indeed, any uid whatever. But to 
an invitation from the Governor-General to an interview with M. Sabatier and 
myself, for the purpose of discussing the course to be pursued in reference to the 


decision of the Commission, we have replied that we can treat only with the 
Commissioner specially delegated by the Porte. 
The questions of claims to indemnity will be entered upon in two or three 
days, if unexpected circumstances do not prevent the preparation of the papers. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) ALFRED 8. WALNE.

(Telegraphic.) Constantinople, January 21, 1859, 9 rom. 

THE Turkish Government gives precise orders to Turkish Commissioner to 
treat with French and English Commissioners as to amount of indemnity. lf 
all opinions agree, the Turkish Commissioner will sign the joint report. If not, 
a separate one, and the Porte will adjudge. 

This Government reserves the question finally for itself, not knowing 
amount of indemnity that may be demanded, nor how it could best be raised ; 
but fully agrees to the principle of indemnity and to the consideration of the 
amount being a portion of Commissioners’ duty.
