Inclosure in No. 356. 
Captain Pullen to the Secretary to the Admiralty. 


Sir, ® Cyclops,” Jeddah, December 14, 1658. 

| BEG to acknowledge the receipt, on the 28th ultimo, of your letter 
of the 23rd of October last, with its several inclosures, relative to the 
British ship “ Eranee,” seized by my authority, for having hoisted Turkish 
colours at this place, and signifying their Lordships’ directions to me to report 
what has been done in the matter. 

® Mv letter of the 2nd of last month will have informed their Lordships 
that 1 had sent the “ Eranee” to Bombay, to be delivered to the Vice-Admiralty 
Court there, and of my reasons for so doing. 

3. With reference to my letter to his Excellency Namick Pasha, dated the 
93rd of June, last, referred to by the Law Olficers of the Crown in their opinion, 
I beg to call your attention to the answer of his Exeelleney thereto, viz., that 
on the terms [ required he could not receive this ship: this would have decided 
me at once in sending her to a British port for adjuc ication, but it was. imprac- 
tieable to obtain ballast in the then state of the populace, and nothing like order 
or government of any kind being restored, it would have been very dangerous 
to the lives of the men placed in her to have allowed them to remain on board 
the ship in the absence of the “Cyclops,” 

4 At the time, however, the crew were withdrawn, and the vessel left in 
charge of the chief mate. | 

5. On my return to this place in July last, she had the Turkish colours 
again flying, contrary to my protest to the Pasha; thus again by act of her 
alleged owner she beeomes forteited. 1 immediately informed the Katmakam of 
this cireumstance, and stated that unless the colours were immediately pulled 
down, | would send the ship outside, and either burn or sink her; after a long 
delay, the authorities complied with my demand, 

“G, On my return in October last, 1 informed his Excellency of my deter- 
mination to send the ship to Bombay, and gave written notice thereof to the 
alleged owner, in order that he should be prepared to defend any action at law 
commenced against him. 

+. Although the various letters have given every information with regard to 
this affair, | will shortly recapitulate facts which were proved, either in evidence 
or by my documents. 

(1,) That the * Eranee” is a British-registered ship. 

(2.) That on two (or more) occasions, namely, on the 15th of June and 
the 23rd of July, she lying at Jeddah, had endeavoured to change her nationality 
and character, by hoisting Turkish colours, and by having her proper name 
erased from her stern. 

he Merchant Shipping Act provides penalties for these offences, for one a 

enalty of not more than 1O0l.: for the other, forfeiture of the ship to Her 
Majesty. 


237 


8. With regard ‘to the question of Turkish jurisdiction over questions 
concerning British subjects, | refer to the Treaties in foree with the Ottoman 
Porte on the subject, and especially to the Act 6 & 7 Vict. cap. 4, establishing 
Her Majesty's jurisdiction, to all mtents and purposes as if the offence had been 
pecs in oe seat dominions. 

. These Laws and Treaties have been my guide in the matter, and which 
I have caused to be fulfilled to the best of aN ‘ability, and Eee. . their 
common-sense meaning and interpretation, 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) W. 1.8. PULLEN.

Inclosure 1 in No. 358. 
Commodore Edgell to Rear-Admiral Sir M. Seymour. 


Sir, “ Chesapeake,” Jeddah, January 1, 1859. 


1 HAVE the honour to forward, for the information of your Excellency, 
a report of proceedings since my arrival at Jeddah, and inclose a copy of a letter 
from Mr. Walne, Her Majesty’s Commissioner, giving me, as | have requested, 
a statement of the pores of the Commission up to this date, which will give 
you (and their Lordships, to whom I send a duplicate of this) all the information 

possess on the subject. 

The letter of Captain Seymour, 25th December, will have informed their 
Lordships of the arrival of the Commissioners, and the instructions of M. Sabatier, 
the French Commissioner. 

The French claims are, | believe, arranged, antl M, Sabatier proposes to 
leave in four or five days in the “ Duchayla” for Suez, to await at Cairo further 
instructions from his Government. 

Mr. Walne trusts that by the 18th instant he will have arranged the claims 
for indemnity as far as the actual sums rec uired are concerned ; but the Turkish 
Commissioner has not brought with him those full powers which were expected, 
and the question will have to be referred to Constantinople, 

It is Mr. Walne’s intention to leave for Cairo when ready, and I shall direct 
Captain Seymour, of the “ Pelorus,” to convey him there, and unless I receive 
other instructions from their Lordships by the return of the “ Roebuck,” which 
vessel carries these despatches to Suez, it is my intention to leave the ‘ Pelorus 
and “ Roebuck” for the present in the Red Sea, as the Commissioner requests,

and proceed to India, touching at Galle and Trincomalee, and, if possible, reach 
Calcutta to meet the Governor-General; returning to Trincomalee immediately, 
as arranged with your Excellency, expected to be there in Her Majesty’s ship 
Calcutta” in March. 

With regard to the two last paragraphs of Mr. Walne’s letter, respecting 
the necessity of employing a naval force in the Red Sea, I would beg to observe 
to your Excellency that the ships of war of the late Honourable East India 
Company have been constantly there, and their officers are perfectly acquainted 
with the various ports, the navigation of the whole being exceedingly difficult, 
owing to the numerous coral reefs which fringe the coast on either side. I 
would therefore beg to suggest to your Excellency that as many of this force 
as are required be employed on this part of the station. 

I have requested Brigadier Coghlan to keep a small depdt of coals at Perim, 
which le will endeavour to do through the Peninsular and Oriental Company ; 
this precaution is necessary, as, owing to the heayy southerly winds which 
prevail from the Island of Jibbel Jeer to Mocha, steamers making the passage 
to Aden run short of coal, and are obliged to work up against the north-east 
monsoon: a few tons from Perim would obviate this, and tune would be gained. 

From the heavy weather the Roebuck” has encountered, she leaks much 
from the upper-deck; Ihave had her caulked, as far as time and the limited 
supply of stores would allow. She had also a leak in the magazine: by removing 
the powder we have, | trust, discovered the cause, and remedied it. 

 Pelorus’' is ready for any work, and, lam happy to say, the health of the 
ships is most satisfactory.

Inclosure 2 in No. 358. 
Consul Walne to Commodore Edgell. 


Sir, Jeddah, December 31, 1858. 

WITH reference to the last paragraph of your despatch of the 28th instant, 
| have the honour to inform you that the labours of the Commission are go far 
advanced that the inquiry into the conduct of the local authorities, and with 
regard to the persons accused of being instigators of the outbreak which 
occurred in June last, is on the point of being brought to a conclusion. 

The consideration of the indemnity to be claimed for losses will occupy the 
attention of the Commission during the next week, and as many of the claims 
are of a very complicated nature, | shall consider myself fortunate if I see them 
reduced to a just estimate in the course of a fortnight. 

The state of Jeddah is not such as will allow of its being left without, at 
least, moral control from without, and os 1 have reported to Her Majesty's 
Government, even when a Consular Officer is again established at this port, he 
will for a long time require the support of a naval force. 

Circumstances have come to my knowledge which make it desirable that 
other iinportant ports of the Red Sea should from time to time be visited by a 
cruizer,

(Telegraphic. ) Constantinople, January 31, 1859. 

THE Jeddah affair is difficult. Porte agrees fully to pay indemnity herself, 
but says the town has been bombarded; some criminals hung, others since 
condemned; that some letters seized show that the Arab population accuses the 
Sultan of being sold to the Christians; and that risings may take place, if 
matters are pushed too far; and confidentially complains of Sabatier, as 
personally hostile. J and French Charge d’Affaires ure doing our utmost, and, 
to-morrow, I shall telegraph final result.

No. 370, 
Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received February 5.) 
(No. 12.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, January 14, 1859. 

I HAD the honour, on the 2nd instant, of laying before your Lordship 
translation of the Report of the Commission sitting us a Court of Inquiry. 1 
stated that it was the clearly expressed intention of my French colleague and 
myself, that the two principal criminals, Abdallah el Molitessib and Sheikh el 
Amoudi, should be immediately executed; but that we were led to expect that 
the Turkish Commissioner would receive from Namick Pasha the least possible 
aid, if, indeed, any aid whatever. 

The anticipations of the Commissioners proved to be correct, Namick 
Pasha, who, in June last, wilfully shut his eyes; who publicly received with 
honour the very persons whom we have found most criminal; who selected 
them to sit in the tribunal formed for the judgment of those who had taken part 
in the mussacre; who executed the orders of the Porte for their arrest only on 
the eve of the departure of the “ Roebuck" for Suez in November last, when 
he knew that his acts must be reported to Constantinople ; who, as it is confi- 
dentially stated, even stooped to give advice to the prisoners as to the course they 
should pursue when called before the Commission: Namick Pasha, the Governor- 
General of the Hedjaz, whose duty it was to act with and support the Turkish 
Commissioner, took upon himself to thwart his proceedings ; and, for a time, 
obstinately refused to exercise the powers which had been expressly apis

on him, under exceptional cireumstances; liy a special firman of the Sultan, and 
by special instructions from the Porte. 

Inclosed is a translation of a letter addressed to me on the 4th instant b 
the Turkish Commissioner, as well as a translation of the letter from Namic 
Pasha therein referred to, At a meeting of the Commission held on the 5th, 
Seid Hamdi Pasha explained to M. Sabatier and niyself all the difficulties which 
he had experienced with Namick Pasha, the little hope which he had of 
yrevailing over his obstinacy, and the possibility of his Le Se to suspend 

i relations with the Governor-General, and retire on board one of the vessels 
of war. 

On that occasion, M. Sabatier intimated his intention of leaving in the 
“ Duchayla,” within two days, to prdceed to Egypt, from whence he would 
immediately report to the Emperor the unwarrantable conduct of Namick Pasha. 
The Turkish Commissioner was requested again to confer with the Governor- 
General, and, if possible, persuade him to carry out the orders of the Porte. 

On the 6th, at-a meeting of the Commissioners, Seid Hamdi Pasha 
reported that Namick Pasha was obstinate, and would take no steps without 
previous reference to the Porte. His object appeared to be to gain time, in 
order to throw all responsibility on his successor, Mahmoud Pasha, whose 
arrival, it'was said, might be shortly anticipated. ; 

M. Sabatier, speaking for himself, stated that he had already announced his 
intention of leaving in the ‘‘ Duchayla,” and should do so; but that he had 
come to the firm determination that if, before the day fixed for sailing, the 
demands of the Commissioners were not complied with, and the necessary 
measures taken to secure the execution of the two principal criminals, Abdallah 
el Mohtessib and Seid Amoudi, the “ Duchayla,” for which soundings were 
taken, should be brought close to the town, and not a single shot or a single 
shell be left unemployed. | 

Looking to the discrepance in our instructions, I was not, of course, in a 
sosition to employ the same language; but, without explaining that discrepance, 
i urzed on the Turkish Commissioner to make one more effort to bring Namick 
Pasha to a sense of his responsibility. : 

The position had become somewhat critical, and one which could not fail 
to be extremely unpleasant to the Commodore in command of a squadron very 
much superior to the French force, but which must necessarily remain inactive. 
Inclosed are copies of a despatch which T addressed to Commodore Edgell, of 
his answer, and of the letter which he thought it advisable to send to the 
Commander of the “ Duchayla.” 

Early on the 7th, the Secretary of the Turkish Commissioner came off to 
M. Sabatier and myself, to announce that Namick Pasha had, at the last 
moment, yielded to the arguments of Seid Hamdi Pasha, backed as they had 
been by a threat of coercive measures on the part of the French Commissioner. 

A’ meeting of the Commissioners was held a few hours later, at which this 
intelligence was confirmed. ‘There was still an attempt on the part of Namick 
Pasha to gain time, on the plea of an outbreak of the Arabs between Taif and 
Mecea, the absence of the Sheriff, and the danger of disturbances in Jeddah 
itself: all of which pretexts were effectually silenced by the offer of such 
material support on the part of the British squadron as should enable Namick 
Pasha to move into the interior, and to take with him any troo ys that he might 
consider necessary for the protection or police of the Holy Cities. ‘Time was 
given to the Turkish authorities to complete any formalities which might be 
held essential to the ordinary course of justice in the cases of the two criminals 
who stood convicted, by their own admissions, of crimes to which the law of the 
Empire has assigned the penalty of death. ahh: 

On the 10th, M. Sabatier and myself received a communication, of which a 
translation is inclosed, to the effect that the execution of Abdallah el Mohtesstb 
and Sheikh el Amoudi would take place on the 12th: in that communication 
mention was also made of the further proceedings which had taken place with 
reference to the criminals—proceedings which, it may be presumed, amply met 
the requirements of Turkish law. 

It having been agreed by the Commission that armed detachments from the 
British and French ships of war should be present at the execution, I addressed 
to Commodore Edgell a communication of which a copy 15 inclosed, together 
with that of his answer.

On the 12th, hulBan-hour after sunrise, Abdallah el Mohtessib and Sheik el 
Amoudi were P blicly decapitated, on the platform of the Custom-house, within 
a few yards 0 ‘the kiosk in'which was held, on the 15th of June, that extra- 
ordinary couneil of the pHictry people of Jeddah, from which emanated the 
order to raise the armed mob of Hadarum, who, a little later, massacred the 
Consuls and other Christian residents, and phindered their estublishments. 

In addition to a considerable body of ‘Turkish and Egyptian troops, there 
were on the ground detachments of Marines from the * Chesapeake” and 
“ Pelorus,’ and of sailors from the “ Duchayla,” the armed boats of the 
squadron lying at a little distance from the landing-place, 

Phere remain to be sent to Constantinople, by the first opportunity that 
may offer, the Kaimakam, six others who rank a6 principal sfisiers, and three 
to whom a less degree of criminality has been assigned. In the second category 
is Saleh Gohar, whose Samanta proceedings with regard to the “ Eranee”’ 
were the indirect cause of the outbreak, and who was himself present at the 
council from which issued the order to raise the Hadarum. Had he been, as 
represented, a British subject, 1 should have thought it necessary to refer his 
case to Her Majesty's Government; but during the inquiry before the Commis- 
sion, | fully ascertained that Saleh Gohar, though born in the Morea, is a 
Moslem, claiming to be an Ottoman subject, and not in any way subject to 
British jurisdiction within the Ottoman territory. 

The principal instigators of the massacre in Jeddah having been now either 

unished, or handed over to the Porte for future punishment, it is my intention 
to farnish the Turkish Commissioner with a list of persons of minor importance, 
who, it is stated, took part, more or less, in the pillage of the houses of the 
Christians, but most of whom have found it convenient to withdraw themselves 
for a time from the direct jurisdiction of the local authorities. 

A more pleasing duty remains to M. Sabatier and myself, that of recom- 
mending to the ‘Turkish Commissioner, and through him to the Porte, several 
public officers who conducted themselves well during a period of difficulty ; as 
well as several private individuals, who, not without great risk, and in some 
cases considerable loss to themselves, gave protection and shelter to unfortunate 
Christians, who during the fearful events of June would, without such shelter, 
have inevitably been sacrificed to the fury of a fanatic rabble, excited to hunt 
them to the death. ‘ 

Acting in accordance with M. Sabatier, I have by a letter, of whieh a copy 
is inclosed, expressed to the Turkish Commissioner my approval of the measures 
taken by him to satisfy the ends of justice. 

It is due to Seid Hamdi Pasha that 1 should call your Lordship’s attention 
to his eonduct during the criminal inquiry which is now terminated. Under 
circumstances of difficulty, this officer has shown much judgment and firmness, 
and: his conduct has contrasted most favourably with that of Namick Pasha, in 
whose hands the Porte had injudiciously placed powers superior to those 
conferred on the ‘Turkish Commissioner. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) ALFRED S. WALNE.

Namick Pasha to Seid Pasha. 
(Traduction.) 


Excellence, Le 28 Gamad Aoual, 1275. (3 Janvier, 1859.) 


LORSQUE vous étes venu chez moi, yous m’avez fait econnaitre quen 
conséquence de la décision prise entre vous et MM. les Commissaires, Abdallah 
Mohtessib et Seid el Amoudi devraient étre mis A mort; que les autres inculpés 
seraient ou envoyés & Constantinople, ou retenus en prison jusqu’d la réception 
d’un ordre; et que si cela n’avait pas lien, on attendratt Varrivée de mon succes- 
seur. Vous m'avez pri d’y mettre de lactivite. 

Bien que je vous aie fait connaitre les inconvénients qui pourraient en résulter, 
vous avez jugé convenable de m’écrire officiellement. J'ai parfaitement, compris le 
contenu de votre lettre, qui m’est arrivée hier au soir. Je vous diral que pour 
lexécution de ces individus j'avance deux excuses. La premiére est celle-ci;— 
Selon usage l'enguéte a eu lieu sécrétement, entre vous et MM. les Com- 
missaires: tout le monde ignore quels sont leurs aveux, quel est le degré de 
leur culpabilité, et le motif du chatiment. Dans l'état actuel des choses dans 
!Hedjaz, cette exécution précipitée augmenterait les troubles qui existent parmi 
les tribus Arabes des environs. D*aprés Ja loi, et de l'avis de tous les hommes 
compétents, Ia peine de mort est considéré comme la peine la plus sévére, 
Puisque vous yous en rapporter 4 moi quant a l’exéeution, jassumerais la respon- 
sabilité de tout ce que cette affaire pourrait avoir de mauvais, et comme 
Vexécution aurait lieu sur vos seules instances, je n’aurais rien en mains pour 
en répondre devant Dieu; et dans ee cas je ne ‘pourrais me soustraire 4 la 
responsabilité qui peserait sur moi dans ce monde et dans l'autre. Pour me 
soustraire & eette responsabilité, il faut que le jugement soit établi par une 
pidce émanée des hommes de la loi. Si ce jugement est rendu, bien; mais s'il 
ne lest pas, l'exécution deviendra trés difficile. 

Aprés m’étre livré & ces considérations, je n'ai pas le courage de faire cette 
exécution. J’espére que vous voudrez bien admettre une de ces raisons, et que 
tous les trois vous voudrez bien m’excuser. Mais dans le cas que ma priére 
n’est pas acceptée, et que l’on me force d’agir, comme je suis destiné, et que je 
dois partir pour Constantinople, j’abandonnerai l'administration du pays, dont je 
ne suis que momentanément chargé, en attendant Varrivée de mon successeur ; 
et je vous ceris la presente pour votre information. 


(Signé) MOHAMMED NAMICK.

being shortly commenced against the town of Jeddah by the French vessel 
“Duchayla,” at the instance of the French Commissioner, M. Sabatier. 

The French, British, and Turkish Commissioners entered, on the 4th 
ultimo, on an inguiry into the causes of the outbreak of June last, which had 
had for its sequel the massacre bf the English and French Consuls, and of a 
sortion of the Christian population at Jeddah, as well as the pillage of their 
hous and establishments. The procés-verbaux of the interrogatories were not 
closed till the 28th of December: and, on the Ist instant, after much ond 
serious discussion, the Commissioners recorded their unanimous opinion. The 
inquiry which had, for so many days, occupied their entire attention, had 
produced a perfect conviction on their minds of the guilt, in their respective 
categories, of the parties enumerated in thatdocument. Of the three considered 
most culpable, Abdallah el Mohtessib, Sheikh el Amoudi, and Ibrahim Kaimakam: 


_ the first confessed that he gave orders to raise the armed mob of THydramaut on 


the 15th of June; the second that he had actually raised them; the third, if not 
equally implicated with the others, had, at least, neglected every duty imposed 
on him by the position of Lieutenant-Governor. 

Reasons were urged by the Turkish Commissioner for placing Ibrahim 
Kaimakan at the disposal of the Porte, with a view to his receiving such 
commuted punishment as the Sultan might, in his clemency, think fit to assign 
him ; but it was the unanimous opinion of the Commissioners that Abdallah el 
Mohtessib and Sheikh el Amoudi should suffer the extreme penalty of their 
crimes in Jeddah itself, a8 a salutary example to those who had taken part in the 
massacre and pillage, or who, for want of such example, might be tempted to 
engage in similar crimes. It was the distinctly-expressed expectation of my 
French colleague and myself that this example should be made as early as was 
consistent with the powers possessed by the Turkish authorities, 

Although the Commission, as a body, in its report expressed a very decided 
opinion as to the culpability of the parties, and went even so fur as to indicate the 
punishments applicable to them respectively, the French and English Com- 
missioners left to the Turkish Commissioncr alone the duty of taking such 
farther proceedings as he might think necessary to the ends of justice. ‘The latter, 
on his part, applied to the Governor of the Hedjaz, Namick Pasha, to execute 
Abdallah el Mohteasib and Sheikh el Amoudi, but received, first verbally, and 
subsequently in writing, a positive refusal to take any part in the measures 
suggested by the Commission ; although we know officially that the Mushir has 
in his possession a special firman from the Sultan authorizing him to punish, 
even capitally, any persons convicted as instigators and abettors of the outbreak 
and massacre of June. 

At a meeting of the Commission held yesterday, M. Sabatier announced 
that if satisfaction were not given by the immediate execution of Abdallah el 
Mohtessib and Sheik el Amoudi, he should, within two days, leave in the 
“Duchayla,” and proceed to Egypt, with a view of reporting to the Emperor 
of the French the conduct of the ‘Turkish authorities. 

But to-day, at a conference of the Commissioners, M, Sabatier communi- 
eated to the Turkish Commissioner, in my presence, that soundings were already 
taken, that the * Duchayla” would be brought near the town, and that, failing 
satisfaction before the time fixed for his departure, he would not leave a shot or 
a shell of that vessel unemployed. 

In the delicate position in which a divergence of instructions has placed us, 
[have endeavoured to work as cordially as possible with my French colleague, 
and have urged the Turkish Commissioner to exert himself once more to obtain 
from Numick Pasha the satisfaction most justly demanded, 

But the time is now arrived in which the instructions of my colleague and 
myself are too much at variance to allow of their being conciliated. M, Sabatier 
has such orders as apparently justify him in employing coercive measures, 
whilst, as you fire aware, my own sui prescribe that hostilities shall not be 
resorted to without previous reference to Her Majesty’s Government. 

The obstinacy of Namick Pashn is such that, knowing the character of the 
man, | have little hope of his yielding; and the position taken up by M. Sabutier 
is one from which he can with difficulty retire. 

Under these circumstances, it is necessary to consider what measures it 
may be advisable to take for the protection of British subjects and propetty on

Consul Walne to Seid Pasha. 


Excellency, Jeddah, January 13, 1859, 

| HAD the honour of receiving your Excelleney’s letter dated the 
Sth Gamad el Ahar, 1275 (10th January, 1859), communicating to me. the 
arders given by the Governor-General of the Hedjaz for the execution of 
Abdallah el Mohtessib, and Seid el Amoudi, convicted of having been the prin- 
cipal instigators of the fearful massacre that took place in this town on the 
15th of June last. 

Justice having now had its course with reference to these criminals, and 
provision being made for carrying into effect the recommendations of the 
Commission with regard to the other prisoners who are to be sent to Constanti- 
nople, the time is arrived in which, in common with M. Sabatier, I am at 
liberty to express to your Excellency my satisfaction at the decided measures 
which have been taken to meet the just demands of my colleague and myself. 
It will be my duty to report proceedings to Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of 
State for the Foreign Department, and I confidently hope that the satisfaction 
given, so far as relates to criminal questions, may be considered sufficient by 
Her Majesty's Government. bes 

The questions of pecuniary indemnity for losses sustained during the events 
of June have still to occupy your Excellency’s attention; but | avail myself of 
this opportunity to thank your Excellency for the cordial concurrence which has 
hitherto been afforded me, and to express to your Excellency my high opinion of 
the judgment and firmness which have enabled you to carry out, under cireum- 
stances of diffieulty, the unanimous decision by which the Commission closed 
the first and most difficult part of its lengthened inquiries. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) ALFRED 8, WALNE,

Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmeshury.—(Recewed February 5.) 
(No, 13.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, January 14, 1859. 


IN my despatch of the 2nd instant, No. 10, I reported to your Lordship 
that the questions of indemnity would be entered on in two or three days, if 
unexpected circumstances did not prevent the preparation of the papers. 

ince then the difficulties experienced with regard to criminal questions 
have so completely occupied the time of the Turkish Commissioner, that it has 
been impossible to enter upon any serious discussion with regard to civil claims, 
though I have myself in some measure profited by the interval to examine 
papers, obtain Seaeatat from the barrister who represents the greater part of 
the claimants, and call for further documents in support of their demands, 
several of which have, by consent, been modified and refused in amount. 

M. Sabatier, who ison the eve of departure in the “ Duchayla,” has sent 
to the Turkish Commissioner a short list of Freneh claims, with brief observa- 
tions; but he.distinctly declines to enter into any discussion whatever upon their 
merits, reserving to himself to report thereon to his Government, with which 
alone, in his opinion, rests the final decision. 

Though without precise instructions for my guidance, [ think Tshall hest 
mect the wishes of your Lordship by pursuing a different course; and | propose 
to enter fairly with the Turkish Commissioner into explanations on each claim. 
But having once formed a deliberate opinion as to the award which ought to be 
given, I shall not readily admit modification on his part, though such award will 
of course be held subject to the approval of your Lordship. 

Two or three of the most important claims present great difficulties even to 
a person having, like myself, local information which it is impossible to convey 
fully to others. The books and documents of Toma Sava and Co. have been 
desionedly destroyed, and proofs in favour of the principal establishment, Toma, 
Myrialaki, A. d'Antonio, and Co., have to be brought from Hodeida, Cairo, and 
other distant places: they are necessarily such as in a Court of law would be 
hardly admissible, though in an equitable point of view, and under the peculiar 
circumstances of the case, they are entitled to greater consideration than could 
be given to them in ordinary suits, 

At best [ can only hope to arrive at on approximative estimate of the 
indemnity to be assigned to that house, for it is questionable whether the 
surviving partners are even now themselves fully aware of the extent of their 
losses. 

Although the paper is incomplete, IL inclose, for your Lordship’s informa- 
tion, a tabular statement of the claims as they now stand, and as they are 
shortly to be presented to the Turkish Commissioner. Under the heading of 
“ Award proposed by British Commissioner,” will be found the conclusions at 
which I have arrived, after due reflection, with reference to eleven cases, the 
others being still under consideration, 

The total amount of claims, in their reduced form, but with reserve for 
interest, if the indemnity be not paid within a reasonable time, say the Ist of May, 
1859, is 579,7654 Austrian dollars. From this it 1s possthle that some further 
reduction may be made in respect of the two large claims Nos. | and 9, in 
support of which additional documents have been called for, and regarding which 
there may be much discussion with the Turkish Commissioner, before even an 
epproximative award can be proposed on my own part, 

Of the claim of Farag Yusur, No.7, 1 have inserted in the list only one 
portion, reserving for reference to your Lordship, in a separate despateh, that 
part of his demands which arises from losses sustained during the bombardment 
of Jeddah by Her Majesty's ship “* Cyelaps.” 

Whether it be decided by the Porte to raise the amount of mdemnity from 
the town of Jeddah, or to draw it from other sources, it is at Cairo that the 
greater part of the payments must be ultimately effected, The suggestion of 
Captain Pullen, made in his despatch of the 3rd of November, thot the funds 
should, in the first instance, be remitted to England, would, if acted on, lead to 
a considerable loss in carriage and exchanges ; and | must submit to ae Lari-

“ My Lord, Jeddah, January 14, 1859. 


IN my despatch of the 22nd of December, No, 4, 1 mentioned the claim 
of Farag Yusur for the loss of two buglehs (large boats) valued at 4,000 dollars, 
which were amongst the vessels destroyed by the armed boats of the “ Cyclops” 
during the bombardment of Jeddah, 

Thave the honour to lay before your Lordship, with copy of the original 
claim of Farag Yusur, copies of two affidavits which have recently been sworn 
before me, and which throw much light upon the circumstances under which 
those vessels and many others, belonging to French and English protégés as well 
as ‘Turkish subjects, were, as it is now very generally considered, unnecessarily 
burnt, sunk, or otherwise destroyed. 

Some explanations of Captain Pullen's proceedings may, perhaps, be found 
in his correspondence with the Admiralty, but among the papers which he has 
handed to me I find no information whatever. 

After talking over the matter with M. Sabatier, who has hesitated to 
advance the claims for losses under this head which have been sent to him, and 
after taking information from naval authorities as to what course they would 
themselves have pursued in the circumstances in which Captain Pullen was

On the same day, the officer commanding Her Majesty's ship ‘‘ Cyclops ” 
bombarded the said town, and, with an armed force, attacked, destroyed, burnt, 
and sunk divers vessels, including among them the above-mentioned two vessels 
of the said Farag Yisr, in the said port, to the damage of the said Farag Yusr 
of 6,500 dollars, being 4,000 dollars on aceount of the value aforesaid of the 
said two yessels, and 2,500 dollars which he would have acquired as profit from 
the use of the said two vessels if they had not been so destroyed. 

Your petitioner is instructed by the said Tarag Yusr to state that he’ has, 
since the said 25th day of July, been informed that the said bombardment and 
attack were executed by order of Her Majesty's Government, in consequence of 
the refusal by the Governor of the said town, after a reasonable lime for 
compliance had been granted to him, and the consequences, as mentioned, of 
such refusal duly notified to him, to afford certain reparation rightfully 
demanded of him for the murder of Her Majesty's Acting Vice-Consul, and of 
the Vice-Consul of His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of the French, and of 
many Christian residents, and for the plunder of their property, and for outra 
to the flazs of England and France, and to divers persons and things nah 
their Majesties’ protection, by Ottoman Mahometan subjects in the said town, 
on the 15th duy of June, 1858, and following days; and that the Sublime 
Ottoman Porte has consented to indemnify all persons under their Majesties’ 
jurisdiction, for losses and damages occasioned to them by the above-described 
acts of murder, plunder, and outrage by Ottoman subjects, or by proceedings 
resulting therefrom: and that a Commissioner has been appointed on the part 
of Her Majesty, and another on that of His Imperial Majesty, to. proceed 
together to the said town of Jeddah, for the purpose of settling the amount of 
such indemnity. 

Your petitioner is also instructed by the said Farag Yasr, to state that the 
said Governor did not, as was his duty, at any time before such bombardment 
and attack, of which he had due notice as aforesaid, afford to the persons, 
including the said Parag Yiisr, residing under foreign jurisdiction in the said 
town and port, or to their property, including the above-mentioned two vessels, 
there, any protection against such bombardment and attack; or give due notice 
thereof to the said persons who could not otherwise obtain such notice; or give 
due notice that there was such property im the suid town and port, to the 
officer commanding Her Majesty’s said ship, 80 as to enable him or the said 
persons to protect such property from such bombardment and attack ; although 
such bombardment and attack was, as mentioned, a proceeding necessary for 
obtaining reparation for the said acts of murder, plunder, and outrage, and was, 
in fact, consequent to and caused by those acts: and that, therefore, the said 
Farag Yiisr, is entitled to be indemnified for his above-mentioned damage by 
the Sublime Ottoman Porte. . 

Wherefore, in the absence of a British Consular Officer at Jeddah, your 
petitioner prays on behalf of the said Farag Yusr, that you will be pleased to 
take such steps in the subject of this petition for communicating the same to 
Her Majesty’s Ambassador at Constantinople, or to Her Majesty's Commis- 
sioner aforesaid, and for obtaining for the said Farag Yiisr the indemnity above 
claimed by him, as the case may require. 

And your petitioner will ever pray, Se.

Deposition. 
Re Farag Yter (“ el Durreh.”) 


THIS Sth day of January, avo. 1859, at Jeddah, before me, Alfred 8. 
Walne, Esquire, Her Britannic Majesty’s Commissioner for the affairs of 
Jenin, appeareth Hassan Khadhr ibn Ahmed, of Jeddah, and maketh oath and 
saith :— 

In the month of Zu-Lhiggeh, a.m, 1274, corresponding to the period 
between the 12th day of July and the 10th day of August, 1858, I was the reis 
or master of the vessel named “el Durreh,” belonging to the Hadji Faraj 

Yiisr, of Jeddah, 

About the middle of the said month of Zu-l-higgeh the town of Jeddah was 
bombarded by the officer commanding Her Britannic Majesty's ship ‘* Cyclops.” 
On the morning following the commencement of the bombardment, the boats of 
the said ship, manned and armed, attacked the merchant-vessels lying at anchor 
in the usual anchorage before Jeddah, Neither the persons on board of the said 
vessel “ Durreh,”’ nor those on board of any of the said vessels, so far as I could 
observe their proceedings, did anything to provoke this attack upon them. We 
we at the time of the said attack, on board the “ Durreh,” tyself and one 
BELT. 

Between 4 and 5 o'clock, corresponding to between 9 and 10 o'clock by 
European reckoning, on the said morning, a boat containing eleven armed men 
irom Her said Majesty's ship came alongside, and nine or ten of the said men 
boarded the said Durreh.” “No one of them could speak our language, which was 
Arabic, nor any of us theirs. We could not comprehend what they wanted. 
Immediately they got on board they collected the sails of the vessel, our clothes, 
and other combustible things together, and placing them in the body of the 
vessel, put gunpowder among them, and fired them. When we saw that, we 
called out to them in Arabie that the vessel they were in belonged to Farag 
Yusr, They teok no notice of us, but re-embarked in their boat, and remained 
at a short distance to observe the progress of the flames. The fire daa 
inereased, and took hold of the vessel. The boat again approached the vessel, 
whereupon I and the sailors with me on board the vessel becoming afraid, 
jumped into the sea and swam ashore, ‘The vessel was completely consumed by 
the fire. We lost everything we had on board. 

The burden of the said vessel ‘el Darreli” was 750 ardebs, and its value, 
including its tackle and furniture, which were also consumed, 2,500 Austrian 
dollars. Ihave been a master of vessels in the Red Sea for more than forty 
years, and know well their value. 

In witness whereof the said Hassan Khadhr ibn Ahmed hath, this day and 
year above written, hereunto set his seal. 

(L.8.) HASSAN KHADHR IBN AHMED. 


Sworn before me the day and year above mentioned. 
(Signed) Atreep $. Watne, Her Majesty's Commissioner.

stood by the deponent,

No. 373. 
Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Recewed February 7.) 


(No. 15.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, January 19, 1859. 


YOUR Lordship’s despatches Nos. 4 to 13 inclusive reached me only on 
the 17th instant, having been browght from Suez by Her Majesty's ship 
* Roebuck.” —, 

As I have already reported to your Lordship, the Commission had previously 
closed its inquiry as to the causes of the outbreak at Jeddah ; had recorded an 
unanimous decision as to the facts established: and given its opinion as to the 
kore degrees of culpability of the criminals implicated in the atrocities of 

une last. 

The instructions intended for my guidance in the direction of this inquiry 
arrived too late to have any influence on my proceedings: those addressed to 
M. Sabatier will meet him at Suez, for which port he left in the “ Duchayla” 
on the 15th instant. 

Inclosed is a translation of a proclamation issued by the Governor-General 
of the Hedjaz immediately alter the execution of Abdallah el Mohtessib and 
Seid el Amoudi, copies of which, it 1s understood, will be published, if not at 
Mecca and Medina, at least in the principal ports of the Red Sea. 

The execution of these criminals, on the very scene of an atrocious con- 
spiracy, was an act of public justice, indispensable as an example, without which 
there would be no security for the lives of Christians in any port of the Red 
Sea, The immediate effect has been to inspire a salutary fear among the inha- 
bitants of Jeddah, who, at the same time, are by no means sorry to be freed from 
such an arch-oppressor as Abdallah el Mohtessib ; but at Mecca public prayers 

have, | understand, been offered up in favour of the criminals, who are, no 
doubt, considered martyrs by a conclave of Mussulman fanatics gathered 
together in that so-called holy city. 
T have, &e. | : 
(Signed) ALFRED §, WALNE. 


Inclosure in No. 373. 


Translation of proclamation published in the quarters of Jeddah, and at the 
Mekkeh gate of the town, on Wednesday, the 8th of Gamad Ahar, 1275 
(corresponding to the 12th of January, 1859), by order of the Local Govern- 
ment, for general information, and as intended to be sent to all the towns 
of Hedjaz and Yemen, that the same may also there be known. 


KNOW all men, concerning the circumstance which happened in Jeddah, 
on the 3rd day of Zilkadeh, 1274 (15th of June, 1858) on the part of the 
lower orders of the people dwelling therein, that they rose np and dared 
to kill the Consul of the honourable Government of France, and the Consul 
of the honourable Government of England, then residing in Jeddah, and 
attacked them in their houses and dwellings, while under the safety and 
protection of the High Ottoman Government; and that they killed the said 
Consuls, and eighteen persons of those dwelling in security, and of the Christian 
subjects of the High Government, and plundered their property, and that the 
event was most grave, and contrary to law, and opposed to the will of the High 
Government of His Majesty, and to the dictates of humanity, and that thereupon 
was sent from the part of the High Government, and from the parts of the two 
honourable before-mentioned Governments, Commissioners for the purpose of 
inquiring into, and ascertaining who were the cause of the occurrence of the said 
event, and who instigated it; and that on their arrival, there took place a 
Council and questions in the presence of the Commusstoners, and that it was 
authenticated and proved in the Council, by the confession of Abdallah, the 
former Mohtessib (Chief of Police) of Jeddah, that it was he who instructed a 
man of the Hadarem, by name Seid el Amoudi, to bring all the Hadarem with 
their arms, and that they presented themselves on his summons, and that by

reason of the assemblage of them, and of the lower orders of the town, the 
disturbance was occasioned, and that they then attacked and killed the said 
Consuls, and those in security, and Christian subjects of the Government, to the 
number above-mentioned, and that they plundered their property ; and that the 
question was put to the said Seid el Amoudi, who also confessed that it 
was he who instructed the Hadarem to assemble for the above-mentioned 
urpose. 

: Phat then, pursuant to the confessions of the said two-named persons as 
mentioned in the Council, the Commissioners demanded the death of the said 
two men who were the cause of the occurrence of the said event, and the 
deportation of those who assisted them with their counsels and presence at 
the time spoken of, to Constantinople, in order to their receiving. fitting 
punishment there, and that after obtaining such confessions, and after the 
demand of execution by the Commissioners, as mentioned, the question was 
again put to Abdallah el Mohtessth and to Seid el Amoudi, concerning what 
they had deposed and confessed at the former meeting of the Commissioners, 
in the presence of the Commissioner of the Sublime Potte, the Mir Liva, his 
Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, and his Excellency Khaleel Pasha, Kaimakan 
of Jeddah, and the representative of the noble law the Cadi, the Sheik 
Abdallah Stnny Effendi, and others, when the said two men again deposed and 
confessed orally, in the presence of the persons mentioned, to the effect of their 
previous confessions at the time of the question; they being perfectly within 
their own diseretion, and not under coercion or intimidation. And that on its 
being established that the said two men stated that they were the cause and the 
instigators of the event which occurred, according to their past and subsequent 
confessions, then, in pursuance of the High Imperial firman, and the Govern- 
ment instructions, and the Vizirial order to put to death and destroy the 
movers in, and originators of, the said event, forthwith and without delay, and 
without reference, took place, by due authority, the death and destruction of 
Abdallah el Mohtessib and of Seid el Amoudi, as a punishment and warning 
and monition, conformably with their wicked deeds and Infamous actions, a5 
proceeding from them, and proved against them by their own confessions. And 
that inasmuch as His Majesty our Lord the Sultan has committed the necessary 
faculty to the Mussulman body to kill whoever is legally deserving of death, 
that was authorized by law: but that, as to whoever among the people should 
have assisted and abetted in the said event, should be sent to Coustantinople, m 
order to receive there, punishment according to his deserts, be it of exile or of 
imprisonment, 

And let this be a warning and a caution to all against the doing of 
evil actions, which may lead to disturbances and guilty acts, and to events such 
as have happened. 

And let all this be knawn to you.

(No. 16.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, January 19, 185%. 


WITH veference to your Lordship’s despatch of the 25th of November, 
No. 7, touching the course to be pursues in regard to Syed Fuzl, | have to 
report that I experience some ifficulty in carrying out your Lordship's 
instructions. 

In my despatch of the 24th of December, No, 8, | explained to your Lordship 
that, during the inquiry before the Commission, | had seen no evidence whatever 
of interference on the part of Syed Fuzl in the outbreak of June; nor have any 
facts since come to my knowledge calculated to criminate him as an accessory to 
the massacre, cither before or after the fact. 

Of crimes committed by Syed Fuzl within British territory, [have not before 
me even « statement; and T am not aware that there exists any Arsaly of Extra- 
dition between Great Britain and Turkey, in virtue of which he could be legally 


261 


Mea up by the Turkish authorities for crimes committed without the Ottoman 
territory. 

Acting, therefore, on the last paragrapa of your Lordship's despatch, | 
propose to limit myself to engaging the Governor-General to remove the tungul 
to some place situated in the Turkish dominions in Europe, 

This fanatic passes here fora saint; and 1 have little hope that even the 
most moderate demand will meet with compliance on the part of Namick Pasha, 
or his successor. 

I beg, therefore, most respectfully to ‘submit to your Lordship whether the 
uestion had not better be at onee referred to Her Majesty's Ambassador at 
‘onstantinople ; as I feel confident that, without positive orders from the Porte, 

directed to the Governor-General of the Hedjaz, Syed Fuzt will neither be 
given up, nor removed from his present asylum.

The Earl of Malmesbury to Consul Walne. 
(No. 17.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, February 8, 1859. 

IN reply to your despatch No. 12 of the 14th ultimo, I have to inform you 
that Her Majesty's Government approve the course which you followed during 
the inquiry at Jeddah. 

I inclose, for your information, a copy of an instruction which I have 
addressed to Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople,* directing him to 
express to the Porte the satisfaction of Her Majesty’s Government at the conduct 
of Seid Hamdi Pasha; and to report the best means whereby the goodwill of 
Her Majesty's Government might be shown to those who afforded such shelter 
and protection as was in their power to Christians at the time of the massacre, 

I have to instruct you also to report to me on this point, and to send me a 
list of such persons as appeared, in the course of your inquiry, to come under 
this category. 

lam, &c. 
(Signed) MALMESBURY,

| HAVE the honour to inclose, for the information of my Lords Commis- 
sioners of the Admiralty, copies of a correspondence between Captain Tricault, 
of His Imperial Majesty’s corvette the “ Duchayla,”’ and myself, relative to the 
affairs of Jeddah, which began to assume a serious aspect. 

Their Lordships will perceive that, after long. delays, the Commissioners 
decided unanimously on the guilt of certain parties brought before them, and, 
after mature deliberation, accorded against their several names the sentences 
which, in their opinion, ought to be carried out by Namick Pasha, the Governor- 
General, who has full authority from the Porte to order any punishments that 
the Commissioners unanimously declared to be commensurate with the crimes 
committed. 

On Namick Pasha’s refusing to carry out the extreme penalty of the law 
upon Abdallah el Mohtessib and Sheikh el Amoudi, the two principals, the 
French and English Commissioners differed in opinion as to what measures 
should be adopted to decide him on rendering justice to the two Governments, 
M, Sabatier determined to resort to force, having full powers to do so from his 
Government, whilst the instructions of Mr. Walne and myself were most, 
explicit in directing us to refrain from any act of hostility, without firat ecommu- 
nicating with the Home Government. Placed in this position, I’was reluctantly 
obliged to inform my colleague, Captain Tricault, that, although I should be 
happy to render him all the moral support in my power, I still, under the 
circumstances, could not assist in the measures suggested and determined on by 
M. Sabatier, viz. the bombardment of the town of Jeddah, which, in my 
opinion, would not enable us to secure the execution of the criminals. 

The Turkish Commissioner was not aware of any discrepancy existing 


263 


between the ordérs of the Commissioners, and by the joint entreaties of 
M. Sabatier and Mr. Walne, proceeded once more to Namick Pasha to point 
out the necessity of his carrying out the power entrusted to him oY the Porte, 
and what misery his obstinacy would entail on the inhabitants, as well a3 himself, 
should he, by his refusal, exposg: the town to a bombardment. Happily the 
Pasha was eventually induced to acquiesce in the decision of the Commissioners, 
and the execution was arranged, and carried out, at the Custom-house (the spot 
where the massacre of the Christians was plotted), at half-an-hour after sunrise 
this morning. . ‘ 

Detachments of Marines from His Imperial Majesty's corvette " Dachavla, 
and from Her Majesty’s ships “ Cheasapeake ” and “ Pelorus,” a8 arranged by 
Captain Tricault and myself, with their colours, were landed under the superin- 
tendence of Captain Beauchamp Seymour, of Her Majesty's ship “ Pelorus.” 
(whose report of the execution I inclose), and J am happy to say that at last the 
principal instigators of the savage outbreak at Jeddah in June Inst, viz. 
Abdallah el Mohiessib and Sheikh el Amoudi, the one the instigator and the 
other the leader of the rabble, met the rewant due to crimes of such fiend-lhke 
cruelty. 
Phe remainder of the prisoners, twelve in number, are to be forwarded to 
Constantinople, and 1 trust these measures will show the Mussulman population 
on the borders of the Red Sea that this fanactical spirit cannot be carried out 
with impunity, and that sooner or later a just retribution will overtake men who 
imbrue their hands in the blood of those who rejoice in the name and principles 
of a Christian. | 

[trust their Lordships will approve of Captain Seymour's measures, whia 
has been in charge here some time, and of my own in this latter part. 

Mr. Walne hopes to conclude his question relative to the indemnity about 
the midde of February, and I purpose leaving this about the end of the month 
for India, placing the ‘* Peloras'” and * Roebuck” at Mr, Walne’s disposal. 

His Imperial Majesty's corvette “ Duchayla” will convey this despatch to 
Suez on the 5th instant. 

I have 


, eee 
(Signed) HARRY EDGELL.

Inclosure 4 in No. 78. 
Captain Seymour fo Commodore Edyell. 


Sir, “Pelorus,’ Jeddah, Janwary 12, 1859. 

I HAVE: the honour to aequaint you that in compliance with your orders 
of yesterday’s date, I left the “Pelorus” at 5°15 «a.m., with the force noted in 
the margin,® in company with four boats from the French ‘ship-of-war 
* Duchayla,” whose commander, M. Tricault, obligingly sent an officer to act 
as my aide-de-camp. 

At break of day we started from the anchorage of the merchant shipping, 
and entered the narrow passage leading to the town of Jeddah. The disembarka- 
tion was effected in the order previously arranged, and the allied force, amounting 
to 62 French and 51 English, exclusive of officers, was drawn up facing the sea ; 
120 Turks, 120 Egyptians, and about 40 Bashi-Bozouks, forming the remaining 
sides of a square facing inwards. ‘The boats were moored in full view of the 
place of execution. 

In a kiosk built on the wall of the town, were seated Seid Pasha and other 
Turkish functionaries, and M. Emerat, Secretary of the French Commission, 
attended for the purpose of identifving the cnealiale 

In about ten minutes’ time the prisoners Abdallah el Mohtessib and Sheikh 
el Amoudi were brought out with their arms tied behind. Apparently no 
previous arrangement had been made to procure executioners, as two Bashi- 
Bozouks were called out from the ranks and told to exeeute the criminals, 
which they proceeded to do with the species of broad and long koife worn in 
their pirdles. 

1 will not attempt to describe the disgusting scene of butchery which 
ensued, Sheikh ei Amoudi was so fortunate as to die almost immediately, but 
Abdallah el Mohtessib received at least three wounds before he fell. Nothing 
could exeeed the stoical indifference with which both met their fate. 

Exclusive of those who attended it officially, not above fifty persons could 
have witnessed the execution, as the Turkish authorities had evidently taken 
every measure in their power to prevent its being numerously attended. | 

Qn the corpses being covered over with sheets, the force re-embarked in 
reverse order to that which they landed in, and returned to their ships. 

The only accident which occurred during the morning shows the dangers of 
the very narrow channel leading to the town. The “ Pelorus’” first-cutter being 
the last boat but one in the line, touched just ‘after dawn on a portion of the 
wreck of one of the buggalows destroyed by Captain Pullen in July last, which 
two feet on either side would have cleared her of, and which ten boats must have 
passed at that distance. Three planks of her bottom were stove, and it was

lt is impossible upon a mere estimate to levy on a small town like Jeddah 
a sum beyond its powers of endurance, But it is in accordance with precedent 
and example after having completed, without loss of time, the means of carrying 
out the best and easiest mode of settling this question, to vote, as an extraordi-

and capable of being borne by the inhabitants, and to provide for the other in

You will, therefore, in the first instance, agree with the Commissioners 
upon the teal amount of compensation, and then the portion of it to be levied 
on the town of Jeddah, in the form of an. extraordinary contribution, will be 
determined between the Sheriff of Mecca, the Governor of Jeddah, and yourself, 
The amount of this portion will be communicated by you to the other Commis- 
sioners, and should they also agree to it, then all the inhabitants of Jeddah, 
whether subjects of the Porte, or of other Powers, with the exception of such as 
suffered during the well-known occurrence, will have to be taxed, an extraordi- 
nary contribution will be assessed, on each one according to his means and 
circumstances, and it will be levied either at once, or by instalments, 

Should unanimity not prevail between you and the other Commissioners as 
to the amount of compensatiou, or as to the portion of it to be levied on the 
town, you will refer the matter for decision here without loss of time. 

Such are the instructions which have been submitted to His Majesty, and 
which His Majesty has commanded to be addressed to you. 

This resolution has been fully communicated to the Sheriff and Governor. 

The importance and delicacy of this matter will not eseape your intelligence, 
It will, therefore, be necessary for you, in the performance of His Majesty's 
commands, to give proofs of acquaintance with business,

The Secretary to the Admiralty to Mr. Hammond,—(Received February 26.) 


Sir, Admiralty, February 25, 1859. 
WITH reference to your letter of the Sth instant, inclosing copies of a 
lesan and of its inclosures from Mr. Walne, the British Commissioner at 
Jeddah, respecting a claim raised by a merchant of that place, established there 
under Her Majesty's jurisdiction, for compensation for two large boats which 
were destroyed when Jeddah was bombarded by Her Majesty's ship “Cyclops,” 
I am commanded by my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to acquaint you, 
for the information of the Earl of Malmesbury, that my Lords have taken 
Counsel's opinion in this case, and I inclose a copy of the same, as given by the 
Queen's Advocate and Mr. Atherton; by which it will be seen that no claim can 
be raised against the Turkish Government for compensation, nor can one be 
enforced at law against Her Majesty’s Government ; but that, under the cireum- 
stances of the ease, it is one rather to be left to the liberality of this Government 
for redress, 
Lam, &c. . 
(Signed) W. G. ROMAINE, 


Inclosure in No. 381. 
Opinion, 


WE do not clearly understand whether the petitioner Farag Yusur, 
described as established as a merchant under Her Majesty's jurisdiction in the 
town of Jeddah, &c., is a British subject, ora person who, although not a subject, 
enjoyed British protection. However this may be, we do not see what claim he 
can have against the ‘Turkish Government, being the State attacked, and whose 
forces in no way interfered in the destruction of the property in question. 

Neither can any recourse be had by the petitioner against Captain Pullen if 
the particular acts of destruction of his vessels were either previously ordered, or, 


267 


with fall knowledge, subsequently adopted in all their circumstances by the 
British Government. The maxim, “Respondeat superior, in that case fully 
pple are also of opinion that no eisim ean be enforced at law against the 
British Government. At the same time, we consider it our duty to point out 
that the destruction of these particular vessels would seem to have been nat 
absolutely necessary to the prosecution of hostilities, nor even uecidental ; an 
that the petitioner would seem to be left without any other redress than suc i . 
the equity or liberality of Her Majesty's Government may be disposed to affort 


under the circumstances. (Signed) J. D. HARDING. 
s W. ATHERTON.

murdered at Jeddah while actively engaged in the discharge of his duty, has lett 
an only child, a daughter about twelve years of age, and that she is now entirely 
dependent on me, her father having left her tomy eare. The Turkish Govern- 
ment, I believe, will grant her an annuity, but in the present state of that 
country, this will be a very precarious provision for her: | therefore trust that 
the Bombay Government Mil. in consideration of ber father having fallen while 
in their service, bring her case to the notice of the home authorities, with a view 
to some permanent provision being made for the unfortunate orphan, 

From Her Majesty’s Government I can expect nothing, as they look upon 
the Jeddah appointment as appertaining to India, Soliciting, therefore, your 
kind interest in this matter, I have, &c.

No. 390. 
Consul Walne to the Earl of Malmeshbury,—(Recetwwed March 16.) 


(No. 19.) 
My Lord, Jeddah, February 21, 1859. 

I HAD the honour of receiving on the 19th instant, by Her Majesty's ship 
“Roebuck,” your Lordship’s despatches Nos. 14, 15, and 16, and by the same 
opportunity I received a despatch from Her Majesty's-Ambassador, furnishing 
me with translation of the new instructions sent to the Turkish Commissioner, 
Seid Hamdi Pasha. 

In my despatch of the 4th instant, No, 18, I stated that from the 15th of 
January the Turkish Commissioner and myself had been constanly occupied 
with the examination of the claims for indemnity, and that much had already 
been effected ; I even suggested the possibility of the greater part of the cases 
being brought to a satisfactory termination in about a fortnight, As l have now 
to report that my expectations have to a great degree been disappointed, it is 
necessary that I should explain to your Lordship the compuratively satisfactory 
manner in which the early part of the negotiations in relation to the indemnity 
were condueted + the sudden and adverse change of conduct on the part of the 
Turkish Commissioner, and the reasons for that change; the little hope that J 
have of arriving at a satisfactory resalt, if the negotiations are continued at 
Jeddah; and my own view as to the best, if not the only, means of bringing 
them to a termination, 

My French colleague having withdrawn from Jeddah, without deigning to 
enter into any discussion with the Turkish Commissioner as to the details of 
French claims, it became a question between Seid Hamdi Pasha and myself as 
to how we could best conduct the examination of the British claims, on which I 
was prepared to enter. It was agreed that we should mect daily at the house 
placed at my disposal by the local authorities ; that a list having been given in 
of the claims, 1 should enter on an explanation of them one by one ; that the 
Secretary should take notes of each case, and of the supporting evidence ; and 
that, finally, the Turkish Commissioner, having obtained such further informa- 
tion on the subject as was available, should ive in, on a future day, © memo- 
randum of his opinion on the case. In this way ten claims were, in the course of 
a fortnight, disposed of in such a way as to show very little discrepancies in 
opinion, although in each case the Turkish Commissioner took care to give his 
decision subject always to the approval of his Government. Seid Hamdi 
had, in his first instructions, been directed to consult, on all matters concerning 
his mission, with the Governor-General of the Hedjaz; but, finding on the part 
of that funetionary only impediments and opposition, he had resolved to finish 
his work with me, and leave Namick Pasha to make, on his final report, any 
observations that pleased him, whether militating or not against his decisions, 

My despatch No. 18 had scarcely lett Jeddah before [ found that my 
relations with Seid Pasha had suddenly undergone a change little favourable to 
the progress of affairs. It was gradually explained to me that the Turkish 
Commissioner had received fresh instructions, brought down by the now 
Defterdar, Ramze Effendi. ‘There was no longer a possibility of treating the 
cases as between Commissioner and Commissioner. Seid Hamdi Pashit had 
been instructed to confer on all questions of indemnity with the Medjlis of 


ee PTS ee 35 Fey Es ee A Gee 0 a We eee a was 


272 


Jeddah: according to the tenour of the instructions the French and British 
Commissioners were even to appear before that honourable body to submit their 
claims, then and there to be adjudged in their presence. The instructions had 
left Constantinople a few days only after the departure of the Turkish Commis- 
sioner, and had obviously been drawn up before the Porte was fully aware of the 
real origin of the outbreak and massacre, 


At the sume time that Seid Hamdi Pasha received from the Porte instruc. 


tions which were well caleulated to embarrass a man not very clear in his 
judgment, or confident as to his position, measures were taken by Namick 
Pasha to intimidate him to the utmost, by leading him to suppose that he had 
committed 2 grievous error in urging the execution of Abdallah el Mobtessib and 
Seid Amoudi—acts that the Governor-General pointed out as in direct opposi- 
tion to the instructions of the Porte, which reached him: after the departure of 
the * Duchayla.” Namick Pasha was so triumphant as to the correctness of 
his own opinion, and the mistake of Seid Hamdi Pasha, that the latter, looking 
to the adverse influence which might be exercised at Constantinople, was fairly 
frightened out of his propriety. Our communications became rare and unsatis- 
factory, and from that day to this] have not received from him a single favourable 
answer to any one of the claims previously placed in his hands. 

Though careful not to play the game of Namick Pasha by taking up a 
position hostile to Seid Hamdi Pasha, I felt obliged to express to the latter in 
strong terms my dissatisfaction at his proceedings, of which, to do him justice, 
he appeared to be thoroughly ashamed. By his instructions he was in the 
hands of the Medjlis, and without the Medjlis he could do nothing. I, on my 
part, had been sent by Her Majesty's Government to treat with the Turkis 
Commissioner, and I had determined, in matters concerning the Commission, to 
have no communication whatever either with Namick Pasha or his creatures, 
constituting the so-called Medjlis, from neither of whom could I expect any 
decisions other than adverse to the claims which it was my duty to protect, 
within the limits of justice. 

I ineclose, for your Lordehip’s information, copies of a correspondence 
which has pnssed relative’to this incident between Seid Hamdi Pasha and 
myself; and also copy of a letter which | addressed him on the subject of the 
largest claim which we have to treat, that of Messrs. Toma Mirialachi, 
A. d’Antonio, and Co,, to which as yet | have received no answer, 

Having received from Her Majesty's Ambassador translation of the instruc- 
tions sent to the Turkish Commissioner on the 6th February, I had yesterday 
an interview with Seid Hamdi Pasha, in which I explained to him the commu- 
nications that had reached me. He had himself received no despatches, the 
bag which arrived by the “ Roebuck ” being directed to Namick Pasha, and sent 
on to Mecea, 

This morning the Turkish Commissioner cailed on me, to read an order 
which he had just received from the Vizier, of a date anterior to that of which 
Her Majesty's Ambassador had sent mea translation, ‘There was no longer a 
question of the Commissioners coming before the Council. Seid Hamdi Pasha 
was to examine the claims to indemnity, in conjunction with the French and British 
Commissioners, and endeavour to arrive speedily at equitable decisions; and if 
he could not agree with his colleagues, to refer to the Porte. It appeared to the 
Pasha, as well as to myself, that this new order relieved him to a considerable 
extent from the trammels in which he had been previously placed. He went so 
far even as to say that he should no longer object to affixing his seal to the 
awards which he had given in, though he bad previously committed himself by 
refusing, in writing, to comply with that formality. 

Notwithstanding this change which has apparently come over Seid Hammadi 
Pasha, I will not conceal from your Lordship, any more than I have concealed 
from the Turkish Commissioner, my impression that it is quite impossible that 
we can agree upon some of the cases brought under our consideration, I trust 
that Tam myself in condition to arrive at an independent judgment, without 
favour or affection; but I have lived sufficiently long in the East to know that a 
Turkish officer in the position of Seid Hamidi Pasha, when treating a question 
which affects his own Government, dares not give a decision that may possibly 
be disapproved of by his superiors, Whatever may be his private convictions, 
Seid Hamedi Pasha will congider it incumbent on him to protect to the utmost 
the interests of the Porte, and with that view he will, probably, in some of the 


273 


cases of most importance, show his zeal by giving awards quite ut variance with 
what 1 must myself propose. Were there a third Commissioner here, he might, 
perhaps, in some measure act as an umpire; but even then there would be an 
opening for reference to the Porte, | 

Looking to the great bulk of the papers which are before me, and to the 
necessity of verbal explanations, a reference could not, by mayselt be made either 
to Her Majesty’s Government or to Her Majesty's Embassy, half so effectually 
in a written communication as by a personal interview. Taking into considera- 
tion the distance between Jeddah and Constantinople, and the very slow and 
imperfect, means of communication, it occurs to me that the best, if not the only, 
means of bringing these negotiations to an end, within a reasonable period, is to 
move the three Commissioners to the capital, there to finish their work, with 
the aid, on one side, of the Porte, and on the other, of the British and French 
Ambassadors. With such an arrangement I consider it probable that questions 
which would here train on for months and months, may there be settled in afew 
days ; whilst in point of expense, as well as of time, a considerable economy would 
be effected; for our present communications with Suez, when by special steamers, 
are exceedingly expensive, 

T have talked over this matter with Seid Hamdi Pasha, who entirely agrees 
in my view, and has promised to submit the suggestion to his own Government. 
He admits that such an arrangement would relieve him of an amount of respon- 
sibity which bears heavily on him; fearing as he does the sinister influences at 
Constantinople of Namick Pasha, who will shortly return there, and who will 
not fail to vilify the Commissioner whose lot it has been to assist in detecting and 
bringing to punishment that band of conspirators whom the Mushir protected 
whilst here, and to whom, doubtless, he hopes to extend his protection 
elsewhere. F 

With reference to the amount of indemnity to be raised from the town of 
Jeddah, nothing can be done till the arrival of Ali Pasha, the new Governor 
General of the Hedjaz, who was at Suez when the ‘ Roebuck ™ left, and who ts 
expected here in a few days. The absence of a French Commissioner, and the 
little probability there is of our being able to agree on the exact amount af 
indemnity to be finally awarded to British claimants, ave difficulties which I may 
or may not be able to get over. Ido not see that in any case the presence of 
the Commissioners is necessary during the operation of taxing the town, which 
will bave to be managed by Ali Pasha, with the advice of the Sheriff of Mecca. 
The amount raised, whatever it may be, can in due time be transmitted through 
the Senior Officer of the British squadron, eetoodere 

Commodore Edgell has informed me that the “Chesapeake” will sail i 
about a week from this time. The previa: of the * Pelorus’’ are so low that 
Captain Seymour assures me that he cannot, in any ease, remain more than. a 
fortnight or three weeks. I shall do my best to push on my discussions with 
Seid Hamdi Pasha, and as soon as 1 have accomplished all that [ can effect 
here, proceed to Egypt to report the result to your Lordship. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) ALFRED S, WALNE.

In reference to your statement that since the arrival of the Defterdar in 
Jeddah, the verification of the claims to indemnity for losses and damages has 
entered on a new phase, and that the same attention is not paid to it as at the 
commencement, | beg to say that the arrival of the Detterdar in Jeddah made 
no alteration, but that the first claims were small and easy, and were verified 
with facility; the claims sent in afterwards, being very large, are difficult to 
verify, and consequently require more time for exact investigation. From the 
verification mae, it was ascertained that Sottiri Moldovano, the agent in 
Jeddah for Messrs. Paleologo and Cochilani, merchants, lost nothing during the 
outbreak; that the goods which arrived afterwards were kept in the Custom- 
house for preservation, and not having been withdrawn, they still remain there, 
It is not in my power to do more for the verification of this claim than 
has been done, 

As to the goods abandoned to the Sublime Porte, as alluded to in your 
letter, I beg to inform you that in my instructions with reference to the 
abandonment of goods or reception of such things on account of the Sublime 
Porte, not tle slightest order has been given me, 

It being my duty to examine into the damages and losses sustained hy 
persons in the outbreak, | have taken for a base the information which you 
lave given me on the cases examined by you, and have lost no time in making 
inquiries in the Medjlis of Jeddah, and from all the officers and persons 
acquainted with them, and of every case verified and adjudged information has 
been given you, 

As to the claims now in my hands, I will do my best to verify then also, 
and acquaint you with the result of my zeal and exertion, but 1 am not 
instructed to examine the indirect damages, : 

(Signature and Seal of) SEID HAMDI PASHA, 
Commissioner of the Sublime Porte in Jeddah,

My Lord, Jeddah, February 21, 1859. 

IN my despatch of the 14th January, No. 14, [had the honour of laying 
before your Lordship the elaim of Farag Yusur, for the loss of two large boats, 
geroved by the armed boats of the “Cyclops,” during the bombardment of 
Jeddah. 

I have now to submit to your Lordship a claim for 4,882 dollars, for 
damages and costs arising from the destruction, on the same occasion, of a sca- 
going vessel named the “ El Aman,” the property of a certain Ruttongy, stated 
to be a subject of Her Majesty. ‘The claim is supported by affidavits, of which 
copies are inclosed. 

In this case, as in the former, it is not my intention to put in any claim 
without the previous sanction of Her Majesty's Government, 

I have reason to suppose that another claim of a similar nature is likely to 
be presented, being for loss of a vessel belonging to Said Mohamed Husseyn, 
Agent at Kosseir to Her Majesty’s Government in India; the amount likely to.

rivately informed that claims of a like nature have been presented to the 
urkish Commissioner by Ottoman subjects.

showeth as follows :— 


ON the 26th day of July of the year 1858, of the Christian era, your peti-

and tackle complete, a sea-going vessel named “ El Amin,” which is to say, 
“The Safety,” of the burden of 800 ardebs, and of the value of 2,800 
dollars. 

Your petitioner was on the same day employing, and had always theretofore 
employed, the said vessel in his lawful calling of a trader and carrier by sea, and 
neither he nor the master of the said vessel, or the crew, or any of the erew 
thereof, ever did anything to cause the lawful seizure or destruction of the said 
vessel by her said Majesty’s naval forces.

eid vessel, and 582 dollars on account of the value of cash and other property

Inclosure 4:in No. 391, 
Affidavit of Abdu ibn Osman. 

(C.) 


THIS 19th day of February, a.p. 1859, at Jeddah, before me, Alfred S. 
Walne, Esquire, Her Britannic Majesty's Commissioner for the affairs of J eddah,. 
appearcth Abdi ibn Osman, late of Loheia, and at this present time of Jeddah, 
and maketh oath and saith: 

On und during the four years next preceding the 14th day of Zul-higeeh, 
A.H, 1274, corresponding to the 26th day of July, of the year 1858 of the 
Christian era, I was employed as a sailor on board the vessel « F] Aman,” 
belonging to Ruttongy, the son of Behim, a British trader established at Loheia. 
On the last-mentioned day the said vessel was lying in the port of Jeddah, 
Abkar ibn Hamid was the master of the said vessel. He went on shore early in 
the morning of that day, leaving on board the said vessel sixteen persons, 
including myself. Five of the said persons were ill of the smallpox. In the 
forenoon of the same day boats, manned and armed, came from Hor Majesty's 
ship ‘‘Cyclops”’ towards the anchorage in which the said yessel was lying. 
One of the said boats, carrying a gun mounted in the bow thereof, approached 
the said vessel. Seven or eight armed men, being of the crew of the last. 
mentioned boat, boarded the said vessel, and called out to the said persons “ jao | 
jao !" which is to say in Hindostani “ go | gol” and then proceeded to break’ the 
boxes belonging to the said master and to the above-mentioned persons, and 
with a portion of the pieces and contents thereof to make a fire in the body of 
the said vessel for the purpose of burning it. Whereupon 1, with the remainder 
of the said persons, became alarmed, and immediately left the said vessel in the 
jolly-boat thereto belonging, and went to the nearest part of the shore. Shortly 
after getting into the said jolly-bont, I saw the said vessel on fire. It, together 
with all the property it contained, including its sails, furniture, and tackle, and 
fourteen boxes, containing the effects of the said master, and of the © kerany,”’ 
and of the said persons, was completely consumed. The twelve of the said 
boxes containing the effects of the said persons were, together with the same. 
effects, worth 100 Austrian dollars. : 

In witness whereof the said Abdu ibn Osman hath, the day and year first 
ubove written, hereunto set his mark.

I AM commanded by my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to send 
you herewith, for the information of Her Majesty’s Secretary of State for Foreign

reporting the progress of affairs at Jeddah.
