(Siened)  H. CORRY, 


Inclosure in No. 392. 
Commodore Edgell to the Seeretary to the Admiralty. 


Sir, " Chesapenke,” Jeddah, February 22, 1859, 

T HAVE the honour to forward, for the information of my Lords Commis: 
sioners of the Admiralty, the report of proceedings at Jeddah since my last 
despatch of the 4th instant, 

The Commission advances but slowly in its progress towards a satisfactory 
termination of the indemnity question. ‘The Commissioner informs me that at 
first they found Seid Pasha, the Turkish Commissioner, ready and willing to 
entertain fair and reasonable views on the various cuses examined into; but 
about three weeks ago Ramsa Effendi, the Defterdar, or Treasurer, arrived in dh 
buggalow, with fresh instructions from the Porte to Seid Pasha, and since that 
time matters have progressed most slowly and far less satisfactorily; and on 
certain pots on each case, such as indemnification for loss the house has 
sustained in its commercial prospects by the stoppage of trade, and the complete 
disarrangement of its affairs, owing to the events of the Lith of J ung, the Purkish 
Commissioner states that he has no authority to entertain such a question, 


ss SS —S——=—= — eS 


“ET be 


ao4 


Namick Pasha, the Governor-General of the Hedjaz, has also thrown every 
obstacle in the way of the Commissioner, and has evidently, since the arrival of 
the Defterdar, made the Turkish Commissioner less willing to act in the straight- 
forward manner he had previously been pursuing. This is much to be regretted, 
for, by the present slow progress, | do not see when Mr. Walne is likely to leave, 
His colleague, M, Sabatier, having left, also retards business; for, if two of the 
Commissioners had agreed on the point of indemnity above mentioned, their 
decision would have been final. . 

I have endeavoured to impress on Mr. Walne the necessity of decision on 
these cases, for I cannot see, after the Turkish Commissioner refusing to enter- 
tain certain points, the use of wasting time in argument, but to finish the claims 
in an official manner, by having the objections of the Turkish Commissioner in 
writing, for reference to the authorities at home, for eventually the question of 
indemnity will have to be arranged at Constantinople. “The Secretary of the 
Turkish Commissioner informed Mr. Walne, privately, that such would be the 
case. 

The “ Roebuck " reported the arrival, at Suez, of the new Governor-General, 
Ali Pasha. I had given instructions to Commander Symonds to receive the Pasha, 
and two of his suite, if he chose to avail himself of the opportunity, but, having 
a very large establishment, he declined the offer. [He is now expected to arrive 
in a Turkish steamer, and | hope will bring more positive instructions for the 
Turkish Commissioner, as the season is fast advancing. Should he not, 
Mr. Walne purposes leaving for Suez in about three weeks. As by that time 
 Pelorus”’ will require provisioning, itis my intention to leave her all the spirits 
I can spare, but we have only sixteen days’ on board. 

Allis quiet at Jeddah, and three vessels, under English colours, have lately 
arrived with pilgrims. 

His Imperial Majesty’s corvette “ Duchayla” was at Suez, waiting for the 
French Consul, shortly expected, when she would convey him to Jeddah. 

I have, &c, 
(Signed) HARRY EDGELL. 


No. 393. 
Mr. Hammond to Mr. Melvill. 


Sir, Foreign Office, Mareh 16, 1859. 
IN reply to your letter of yesterday's date, recommending to Lord 
Malmesbury's favourable consideration the case of the daughter of the late 
Mr. Page, of Jeddah, Lam directed to acquaint you, for the mformation of Lord 
Stanley, that Miss Page is not the object of charity his Lordship has been 
led to suppose,-as she will receive a large amount of the compensation obtained 
on account of the destruction of British property at Jeddah, and probably a 
pension of 1,000 franes per month, which the Sultan has expressed his intention 
to grant to the person who shall prove to be the legal representative of the late 
Mr. Page, 
: Lam, &c. 
(Signed) MALMESBURY,

After much verbal discussion, a note, of which a copy is inclosed, was, by

In the instructions sent to the Turkish Commissioner it is stated, that ** all 
the inhabitants of Jeddah, whether subjects of the Porte or of other Powers 
with the exception of such as suffered during the well-known occurrence, will 
have to be taxed." ‘This part of the order may, perhaps, have escaped the 
observation of Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople, but it has by ne 
means escaped that of the authorities at Jeddah. It involves a principle, not 
only dangerous for the future to the interests of Europeans residing in the 
Ottoman Empire, but one, the application of which in Jeddah itself would 
probably, immediately lead to the infliction of grievous acts of injustice on many 
of the ndian subjects of Her Majesty now resident at that port. ‘The attention 
of the French Government has been already drawn to this subject, and I have 
respectfully to submit it to your Lordship's consideration, 

I had hoped that the new Governor-General of the Hedjaz, Ali Pasha, 

4 D 


286 


might have brought with him instructions from the Porte calculated to facilitate 
the solution of the difficulties which had arisen between the Turkish Commis- 
sioner and myself. So far as 1 could judge of his conduct during my stay at 
Jeddah, he had, on the contrary, been directed to obstruct our proceedings. 
Seidl Hamdi Pasha, the Turkish Commissioner, had no liberty of action, but 
was obliged, in every matter of doubt or difficulty, to take instructions from Ali 
Pasha. 

The Porte having taken no measures for selling by public auction the goods 
which had been abandoned, a proposal was made on the part of Messrs. Toma 
Mirialaki, A. D'Antonio, and Co., to receive the merchandize formerly belonging 
to their house, at a valuation to be fixed by competent persons named by the 
British and ‘Turkish Commissioners. A considerable portion had probably been 
damaged during the last rainy winter, and, as it is well known, another portion 
had actually been sold by the authorities previous to the arrival of the Commis- 
sioners. ‘To so reasonable a proposal Ali Pasha caused a negative answer to be 

ven, although, as I have good reason to suppose, the Turkish Commissioner 
himself entertained an opposite opinion. I have the honour to lay before your 
Lordship copies of the correspondence on this subject. 

Previous to the arrival of Ali Pasha, I had received from the Turkish 
Commissioner answers respecting most of the British claims, not, certainly, of a 
satisfactory character, but such as, by their admissions, must materially assist 
the ultimate settlement of these questions, It was, however, with great difficulty, 
and only an hour before my leaving Jeddah, that | obtained for these documents 
the signature and seal of Seid Hamdi Pasha. His conduct at the last suffi- 
ciently indicated that, however well-disposed Haitire he had received, directly 
or indirectly, instructions to ignore the abandonment of goods, to make light of 
losses, and reduce the indemmity to the lowest possible figure. His Report is 
now on its way to Constantinople. 

Inclosed is copy of the letter which accompanied my complete list of claims, 
with the respective awards proposed by myself; but on the present occasion, 
us the mail is on the point of leaving, | add only a summary note of the 
latter. I propose, a3 carly as possible, to submit to your Lordship a short 
analysis of each case, but this is a work which will necessarily require some time 
for preparation. 

M. Rousseau has reported to the French Government his opinion as to the 
utter inutility of negotiating at Jeddah, and his concurrence with the Turkish 
Commissioner and myself as to the advisability of transferring the Conferences 
to Constantinople. | 

The French claims, which, when M. Sabatier left Jeddah, were estimated at 
1,157,594 franes, are now increased, I understand, to 2,500,000 francs. There 
appears to be great unwillingness on the part of the French Commissioner to 
allow any minute examination of these claims, and | am disposed to think that 
they would scarcely bear an ordeal such as that through which the British cases 
have already passed. ey he 

1 do not consider it desirable that the British Commissioner should be 
called upon to assist in the examination of the French claims, as such a proceed- 
ing might possibly give rise to differences of opinion which had better be

Jeddah, March 7, 1859. 


THE Undersigned, Her Britannic Majesty's Commissioner, has the honour 
to inform his Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, Commissioner for the Sublime 
Porte, that he has been instructed by Her Majesty's Secretary of State for 
Foreign Affairs that, after taking the matter into consideration, Her Majesty’s 
Government haye come to the conclusion that it is pao ely indispensable to 
levy an indemnity on the town of Jeddah itself; that such indemnity should be 
calculated in proportion to the pecuniary resources of the inhabitants of that 


287 


place, and in such a way that the fines may fall more especially upon the cuilty : 
and that if the amount raised is insufficient to meet the claims on account of 
losses sustained, the surplus required may be paid by the Ottoman Government. 
He has also received from Hor Majestyra Atibaehader it Constantinople a trans- 
lation of the instructions sent to his iixeellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, 

Looking to the facilities for consultation now afforded by the presence in 
Jeddah not only of the three Commissioners, but also of his Excellency the 
Governor-General of the Hedjaz, and of his Excellency the Sheriff of Mecca, the 
Undersigned considers the occasion peculiarly favourable for considering anil 
deciding on the Rovian of the indemnity which should be paid by the town. 

,__ itis true that, according to the strict letter of the instructions sent to his 

Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, the total amount of indemnity should be first 
established by the Commissioners; but as, pending reference to their respective 
Governments, this cannot be immediately effected, it appears to the Undersigned 
that there can be no possible inconvenience, but, on the contrary, great advan- 
tage, In his Exceilency’s at once proceeding to examine, in conjunction with 
his Excellency the Governor-General of the Hedjaz and his Excellency the 
Sheriff of Mecca, what amount of fine the town can fairly support, seeing that 
their judgments in this matter have to be guided, not by the actual and precise 
amount of the indemnity to be sally adjudicated, but by the means of the inha- 
hitants to ey that portion of the indemnity which has to be imposed on them, 

The Undersigned having examined the British claims to indemnity, a report 
on which he reserves to himself to submit to Her Majesty's Government, is on 
the point of leaving Jeddah ; and he believes that it would be highly satisfactory 
to Her Majesty’s Government to be informed that the Ottoman authorities had 
in this matter afforded facilities sanctioned by the spirit, if not the letter, of their 
instructions, and that they had done all that was in their power to hasten the 
final arrangement of those questions which have so long and so seriously oceu- 
pied the attention of the three Commissioners, and which the Sublime Porte 
itself must be anxious to bring to aspeedy and honourable settlement. 

The Undersigned, &c. (Signed) ALFRED §. WALNE,

Seu Pasha to Consul Walne: 
(‘Translation.) 


(After the usual compliments.) 3 Shaan, 1275. (March 8, 1859.) 

1 HAVE to acknowledge the receipt of your highly esteemed note, dated 
the 7th March, pointing out to me the instructions of the Sublime Porte, which 
refer to an extraordinary tax to be levied on the inhabitants of Jeddah for reco. 
vering that portion of the indemnity which has to be established and agreed 
upon by the Commissioners, and that, although the amount of indemnity is not 
yet fixed, the instructions should not be carried out word for word, but that, for 
factlitating the business in future, a sum should be recovered from the said 
inhabitants, 

In order to learn what sum might, by supposition, be now fixed on the 
town, I communicated with his Excellency the Sheriff and his Excelleney the 
Governor-General of Jeddah, and informed them of the note you addressed me 
on the subject. They-said that the fixing a sum by supposition, without the 
Commissioners having previously established the total amount of the indemnity, 
is a proceeding contrary to the orders expressed in the instructions, and even if 
this would afterwards facilitate the matter, it is impossible in this affair of taxing 
the town, that they could in ignorance fix a sum by supposition. In any case, 
the amount of the indemnity should be first known, and then everybody shoul! 
be taxed according to his means, Now, the amount of the indemnity being 
unknown, it is impossible, by mere supposition, to fix the sum of contribution. 
Consequently [ address you the present for your information,

Mr, Ayrton to Consul Wulne, 
Sir, Jeddah, February 25, 1859, 

IN reply to the verbal intimation I had the honour to receive from you, 
yesterday, of the willingness of the Ottoman Commissioner to order the delivery 
to me, as the representative of Messrs, Mirialaki A. d’Antonio and Co., of the 
property in their name, in the hands of the Local Government, as on account of 
the indemnity payable to them by the Sublime Ottoman Porte, in respect of the 
late outbreak at Jeddah, | have to express my consent to receive such property 
on the following terms, which T believe fairly meet the proposal made to me, 

All cash which has been recovered by the Local Government, or realised by 
it, from the sale by it of goods consigned to Messrs. Thoma Saya and Co.. or 
otherwise received by it in their name since June 15, 1858, to be paid to me. 

All goods or other things recovered from those plundered from Messrs. 
Thoma Sava and Co., on the 15th of June, or since, in their name received by 
the Local Government, excepting timber in planks or picees, so far as the same 
goods or things may be in a sound and saleable condition, to be delivered to me. 

Provided, however, that such goods shall be taken by meat the price 
to be agreed upon by two persons to be named in that behalf by yourself and 
the Ottoman Commissioner; or in the event of such two persons not being able 
So fo ugree upon a price, then at such price as shall be indicated by any third 
person of sufficient experience, to be named by yourself and the Ottoman 
Commissioner; and, provided also, that the price when so determined, shall be 
reckoned as so much cash, and, together with the above-mentioned cash, be 
received by me on account of the indemnity payable by the Sublime Ottoman 
Porte to Messrs, Mirialaki A, d’Antonio and Co, 

Of course the prices of many articles of merchandise have varied with the 
changes of the market, and are not now what they were on June 15, 1858. 
Some articles, however, have remained nearly unchanged in price: such are, 
bees'-wax, cardamoms, rhinoceros’ horn, mother-o'-pearl, white leef, and sumu, 
any quantities of which, ina condition as sound as that in which they were on 
the 15th of June, [am ready to take at the prices stated in the affidavits of the 
Sheik Hassan Mohamed and Ahmed Bakheidhar. 

The reason why I have excepted the timber from the articles to be taken, 
is, that it might not be quickly saleable at what might be considered its extreme 
value, and that, were I to leave it for sale with an agent here, the sum at which 
it might be valued would be considerably reduced by the expenses of agency 
and allowance of interest; but if the Ottoman Commissioner is disposed to 
concede such timber, in the event of there being any, at a price to ensure its 
immediate sale, | am reudy to accept it. 

 Lhave, &e. 
(Signed) F, AYRTON, 
Representing Messrs. Mirialaki A. IY Antonio & Co,

who have come to my knowledge as having conducted themselves in a manner 
more or less praiseworthy on the occasion of the massacre and plunder of the 
Christians in Jeddah on the 15th of June, 1858, and following days. 

Among them, Mohamed Khaily, of the town of Khoi; Ahmed Acha Emin- 
el-Shouch, Director of the Government magazines, and a poor man, Aly-cl- 
Seramaty (the shoemaker), deserve more particular notice. Mohamed Khéily, 
for his attempt to protect the people who sought shelter with him from 
Messrs. Thoma Saya and Co.'s house, was plundered by the rioters of all 
the property he possessed in the world, consisting of 1,080 dollars in cash, and 
effects to the value of 120 dollars, making together 1,200 dollars. ‘The late 
Kaimakam afterwards presented him with | dollar. He has since been living 
on money borrowed, in-small sums, from Messrs, Myrialaki A. d'Antonio and 
Co., his means of repaying which will depend upon his obtaining an indem- 
nity for his losses. He has also had to bear the expense of a journey to 
Cairo, 

Aly-cl-Seramaty was likewise plundered of his small stock of furniture, of 
the walue of 15 dollurs, for having befriended Shabin Békas. 

I also subjoina list of names of persons who are yet at large, but who, if 
it is thought expedient, may be brought to the notice of the local authorities as 
having taken a part, direct or indirect, in the disorders of the 15th of June.

The Earl of Malmesbury to Str H. Buliver. 
(No. 189.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, March 30, 1859. 

I TRANSMIT, for your Excellency’s information; copies of two despatches 
and of their inclosures, from Mr. Walne,* giving a most unsatisfactory account of 
the progress of the business with which the Jeddah Commission has to deal, and 
showing the unexpected course which the Turkish authorities have pursued in 
throwing constant obstructions and difficulties in the way of the British and 
French Commissioners, 

Yon will not conceal from the Porte the regret and surprise of Her Majesty's 
Government at the extraordinary conduct of its officers, as reported by Mr. Walne, 
which proves how little reliance ought to have been placed on the distinct 
assurances of the Turkish Government that their agents had been empowered to 
co-operate honestly and efficiently with those of England and France in working 
out a satisfactory settlement of the Jeddah claims. 

Mr, Walne is inclined to think that, as matters now stand, the question as 
to the indemnity to be paid by the town might be more casily arranged at Con- 
stantinople; and Mr. Walne likewise concurs with the French and Turkish 
Commissioners as to the advisability of transferring the further discussions on 
these affairs generally to that capital ; but, before coming to a decision, | would 
wish you to report to me your opinion upon these: points, as well as upon the 
question of calling on the Porte to grant rewards and gratuities to all the 
subjects of the Sultan who conducted themselves well and suffered on the occasion 
of the outbreak. 

I have further to direct your Excellency's attention to the fact that, accord- 
ing to the orders sent to the Turksh Commissioner, the fine will have to be paid 
by all the inhabitants of Jeddah, whether subjects of Turkey or of other Powers ; 
and I have to instruct you strongly to remonstrate on this with the Porte, and 
positively to declare that Her Majesty's Government will not permit a fine to be 
exacted from any Indian or other subject of Her Majesty at Jeddah. 

Dhave, &c. 
(Signed) MALMESBURY,

Phe Law Officers of the Crown to the Karl of Malmesbury.—fRecetred March 25.) 
My Lord, Doctors’ Commons, March 24, 1859. 

WE are honoured with your Lordship's commands, sienified in Mr, 
Hammond's letter of the 4th March instant, stating that we are aware of the 
massacre of Christians which took place at Jeddah in the month of June fast, 
Among the victims on that occasion was Mr, Page, the British Viec-Consul. 

That the Sultan, as we should see by the inclosed copy of a telegram from 
Sir Henry Bulwer, announced his intention of giving a pension of 1,000 franes a 
month to the heirs of the British Consul, if he has any; and that we should 
also see by the inclosed copy of a despatch from the Minister for Foreign Affairs 
at Constantinople, that the Turkish Ambassador at this Court was instructed to 
inquire about a daughter supposed to have been left by Mr. Page. 

Mr, Hammond was further pleased to inclose a collection of correspondence 
which has passed between the Foreign Office and Mr. Cole, claiming to repre- 
sent the interests of the said daughter under-a will made in her favour, of which 
he was executor, and between the Foreign Office and Mr. Fenwick, claiming to 
represent the interests of the mother of the deceased. 

That the original will left by Mr. Page, and a copy of which is inclosed, 
having been transmitted to this country from Egypt, has been proved by 
Mr. Cole, and it will be seen that by it he leaves everything he possesses to his 
natural daughter, a 

That the time appears now to have arrived for claiming the fulfilment of 
the promise of the Porte to provide for the heirs of Mr, Page; and Mr, Cole, as 
we should see by his inclosed letter, requests that the fact of the will in favour of 
Miss Page having been proved, should be notified to the Turkish Ambassador in 
this country, 

* Tnclosure in No. 346.

Tae fe Pe ee | — =, 


[ae 


Mr. Hammond was, by your Lordship’s direction, pleased to request our 
opinion as to the course which, under existing circumstances, should be pursued. 

Mr. Hammond states, that the promise having been made by the Porte to 
Her Majesty's Government, it is for Her Majesty’s Government to apply for its 
fulfilment. 

That your Lordship’s first impression has been that a communication should 
he made to Mr. Cole and Mr, Fenwick respectively, to the effect that the will 
having been proved, your Lordship is now prepared to receive cither a separate 
statement from each of them, or, if they can agree, a joint statement from both, 
setting forth the grounds on which they severally claim for their respective 
clients the pension promised by the Sultan ; and that your Lordship, on receiving 
such statement or statements, will instruct Her Majesty's Ambassador at Con- 
stantinople to lay the same before the Sultan, in order that His Majesty may 
decide to which of the parties the pension should be paid, 

That your Lordship presumes that os no other parties have claimed to be 
Mr. Page's heirs, it may be taken for granted that no other heirs exist, but that 
it is a point for our consideration whether any public invitation should be issued 
calling for heirs to come forward; and further, whether any further, and if so 
what proof, should be required of Mr, Cole and of Mr, Fenwick in regard to the 
identity of the parties whose interests they represent. 

Mr. Hammond stated that your Lordship would be glad to have our opinion 
as to the course to be pursued in these matters at our early convenience, 

In obedience to your Lordship’s commands, we have the honour to 
report ;— 

, That Mr. Page, having left a will, of which probate has been granted, the 
executor of that will (Mr. Cole) is primd jfacie the person legally entitled to 
receive the indemnity in trust for the sole legatee, the illegitimate daughter of 
the decensed, who is a minor. 

It appears, however, from a letter written by the deceased to Mr. Cole, 
dated September Sth, 1856, inclosed in Mr. Cole's letter to your Lordship of the 
8th September, 1858, that deceased was in the habit of making a small allowance 
to his mother; and, inasmuch as he appears to have left a considerable private 
fortune (estimated at 11,0001), all of which, together with the indemnity, will 
pass to the daughter under the will, his mother might, in our opinion, properly 
receive out of the pension or indemnity an annuity equal to the allowance which 
he was in the habit of making her, whatever this may have been. 

We therefore recommend that Her Majesty's Government should apply to 
the Sultan to make to or for the benefit of the mother of the deceased a prant of 
an annuity, during her life, equal to the allowance before mentioned ; and, subject 
to that partial life-interest, to make a grant of the 1,000 francs per month to or 
for the illegitimate daughter of the deceased. 

Whenever the indemnity shall be received, we would suggest the appoint- 
ment of at least one proper person as co-trustee with Mr. Cole, and an ‘application 
to Chancery to make the minor a ward of Chancery. 

We have, &c., 
(Signed) J. D. HARDING, 
FITZROY KELLY, 
H. M. CAIRNS.

The Turkish Commissioner concludes by stating that, having made inquiries 
from competent persons, and examined the officers and books of the Custom-. 
house, he has arrived at the above conclusion; that on some questions he is 
eonvineed, and that on others he refers to the Porte. . 

This is, of course, an evasive and unsatisfactory answer on a very important 
claim, by which the Turkish Commissioner has endeavoured to throw off his 
own shoulders the responsibility of giving a decision which must, in any case, 
result in the payment of a large indemnity by the Porte. But it must not be 
forgotten that Seid Hamdi Pasha was officially invited by the British Commis- 
sioner to communicate to him any observations which he had to muke on the 
part of the Porte in opposition to the demands of the claimants,” On one or 
two trifling questions lhe has raised objections scarecly worth notice, and his 
silence on important items of claim: may fairly be taken as admissions of their 
justness. He was offered every facility for examining, or having explained to 
him, the numerous affidavits by which the case is supported; and he having on 
more than one occasion professed his incompetency to understand mercantile 
accounts, it was suggested to him that he might cause them to be examined by 
merchants, or other competent accountants. Of neither of these offers did 
Seid Hamdi Pasha avail himself. hate 

The final statement by which the claim of Messrs. Toma Myrialaki, A. 
D' Antonio and Co. is accompanied, occupies not less than forty-two folio pages, 
and it is impossible to do justice to it by any summary of the arguments 
adduced. ‘The case was, in the first instance, commenced at Cairo, in ignorance 
of many facts which became known to the barrister in charge during his three 
months’ stay in Jeddah. Most important information was obtained upon the 
spot, such as, if time had allowed, would have enabled Mr. Ayrton to put in his 
claim under an entirely different form, basing it on the actual. losses proved in 
evidence, instead of resting it, as he has done, on the accounts furnished by the 
principal house at Cairo, and by the branch house at Hodeida, oe 

According to the affidavits of the surviving partners, and of the surviving 
clerks of the house, and other sworn evidence, as well as by reference to the 
books of the Custom-house, the amount of property in possession of Messrs. 
Toma Sava and Co.,, on the 15th of June, 1858, was equal to 256,162 dollars ; 
and as this calculation is made in great measure from memory, it is probably 
rather under than over the mark, It is caleulated that there is still in the 
hands of the Local Government property of the value of 49,360 dollars, besides 
vessels worth 7,875 dollars, and a house worth 5,700 dollars, abandoned to the 

Porte. ;

The first item is supported by a document signed by Toma Sava and Co.. 
the other items by affidavit and the evidence of several respectable persons, So 
far from being disputed by the Turkish Commissioner, the: first part of the 
claim receives confirmation from the information which he obtained at Jeddah, 
and is recognised as real and just. The additional charge for profits aceruing is 
submitted by him to the Porte. 

As to the loss of jewels, furniture, and other property, left in the care of 
Toma Sava and Co., the Turkish Commissioner recognises that Autun Yousouf 
Abd el Messieh did reside at Jeddah, and that he has been informed that on 
his departure he actually did leave furniture, and a large Indian case, contents 
not known, The claim is considered by him as not unfounded, but he expresses 
surprise that a document having been taken for the securities, none should have 
been taken for the jewels, furniture, and other effects. He refers the case 
including damages and costs, to the Porte. 

Captain Pullen, having examined this case at Cairo, had formed a favour. 
uble opmion of it, and calculated the indemnity ut 47,089 dollars. The 
securities were handed over to ‘Toma Sava and Co., as a mercantile transaction. 
Phe sealed box of jewels, the furniture, &e., were, no doubt, left with Sava as 
one friend may leave his effects in charge of another friend, ino which case 
documents are seldom asked for or given. Looking upon the claim in an 
equitable rather than a strietly legal point of view, the British Conwmissioner 
considers it sufficiently supported to allow of his giving an award of 34,157 
dollars, as by consent of claimant. | ate

No. 9. Messrs, Duea Paleologo, Cochilani and Co., established at Cairo, 
under British protection.

In this ease the British Commissioner has been obliged to reserve his 
decision till a further examination can be made at Cairo. The affidavits sent 
down in support of the case were, by themselves, as to some matters, insufficient ; 
as to others, they did not arrive in time. 

There are French, as well as British, claims, having their origin in the same 
locality at Jeddah, the Hosh-el-Sheriff ; and it enhea? to have been the object 
of the Turkish Commissioner, as well as of the local authorities, to prove that 
the Hosh-el-Sheriff was not, during the events of June, in any way plundered, 
though it is amply proved that at least one of the lodzers was driven out, at the 
demund of the mob, and murdered at the door of that okella. The witnesses 
brought forward at Jeddah on the part of the Porte have given in statements 
the falsity of which will probably admit of proof in Cairo; but the British 
Commissioner requires time for the full examination of a case on which he is not. 
unlikely to form an opinion much at variance with that put forward by Seid 
Hamdi Pasha. Even in its reduced form, the claim of Messrs. Duca Paleologo, 
Cochilani and Co. has the appearance of being exaggerated; but, in any case, 
their establishment at Jeddah could not be broken up, their agent and partner 
driven away, after imminent risk to his life, and their extensive business with the 
Red Sea interrupted for at least a year, without the house being entitled to 
indemmity for losses. ‘The verification of these will be made as early as circum- 
stances permit, and the case will be reported on separately, 


No. 10. Mohammed Ali Buzruk, o Persian, naturalized in India. 


£

Dollars: 
Tediueod elm. . “a a ae ‘710 


This claim is for the value of two bales of silk, sent by Abdel Gawad, the 
agent at Cairo of Mohammed Ali Buzruk, to the house of Toma Sava and Co., 
but which arrived at Jeddah shortly after the massacre, and were kept at the 
Custom-house, As is fully admitted, they were subsequently handed over, on 
the application of the Persian agent, and by order of the Kaimakam, to a certain 
Persian, named Ali Akbar, who presented letters purporting to be from Abdel 
Gawad, authorizing him to withdraw them, The authenticity of these letters 
being disputed, Ali Akbar refused to submit them to the British Commissioner 
for the purpose of being examined by persons conversant with the handwriting of 
Abdel Gawad, and the Persian agent supported Ali Akbar in this refusal. There 
ure good reasons to suspect that the letters, in virtue of which the goods had 
been withdrawn, were forgeries. In any case, the Turkish Commissioner would 
take no proper measures for insisting on the re-delivery of the goods to the 
legally-constituted procurator of Mohammed Ali Buaruk ; and as they are the 
property of a British naturalised subject, and he is illegally deprived of them 
through the negligence of the Turkish authorities, the Porte ought to be made 
responsible for the loss oceasioned by the acts of its subordinates. ‘This ts 
disputed in tota by the Turkish Commissioner, but without evidence, or valid 
reasons to support his opposition. ae 

Award proposed by British Commissioner, 1,710 dollars, as by consent of 
claimant.

No. 11. Executor of the late Mr, Page, Her Majesty's Acting Vice-Consul 
at Jeddah, murdered on the ith June, 1858, Claim, 11,0002, equal to 
62,250 dollars. 

In the absence of any one authorized to represent the estate of the deceased, 
reservation had, in the first instance, been made for 60,000 dollars, but, pending 


Sl 


the proceedings, the executor put in, by the channel of the Foreign Department 
a claim of 11,0001, though unsupported by evidence. : . 
Inquiries having been made at Jeddah, it was found that Mr. Page con- 
dueted his business, to a considerable extent, in the names of third parties, so 
that it was difficult to estimate its amount, But Farag Yusur had last year been 
left in temporary charge of the Vice-Consulate, and to some extent in charge of 
Mr. Page's commercial affairs during his absence ; and, being examined on oath 
give evidence that, to the best of his knowledge, Mr. Page was in POSSERSION, i 
short time before his death, of from 8,000/ to 10,000/, and that 1,300/. had 
been paid over to him on the very day of his murder, It is understood that there 
Were considerable stims of money in the house at the time of the outbreak, 
Chere is in the hands of Farag Yusur merchandize belonging to the estate worth 
about 7,000 dollars; and, on the other hand, itis stated that there are in Eneland 
heavy claims to be met. The general tenour of the Turkish Commissioner's 
observations is rather favourable to the claim than otherwise, but he submits the 
mutter to the decision of the Porte. | 
Taking all the cireumstances into consideration, 11,0001. must be considered 
a5 u moderate indemnity for the losses arising from the murder of Mr, Pave, 
looked on merely as an English merchant. It is worthy of the consideration of 
Her Majesty’s Government whether something more ought not to be added on 
account of the official position which he held at the time, 
_ ‘As an approximative indemnity, the British Commissioner sees no reasonable 
objection to admitting the sum claimed. Award proposed, 52,250 dollars 
payable without deductions.

No. 16. Elias Hanna Antun, late Interpreter to Her Majesty's Vice-

The property of the deceased has been differently estimated at from 
6,000 dollars to 10,000. The Turkish Commissioner admits that, according to 
the information which he had received, the former estimate is not exaggerated, 
but submits the claim to the decision of the Porte. Award proposed by British 
Commissioner, 6,000 dollars; but as it is reported that the heirs are likely to

as final,

allawecl for indemnity, whatever it may be, should be paid over to Her Majesty’s 
Consul at Jeddah, with instructions to liquidate the estate, pay the debts proved, 
and hand over the balance to the heirs.

My Lord, Constantinople, April 22, 1859. 

IN reply to your Lordship's despatch No. 189 of the 30th ultimo, which 
reached me by the last messenger, | have the honour to. state that the Porte’s 
officers, at a distance from the capital, are so afraid of responsibility, and the 
instructions, written in the Turkish language, are always so vizue, that [ agree 
with Consul Walne’s opinion that it would be more conducive to a speedy 
settlement if the Jeddah Indemnity Commission were transferred to Constanti- 
nople, and, indeed, | inquired your Lordship's opinion on this subject hy 
telegraph on the 6th instant. I should add that, having since sounded Fuad 
Pasha, I find that the Porte would be dispozed to assent to such a proposal 
as 1 telegraphed on the 13th. 

I have also to state that, on being acquainted with the facts alluded to by 
your Lordship, I lost no time in making the general complaint as to the conduct 
ot the authorities of Jeddah, which you enjoin, whilst I have protested against 
the intention of exacting the fine to be levied on Jeddah from any Indian or 
other subject of Her Majesty. 

As to rewarding those subjects of the Sultan who, for their good conduct, 
suffered on the occasion of the outbreak, I think such a recommendation is 
highly desirable on our part, and would counterbalance the severity which it has 
been necessary for us to exercise against the guilty, ‘ 

I have, &e.

Inclosure in No. 421, 
The Soltertor to the Seeretary to the Treasury. 


Sir, Treasury, June 9, 1859, 

MY Lords have been pleased to refer to me the papers noted in the margin, 
relative to an annuity, or pension, proposed to be granted by the Grand Sultan, 
for the beneht of the heirs of Mr. Page, late Viee-Consul at Jeddah, and to direct 
me to examine into the ease, and to report what steps had best be taken, in 
order to protect the interests of Miss Page, his daughter and sole lezatec. | 
have communicated on the subject with Mr. Cole, executor of the late Mr, Page, 
and, as allesed, the guardian of his infant daughter; and with reference to the 
letter from that gentleman in answer to the suggestions made to. him by the 
Foreign Office respecting the steps to be taken for securing the pension for the 
benefit of Miss Page, which letter did not appear lo be satisfactory to the law 
officers, | am informed by Mr, Cole that his letter was written under the impres- 
sion that it was desired on the part of the Government to interfere with his 
legal rights as administrator over the general property of Mr. Paze, and not 
merely to protect the interests of Miss Page, in the pension proposed to be 
granted by the Sultan, 

This, | apprehend, ig a mistake, and Iso informed Mr. Cole; whereupon 
he assured me that he had no wish to oppose the views of the Government in 
regard to the peosion, but that he was willing to act as a trustee for Miss Page, 
or otherwise to concur in any act that might be considered beneficial to her in 
respect of the pension. 

The Law Olficers, on the supposition that Mr. Cole's views regarding the 
pension were not satisfactory, have advised that it should be placed in the hands 
of trustees, and that Miss Page should be made a ward in Chancery. 

But these steps cannot, | apprehend, be taken, until the pension has been 
remitted to the Government; and I would submit, with a view to the most 
effectual protection to Miss Page's interests, and in order to secure payment of 
part of the amount to Mrs, McLean, the late Viee-Consul’s mother, that the 
Sultan should be requested (if there be no objection to that course), to transmit 
to Hor Majesty’s Government a sum of money equivalent to the value of the 
annuity proposed to be granted to Miss Page; and that this sum, when received, 
should be invested in the pac funds, in the names of Mr. Cole and some other 
person appointed by Her Majesty's Government; and adeed of trust executed 


by them, whereby, after payment of the intended annuity to Mrs, McLean, the 
interest of the residue should be appropriated for the maintenance and education 
of Miss Page, until she comes of age, and the fund be then transferred to her 
absolutely. Should the Sultan prefer to pay an annuity yearly during the life-of 
Miss Page, instead of a sum by way of equivalent for the pension, a deed of trust 


319 


applicable to such a state of things may be prepared; and should it become 
necessary or advisable, Miss Page may then be made a ward in Chancery, for the 
more effectual protection of her interests. 
Tam, &c. 
(Signed) H. R. REYNOLDS.

Lord J. Russell to Sir A. Bulwer. 
(No. 10) 


Sir, Foreign Office, June 28, 1859, 


WITH reference to your Excelleney’s telegram of the 2lst of July, 1858, 
reporting the gracious decision of the Sultan to grant to the heirs of the late 
Mr. Page, a pension of 1,000 francs a month, I have to instruet you to inform 
the Porte that the will of that gentleman has been legally proved in this 
country by his executor Mr. Cole, and that his daughter, Miss Page, is, under 
that will, constituted his sole heiress. This lady, therefore, will be the proper 
recipient of His Imperial Majesty's bounty; but as, by Mr. Page’s death, bis 
mother, Mrs. McLean, hes been deprived of an allowance of 50/. which he 
annually granted for her support, Her Majesty's Government think it right that 
an annuity to the above amount should be paid to that lady, till her death, out 
of the pension promised by the Sultan to the heirs of the late Mr. Page: and 
with a view to the most effectual protection of Miss Page’s interests, and in 
order to secure pasment of part of the pension to Mrs. MeLean, | have to 
instruct your Excellency to suggest to the Porte the expediency of transmitting 
to Her Majesty’s Government a sum of money equivalent to the value of the 
annuity proposed to be granted to Miss Page, in order that the same may be 
invested in the public funds in the name of Mr. Cole and some other person 
appointed by Her Majesty's Government, and a deed of trust exeeuted by them, 
Whereby, after payment of the proposed annuity to Mrs. Melean, the interest 
of the residue may be appropriated to the maintenance and education of 
Miss Page until she comes of age, and the fund may then be transferred to her 
absolutely. Should, however, the Sultan prefer to pay an annuity yearly during 
the life of Miss Page, instead of a sum by way of equivalent for the pension, i 
deed of trust applicable to such a state of things will be prepared, and should it 
become necessary or advisable, Miss Page will then be made a ward in Chancery 
for the more effectual protection of her interests. 

[am, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

THIS Slst day of the month of May, 4.p. 1859, at Alexandria, before me, 
Alfred 8. Walne, Esquire, Her Britannic Majesty's Commissioner for the affairs 
of Jeddah, appeareth Kalil Abd-el-Rahim of Kenneh, and at this present time 
at Alexandria, and maketh oath and saith:—I am established as a merchant at 
Kenneh; 1 know the vessel “ Attict el Rahman Dangour,”’ which belonged to 
Said Ahmed Hossein, the agent at Kenneh of Her Majesty’s Government of 
India. The said vessel was built at Kosseir: J saw it at times when building, and 
L know from conversation with the said Said Ahmed Hossein at such times and 
after the said vessel was finished, which was in the year 1857-58 of the 
Christian era, that it was well provided with sails, tackle, and furniture, and 
that inclusive of such sails, tackle, and furniture, it cost 8,000 dollars; it was 
estimated to be of the burthen of 2,000 ardebs. I know that the sari Said 
Ahmed Hossein received at Kennch in the month of Moharram 1275, corre- 
sponding to the month of August of the year 1858 of the Christian era, advices 
from his correspondent at Jeddah, to say that the said vessel “ Dangour” had 
been completely burnt and destroyed in the anchorage where it was lying at 
Jeddah, by armed boats sent from Her Britannic ship. “ Cyclops,’ on the 14th 
day of Zul Hugge, a.u. 1274, corresponding to the 26th day of July of the said 
year 1858. 3

Sir, Alerandnia, June 23, 1554. 


[HAD the honour of receiving, on the 20th instant, your Excelleney’s 
despatch of the 28th ultimo, inclosing copy of a telegram from the Earl of 


aot O2EE ree oe So ie

gah 


Malmesbury, relative to the proposed removal of the Jeddah Indemnity Com. 
mission to Constantinople, ; 

His Excellency Seid Hamdi Pasha, Turkish Commissioner, recently returned 
from Jeddah, leaves to-morrow for Constantinople. 

T had yesterday an opportunity of ascertaining the intentions of M. Sabatier, 
He informed me that the state of political aifairs would not for the present admit 
of his leaving Egypt, and that he had instructions to remain at his post. 

For myself, my movements must depend on the arrangements necessary for 
carrying on the business of Her Majesty’s Agency and Consulate-General in 
Egypt, and also for making provision for Her Majesty’s Consulate at Cairo, in 
the event of Mr. Ayrton, who is temporarily in charge of that office, consi- 
dering it necessary to proceed with the Commission to Constantinople. 1 have 
as yet no certain information about the movements of Mr. Colquhoun, but am 
led to suppose that lie can scarcely be expected here before the end of August, 
and I think it possible that M. Sabatier may not be able to leave Egypt before 
the probable period of Mr. Colquhoun’s arrival, if then. 

In the interval, 1 propose to take some further evidence bearing on the 
claim of Messrs. Paleologo, Cochilani and Co., respecting which I reserved to 
myself to make a separate Report, I have suggested to Seid Hamdi Pasha 
the propriety of joining me in the examination, but he has shirked this duty, 
I presume, because he gave an opinion upon the case prematurely. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) ALFRED S. WALNE.

The Secretary to the Admirally to Mr. Hommond.—(Recewed July 22.) 


Sir, Admiralty, July 21, 1859. 
HAVING laid before my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty your 
letters of the 12th and 18th instant, on the subject of further claims which have 
been preferred for compensation for damage sustained during the bombardment 
of Jeddah by Her Majesty's ship “Cyclops,” I am commanded by my Lords 
to acquaint you, for the information of Lord John Russell, that their Lordships 
are not in possession of any information which can enable them to judge of the 
validity of the claims put forward in the cases referred to, and that they can 
only stiggest, with reference to the opinion. of the Law Officers on the claim of 
Farag Yusur, which was forwarded to your Department from this office on the 
25th of February last, that there would appear to be no legal claim against the 
British Government, and that tt must rest with Lord John Russell to determine, 
upon such information as Her Majesty's Consul may be able to furnish, how far, 
in equity or liberality, it would be proper for Mer Majesty's Government. to 
afford redress to the present claimants, who may or may not be deserving of 
favourable consideration. 
Tam, &c. 
(Signed) C. PAGET.

My Lord, Foreign Office, July 26, 1859, 

YOUR Excelleney is aware that certain persons have brought forward 
claims against Her Majesty's Government and that of the Emperor of the 
French, for compensation on account of losses sustained by them on the 
occasion of the bombardment of Jeddah, My predecessor, in his despatch to 
Lord Chelsea, No. 48 of the Sth of March last, transmitted a copy of the 
instructions which be had addressed to Mr. Walne, instructing him with refer- 
ence to one of these claims, that of a person named Farag Yusur, to settle it 
out of the fine to be levied on the town. Lord Chelsea was at the same 
time instructed to appeal to the French Government to send similar instructions 
to their Commissioner. In a further despatch to Mr. Walne, copy of which 
was transmitted to you by Lord Malmesbury in his No. 283 of the 19th of 
March, that gentleman was informed that his Lordship had arranged with the 
French Ambassador at this Court that another claim of the same description 
which had been sent in, that of a person named Ruttongy, should be settled in 
the same way, and he was instructed accordingly to arrange the settlement 
with his French colleage. reece 

It appears, however, from a despatch which has just been received from 
Mr. Walne, and of which I inclose a copy,* that the French Commissioner had 
not, when he last spoke to him on the subject, received any instructions respect- 
ing these claims. Mr. Walne in the same despatch, as your Excellency will see, 
incloses papers respecting a further claim brought forward by a man named 
Ahmed Hossein: and as other claims are coming in, and are likely to come, at 
is desirable that some measures should be taken for dealing with them without 
further delay, 1 have, therefore, to instruct your Excellency to bring the 
subject again before the French Government, and to request that instructions 
may be forwarded to the French Commissioner in conformity with those above 
alluded to which were addressed by Her Majesty’s late Government to 
Mr. Walne, Lam, &e. at

Inclosure in No. 431. 


Sir Al, Bulwer to Fuad Pasha. 


Constantinople, July 9, 1859, 

THE. Undersigned, Her Britannie Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary 
to the Sublime Porte, has received special instructions to inform the Sultans 
Government that the will of the late Mr. Page, Vice-Consul at Jeddah, has been 
legally proved in England by his executor, Mr. Cole, and that his daneliter, 
Miss Page, 19, under that will, constituted his sole heiress. Thus this young 
lady will be the popes recipient of the pension of 1,000 frames a-monthi, 
graciously granted by lis Majesty the Sultan to the heirs of the late Mr. Pace. 
But as, by Mr. Page's death, his mother Mrs. Me Lean has been deprived of an 
allowance of 50/. which he annually granted for her support, Her Majesty's 
Government think it right that an annuity to the above amount should be puid 
to that lady till her death, out of the pension promised by the Sultan to the 
heirs of the late Mr. Page. And with a view to the most. effectual protection 
of Miss Page’s interests, und in order to secure payment.of part of the pension 
to Mrs. Me Lean, the Undersigned is further instructed to suggest to the Porte 
the expediency of transmitting to Her Majesty's Government a sum of money 
equivalent to the value of the annuity proposed to be granted to Miss Pare 
in order that the same may be invested in the public funds in. the name of 
Mr, Cole and some other person appointed by Her Majesty’s Governnieat, and 
a deed of trust executed by them, whereby, after payment of the proposed 
annuity to Mrs. Me Lean, the interest of the residue mav be appropriated to the 
maintenance and education of Miss Pare, until she comes of ave, and the fund 
may then be transferred to her absolutely. 

Should, however, the Sultan prefer to pay an annuity yearly during the life 
of Miss Page, instead of a sum by way of equivalent for the pension, a deed of 
trust, applicable to such a state of things, will be prepared, and, should it become 
necessiry or advisable, Miss Page will then be made a ward in Chancery, for 
the more effectual protection of her interests. , 

The Undersigned, &e. (Signed) H. lL, BULWER.

[ WAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your note of the 27th

Vice-Consul at Jeddah, who was murdered on the occasion of the outbreak at 
that place, and that in accordance with the communications which have taken 
place between the Sublime Porte and Her Majesty’s Ambassador at Constanti- 
nople, the sum of SOL a year will be paid out of that grant to the wife of the 
late Mr. Page, and the remainiog 430/. to his daughter, 

_ In requesting you to convey to the Sultan the satisfaction of Her Majesty's 
Government at the arrangement which His Imperial Majesty has been pleased 
to make for the payment of the pension to the family of the late Mr, Page, 
I] beg to explain to you that the late Mr. Page did not leave any widow, but 
that the annuity of SO/, a year was intended for his mother, Mrs. McLean, 
towards whose support he was in the habit of contributing that sum during his 
lifetime. Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople was accordingly 
instructed to recommend to the Porte that an annuity of 50! a year should be 
paid to Mrs, McLean until her death, out of the pension promised by the Sultan 
to the heirs of the late Mr. Page, and that on her death that sum should revert 
to Miss Page, who would therealter be in the receipt of the entire sum granted 
by the munificence of the Sultan,

Sir H. Bulwer to Lord J, Russell —(Received September 30.) 
(No. 157.) 
My Lord, Therapie, September 16, 1859. 

[ HAVE spoken to M. Thouvenel on the subject of the transfer of the 
Jeddah claims to Constantinople. 

He seems to think that it would be absolutely necessary for the Cominis- 
sioners to come here, and that it would be very difficult, if not impossible, for us 
to investigate the claims at issue without their assistance. 

What he suggests is, that to them should be adjoined a gentleman from 
each Embassy, and one from the Porte, and that all points on which doubts 
arise should be submitted to our decision. 

If this course is not adopted, | should venture to recommend that the 
Commissioners sent some person to whom they had explained their views on the 
various eases at issue, and that the two Embassies should adjoin this gentleman 
to a Commission named by them and the Porte, 

At all events, a Commission of some kind will be necessary to aid the 
Ambassadors, who will not be able to go minutely into facts with which they 
are at present wholly unacquainted, and the examination of which would occupy 
more time than they are able to give, without neglecting the ordinary business 
they are charged with. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) HENRY L. BULWER,

No. 442, 


Lord J. Russell to Sir H, Bulwer, 
(No, 151.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, October 1, 1859. 

WITH reference to your despatch No. 157 of the 16th ultimo, reporting 
your conversation with M. Thouvenel, on the subject of the transfer of the 
Jeddah claims to Constantinople, and the necessity for the presence of the 
Commissioners, 1 have to state to your Excellency that you are at liberty to 
summon Mr, Walne to Constantinople if you consider it necessary to do so, 
Her Majesty’s Government, however, do not understand that the reference to 
Constantinople for the settlement of the Jeddah claims, at least so far as those of 
British subjects are concerned, was intended to involve the re-examination of 
such claims as had already been pronounced upon by the Commissioners at 
Jeddah. 

Such a course seems wholly unnecessary, and it would occasion much 
vexatious and additional expense to the claimants, and a very needless delay in 
the payment of their claims. ‘The ground on which the final settlement of the 
claims was remitted to Constantinople was, to facilitate, not to impede, the 
payment of the sums awarded at Jeddah. 

The point in dispute, in regard to the main part, if not the whole, of the 
British claims, was not the amount to which the claimants were entitled, but 
the manner in which they should be paid. 

The British and French Governments considered that the town of Jeddah 
should be made exelusively responsible for the payment. The Porte, on the 
other hand, admitting that payment was due, desired to reheve the town from 
making it altogether, by undertaking to pay a portion of it out of the general 
revenues of the Empire. It was to settle this point, and this alone, at least as 
far as adjudicated claims were concerned, that the reference to Constantinople 
was assented to by Her Majesty's Government, and your Excelleney will, there- 
fore, refuse to reopen cases already determined, and, as regards such eases, confine 
vour action to pressing for immediate payment, 

Tf there are any eases still undetermined, they may be fit subjects for 
investigation at Constantinople, and if you require Mr, Walne’s assistance, you 
will, as I have said before, be at liberty to call him up. But you wil remind 
the Porte that much unnecessary delay has already taken place in settling these 
matters, and you will say that Her Majesty’s Government expect that in all cases 
that are closed, the sums awarded to the claimants shall be forthwith paid, 

. lam, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

No, 446, 


Messrs. Ducw Paleoloyo & Co. to Lord J. Kussell:—(Received October 29.) 


My ror) : Manchester, October 26, 1859, 

HAVING received from our establishment at Cairo, by last mail, advices 
to the effect that our claim against the Sublime Porte, for the losses and 
damage occasioned to us by the outbreak, massacre, and pillaze at Jeddah on 
the 15th of June, 1858, has, together with the claims of the other sufferers 
under Her Majesty’s protection, been definitively examined by Her Majesty's 
Commissioners, we take the liberty of expressing our hope to your Lordship 
that as little further delay as possible may be allowed to intervene in obtaining 
the amount of the indemnity ; because (wo need hardly trouble your Lordship to 
say) the settlement of this question is of great importance to us, both in respect 
of past losses and of our future trade, which we do not see much prospect of 
re-establishing in the direction of the Red Sea, so long as the question of the 
Jeddah indemnities remains unsatistied, 

The people of Jeddah, under the impression that their Government desires 
to resist their claims, are still acting in a spirit of combination, to shut out 
commerce by Europeans with Jeddah ; but theiridea of the possibility of effecting 
this object would soon be dissipated, or at least very much diminished, if they 
had the example of the payment of the indemnity for their former proceedings 
before them. This idea has been, perhaps, strengthened by the line of conduct 
adopted by the Sublime Porte, since the conviction by the Commission, in 
December 1858 and January 1859, of the principal offenders in the outbreak, 
Although two of these offenders were executed, and the rest sentenced to long 
terms of imprisonment and hard labour, and although all of them, with the 
exception of the Cadi, were men possessing property enough to have made good 
among them the total amount of the indemnity admitted by the French as well 
as British Commissioner, the Sublime Porte has not confiscated or even seques:: 
trated the least portion of such property. 

This is, it is true, the affair only of the Sublime Porte; but we reeall it to 
vour Lordship’s attention, as showing how entirely the responsibility of satis- 
fying the indemnities due, now rests with the Sublime Porte, 

We would also venture to urge another consideration which may induce 
your Lordship to think that it is nota matter of unimportance to re-establish 
confidence by the early settlement of the present ‘claims in the Jeddah and Red

The first question that has to be considered, as the one most materially 
affecting the claim of Messrs. Paleologo Cochilani & Co., is, whether the Hosh- 
e-Sherif was or was not more or less subjected to plunder during the outbreak. 
After am examination of the oral evidence produced before the Ottoman and 
Gritish Commissioners, and careful comparison of it with the recent affidavits of 
Sottiri Moldovano and Georgios Antonios, which throw a new light upou 
the whole case, there can be but one answer. {t does not, indeed, appear that 
the Hosh-e-Sheriff was forcibly attacked from without, and openly plundered, 
like the isolated houses of Sava, and the French and English Consuls. Being 
for the most part the residence of Moslems, it was hardly likely that such an 
open attack would be made on it. But, on the other hand, there cannot exist a 
doubt that the apartments of the few Christians who had resided within this 
okela, were ransacked during the absence of their tenants, of whom some had 
been killed, and others were confined inthe houses of the Cadi or Katmakam, till 
they finally took refuge on bourd the ‘* Cyclops.”’ The plunder of the property of 
Christians lodged in the Hosh-e-Sheriff may have been effected by the Moslem 
residents of the Tosh itself, by persons living in the adjoining houses, or by 
‘some of the hundreds of townsmen who have, every day, access to this.extensive 
okela. 

It is not improbable that the most portable and valuable articles ultimately 
found their way to the secret stores of the Molitessib and Kaimakam, who 
themselves, as is well known, laid plunderers systematically under contribution. 


The claim of Messrs. Duca Paleologo & Co. is not the only one of 


Inportance having tts origin in the Hosh-e-Sheriff; that of Messrs, Pastre 
Fréres, whose agent lived in the same okela, has also its origin there, ‘The 
French Commissioner has, as I have learnt from him, fully convinced himself 
that a part of the Hosh-e-Sheriff was subjected to pillage, having arrived at 
that conclusion by evidence which has not been brought before either the 
Ottoman or the British Comimissioner, When there was a question of levying on 
Jeddah indemnity for the losses occasioned to two houses of such known 
standing and respectalnlity as those of Messrs, Pastré Fréres and Messys. 
Paleologo Cochilani & Co., the one under French and the other under British 
wrotection, it was quite natural that the residents of the Hosh-e-Sherilf should 
fe afd of having levied on them very heavy contributions: hence their 
anxiety to convinee the Turkish Commissioner that no plunder whatever had 
taken place within the walls of the Hosh, and the putting forward of -witnesses 
who, as is well stated hy Mr. Ayrton, “proved too much,” and whose evidence 
was in several mutters directly opposed to well-known and proved facts. Such, 
for instanee, were the assertions that Sottiri Moldovano left the * Cyclops” to 
go on shore, obtained all his effects, and gave the Kaimakam a receipt for 
them.

The item of 439/. 15s, 1d., originally claimed as the calculated loss on fifty 
bales of manufactured goods, detained at Suez in consequence of the outbreak at 
Jeddah, bas now been replaced by a demand of only 94f. 7s. 7d., for eight

here held to be a legal rate, and, all things considered, there does not appear to 
be any valid reason for rejécting this portion of the claim. 

The sum of 16,244,545; dollars, or 3.5382. 9s,, is claimed as compensa- 
tion for losses, direet and contingent, on the sale in Cairo of 227 bales of manu- 
factures ordered for the Jeddah market, and which had already reached that 
city, on their way to the Jeddah house, when the news of the outbreak reached 
Egypt, The quality of goods appears to have been specially adapted to the 
Hedjaz markets; and whether the whole was intended for direct transmission to 
Jeddah, or a portion to be sent to the house there, and another portion disposed 
of at Cairo to Hydramout and native dealers trading with the Hedjaz, there 
must, in any case, have been a great deprivation of profits as usually derived 
from this braneh of trade. he outbreak at Jeddah, with its fearful massacre, 
fullowed by the bombardment, for some time completely paralysed the establish- 
ments at Cuiro having relations with the Hedjaz, and so far from venturing to 
effect sales in Cairo, the merchants had to eall upon the Egyptian Government 
to prevent the departure of the Hadarem, who were largety thei debtors for 
goods previously consigned to them. ‘Yo the present day the trade has not 
recovered itself, nor is it likely to again resume its former importance,

should not be lield responsible to make good this unavoidable loss, obviously the 
result of the funatical outbreak at Jeddah, abetted, if not originated, by the 
authorities of (hat town.
